articles.title: Zelenskyy furious as Trump announces deal to buy Russian diesel
articles.body:
Donald Trump is on a fresh collision course with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European allies after his stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel upended years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.
Zelenskyy reacted furiously to Trump’s announcement of the deal with Vladimir Putin on Friday, calling it “absolutely terrible” and “not fair and not honest”.
The Ukrainian president said “back room deals” with the Russian leader would give Putin more chances on the battlefield. On Saturday morning, Ukrainian officials reported that a Russian attack had killed 12 people in the south-east, including three children, and Moscow claimed its troops were advancing in the east.
In a move likely to create a fresh crisis with Washington’s Nato allies, Trump announced the deal with Putin on his Truth Social network, saying it was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared as a result of his decision to go to war against Iran.
“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia,” he said, to deliver millions of tonnes of diesel fuel over the next few months.
He added: “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority.”
Fuel prices have soared since Iran closed the strait of Hormuz, a strategically sensitive choke point that was the passageway for 20% of global oil supplies before the war. While costs have risen for motorists – a gallon of regular fuel in the US is about $4.20 (£3.17) – it is the price of diesel, which last month hit a record high of $6.52, that has inflicted the most damage on Trump and the Republicans as November’s midterm elections approach.
Diesel is the main supply chain fuel, and a rise in its costs feeds into consumer prices and also hurts US farmers, who need it to operate machinery.
Democrats said the agreement undercut a law Trump signed last month allowing for a broad range of sanctions on Russian banks, officials and tankers, as well as directing him to impose steep tariffs on the top five importers of oil or natural gas from Russia. The law gave Trump wide discretion to make exceptions to its provisions.
“This is what failure looks like. Failure for President Trump to live up to his promises to lower costs for Americans. Failure to protect America from its adversaries,” said a statement from the Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the foreign relations committee, and Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the banking committee.
Some Republicans also criticised the agreement.
“Propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities,” congressman Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican, wrote on X. “The President’s policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures. We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity.”
Zelenskyy told Axios that it “looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible.” The Russian leader turned 74 this week.
In a long social media post, Zelenskyy, who has had an uneasy relationship with Trump, said the deal amounted to “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. Russia was likely to repay it with “further terror and perfidy”.
“It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.
Referring on Saturday to the attack on the south-eastern city of Zaporizhzhia that killed 12 people, Zelenskyy wrote on X: “Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia.
“Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed.”
Separately, Russian media cited the defence ministry as saying its forces had captured the settlements of Lukashove and Lobanivka in Ukraine’s eastern Kharkiv region.
Zelenskyy previously said Putin had been playing games with Trump, and on Saturday, a Kremlin spokesperson said the Russian leader had responded with “understanding” to Trump’s proposals to de-escalate the conflict.
Trump announced the diesel deal as his envoys, Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, met Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss proposals to end the war.
Zelenskyy, in a separate statement released by Ukraine’s embassy in Washington on Friday, said the Ukrainian negotiators had been “used as a smokescreen for the deal”, which he called “a weak decision by strong partners”.
“That is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” he said.
Trump recently criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries, calling on Zelenskyy to choose alternative targets. The Ukrainian leader rejected the request unless Russia stopped attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Tensions have been rising between Russia and European Nato members amid speculation that Moscow might be preparing military action intended to test the alliance’s resolve.
The latest development is likely to worsen Zelenskyy’s relationship with the Trump administration. He was infamously ambushed by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, last year in an explosive White House encounter when the president told him: “You don’t have the cards.”
But Trump has since reportedly grown disenchanted with Putin, expressing disappointment at his failure to reach a peace deal.
Trump’s willingness to reach a fuel agreement with Putin comes despite Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the US. Russia is believed to have given Iran satellite intelligence and overhead surveillance data detailing the locations of US forces, ships, aircraft and military bases. It has also provided drone components and ammunition.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits Russian Pantsir-S1 Air Defense System, Drone Launch Site and Ammunition Depots
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Russian Pantsir-S1 Air Defense System, Drone Launch Site and Ammunition Depots
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Pantsir-S1 air defense system, a drone launch site, and several military logistics facilities across Russian-controlled territories and Russia on October 8 and overnight on October 9.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported that the strikes targeted multiple military facilities supporting Russian operations against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff, Ukrainian forces hit a Pantsir-S1 self-propelled anti-aircraft missile and gun system near Kudepsta in Russia’s Krasnodar region.
In the Donetsk area, Ukrainian troops also targeted a facility used to store, prepare, and launch Russian attack drones, as well as a command and observation post belonging to a Russian military unit.
The operations extended to Russian military logistics infrastructure in the occupied territories of eastern Ukraine.
Ukrainian forces struck ammunition and military supply depots near Rubizhne, Sentianivka, and Luhansk in the Luhansk region, as well as near Vesele in the Donetsk region.
Another strike targeted a field fuel and lubricants depot near Stroitel in Russia’s Belgorod region.
The General Staff also provided an update on an earlier operation, confirming that Ukrainian forces destroyed a command and observation post belonging to a unit of a Russian airborne assault division near Ukrainsk in the Donetsk region on October 6.
The latest operations also targeted infrastructure associated with Russia’s missile program. Overnight on October 9, Ukrainian forces struck two missile-related facilities in the Nizhny Novgorod region, including sites involved in missile launch systems and the dismantling of intercontinental ballistic missiles.

articles.title: US Envoys Pressure Kyiv on Refinery Strikes
articles.body:
US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have warned Ukrainian negotiators during high-level talks in Miami that Washington could cut off intelligence sharing if Kyiv does not halt long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Accodring to Axios, the reported ultimatum came amid escalating friction over a bilateral agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel to US and international markets – a transaction the White House claimed would alleviate elevated consumer fuel prices.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A US official disputed that the American envoys issued an explicit threat, but confirmed that Witkoff and Kushner conveyed that Washington expected reciprocity from Kyiv given US deliveries of ammunition and intelligence, warning that Ukrainian actions should not harm American consumers.
“The attacks on the refineries cause pain in Russia, but it causes pain for the US, too,” the US official told Axios. “[President Volodymyr] Zelensky is misreading the room. By continuing to hit refineries, he is eroding the goodwill that he has built with Trump over the last six months.”
According to Axios, the talks in Miami centered on finalizing post-war security guarantees that the US, Europe, and NATO would provide to Ukraine as part of a settlement framework to end the conflict, alongside prospective territorial compromise proposals.
Putin Rejects Peace Talks in Trump Call, Vows to Press War
Witkoff and Kushner presented a post-war reconstruction and security package, with discussions addressing Ukraine’s accession path to the EU, post-war relations with NATO, and a durable European security architecture.
Trump’s diesel pivot
The diplomatic rift deepened after Zelensky rejected US demands for a unilateral halt to deep strikes on Russian petrochemical assets.
Ukrainian officials had proposed a mutual energy armistice, conveying to Trump, Witkoff, and Kushner that Kyiv would suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow concurrently halted missile and drone bombardments against Ukraine’s electricity grid and heating plants.
However, Trump insisted on an unconditional, unilateral suspension of strikes on Russian refining facilities, arguing that the operations contributed directly to domestic fuel inflation ahead of winter.
The US president did not view strikes on Russian commercial refineries as equivalent to Russian attacks on Ukraine’s power and water infrastructure, the US official told Axios.
“President Trump decided to strike the diesel deal with Russia after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky ignored half a dozen US requests to stop attacking Russian refineries,” the official stated.
In an interview with Axios following the White House announcement, Zelensky described the agreement as an unexpected and “unfair” development, characterizing the sanctions waiver as an unjustified concession to Putin.
The US official maintained that the administration seeks to engage Moscow in diplomatic negotiations, asserting that while Putin continues to strike Ukrainian territory, Washington assesses the Kremlin remains open to discussions on concluding the war if an acceptable framework is presented.
Refining deficits and operational defiance
The friction over refinery targeting unfolds as Ukrainian officials reaffirm that Kyiv will not abandon asymmetric deep strikes against Russian energy infrastructure.
A senior Ukrainian official told the Financial Times on Saturday that Ukraine intends to press ahead with drone strikes on refineries, stating plainly: “We will burn [Russian] refineries.”
Energy market analysts have expressed skepticism regarding Moscow’s physical capacity to fulfill the export volumes announced by Trump, citing extensive operational damage across the Russian refining sector.
Independent market tracking by intelligence firm Kpler indicates that Russian refineries are currently operating at approximately 60 percent of installed capacity due to emergency maintenance and equipment deficits caused by Ukrainian drone waves.
“The biggest question for me is: where are they going to get the diesel from?” said Michelle Brouhard, head of policy and geopolitical risk at Kpler. “Russia does not have an export problem. It has a refining problem.”
Prior to 2025, Russia exported an average of 2.6 million metric tons of diesel monthly by sea, but maritime shipments collapsed throughout 2026 as successive strikes idled primary distillation and cracking units across European Russia and Siberia. Constrained refining output prompted the Kremlin to enact an export ban on domestic diesel in July to stave off domestic fuel deficits.
Trump’s announcement claimed Moscow had agreed to supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter, potentially scaling to 3 million tons depending on refinery operations.
Following the announcement, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
The waiver was enacted only three weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which aimed to expand statutory sanctions across Russia’s energy, banking, and defense sectors.

articles.title: Live: Russian strikes on Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia kill at least 12, including children
articles.body:
Russian strikes on the southeastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia killed at least 15 people, including three children, regional authorities said on Saturday. The attack also caused "large-scale power outages" in the capital Kyiv and the surrounding region. Follow our liveblog for the latest developments.
EU top diplomat says lifting diesel sanctions gives Russia 'revenues to wage war'
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said lifting sanctions on Russian diesel helped fuel the Kremlin's war on Ukraine, after US President Donald Trump announced a deal for Moscow to supply fuel.
"Russian strikes killed over 80 Ukrainian civilians in two days. Moreover, it has stepped up its hybrid attacks against Europe, both EU Member States and NATO allies," Kallas posted online.
"Suspending sanctions on Russian diesel provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war. This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't," she wrote.
Macron expresses 'solidarity' with Zelensky 'in the face of ongoing attacks'
Fresh strikes on Ukraine are Russia's 'thanks' for US diesel deal, Zelensky says
'Large-scale power outages' in Kyiv following Russian strikes
Ukraine's capital Kyiv suffered "large-scale power outages" on Saturday because of Russian strikes, the country's largest private energy provider said.
"New large-scale power outages in the capital due to attacks. Stabilisation schedules are currently not in effect," DTEK, a private energy firm, said in a statement on Telegram.
🎥 Trump hails Russia deal to release diesel as midterms loom
US President Donald Trump said Friday that he had secured Russia's agreement for a major release of diesel, as he eased sanctions on Moscow to lower energy costs ahead of midterm elections.
Four civilians killed in Russian-held Luhansk region over past 24 hours, Moscow-installed governor says
Four civilians were killed and five others were wounded as a result of Ukrainian attacks on the Russian-controlled Luhansk region in eastern Ukraine in the past 24 hours, the region's Russian-installed governor Leonid Pasechnik said.
Reuters could not independently verify the report and there was no immediate comment from Ukraine.
Parts of Kyiv and the surrounding region left without power after Russian attack, Ukraine energy ministry says
Germany to pursue new sanctions on Russia despite US diesel deal
Germany said it would continue to push for new EU sanctions against Russia despite Moscow's agreement with Washington to release diesel to ease a fuel crunch.
"The German government sticks to its measures sanctioning Russia and is working jointly with its European partners on new sanctions," government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said in a statement sent to AFP.
Major backer Germany's "support for Ukraine in its struggle to defend itself remains unfailing", he added.
"Diplomatic efforts for a peaceful solution continue."
Moscow has been hit with waves of sanctions by the United States and partners since its 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Kremlin says Putin, coordinating with Iran, shared Tehran's views with Trump
The Kremlin said that President Vladimir Putin relayed to US President Donald Trump Iran's position on a possible resolution to the US-Iran war, with the backing of the Iranian president, Russia's Interfax news agency reported.
"In coordination with the president of Iran, Putin conveyed to Trump the Iranian side's view on a possible resolution of the
conflict," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted as saying.
Russian combat losses in Ukraine, according to Kyiv
Putin showed 'understanding' for some Trump ideas on Ukraine, Kremlin says
Russian defence ministry says forces capture two settlements in Kharkiv region
The Russian defence ministry said that its forces had captured the settlements of Lukashove and Lobanivka in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, Russia's Interfax news agency reported.
Reuters could not independently verify the battlefield reports.
Ukrainian attack drones hit a key Russian railway bridge
Seoul's ambassador to Ukraine returns home after POW row
South Korea's ambassador to Ukraine returned home today, Seoul's foreign ministry said, as a diplomatic row deepens over the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul.
The announcement came days after South Korea said it recalled him following Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's disclosure last month of the prisoner transfer, which Seoul said put their families in North Korea at risk.
"We inform you that Park Ki-chang, Ambassador to Ukraine, returned home this morning," Seoul's foreign ministry said in a statement sent to AFP.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has demanded an official apology over the prisoner revelation.
Eight killed including three children in Russian strikes, according to regional authorities
Russian strikes on Ukraine's southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia killed at least eight people, including three children, according to regional authorities.
The strikes came a day after Ukrainian and European officials met in Miami in a renewed diplomatic push to end Russia's war in Ukraine.
"The death toll from the air strikes on Zaporizhzhia has risen to eight. Among them are three children," said Ivan Fedorov, co-chair of the Defence Council of the Zaporizhzhia region.
At least 16 people were wounded, he said, and 12 were missing.

articles.title: One strike takes out more Russian officers than ever during the entire war.
Zelensky: Ukrainian Peace Team in Florida Used as ‘Smokescreen’ for US-Russia Diesel Deal
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky delivered a blistering rebuke of Washington on Friday, Oct. 9, after US President Donald Trump struck a separate energy deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin while Ukrainian peace negotiators were in Florida – handing Moscow a massive financial lifeline to sustain its invasion.
The diplomatic contrast could hardly have been sharper. As Ukrainian officials sat down with their US counterparts in Miami to explore ways to halt Russia’s war, Trump spoke directly with the man who launched it, agreeing to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The arrangement stands to generate substantial new revenue for Moscow at a time when Ukraine and its European partners have been pressing for maximum economic pressure to cripple the Kremlin’s war machine.
Speaking to journalists Friday evening, Zelensky sharply questioned Washington’s approach, challenging how the US could credibly mediate peace while simultaneously offering Putin sudden economic relief.
Ukraine seeks ceasefire as Trump cuts deal with Moscow
According to President Zelensky, Ukraine’s negotiating team traveled to Florida to seek a pathway toward ending Russia’s full-scale invasion – or, at the very least, securing an initial ceasefire.
“Right now, our Ukrainian team, our negotiating team, is in Florida, holding talks with the American team about ending this terrible war – or, at the very least, achieving a ceasefire,” Zelensky said.
Trump Names Truth Social Adviser Katie Zacharia as New White House Press Secretary
He emphasized that an agreement to halt attacks on energy infrastructure could provide an urgent first step toward a broader de-escalation, particularly as relentless Russian strikes threaten Ukrainian homes, the power grid, and essential services ahead of winter.
“An energy ceasefire could be the first step toward a broader ceasefire. This is extremely important for our people, for our families.”
The high-level Ukrainian delegation in Florida includes Presidential Chief of Staff Kyrylo Budanov, National Security and Defense Council Secretary Rustem Umerov, First Deputy Chief of Staff Serhiy Kyslytsia, and parliamentary faction leader Davyd Arakhamia. They have been holding talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, alongside representatives from Britain, France, Germany, the EU, and NATO.
But as those sensitive negotiations unfolded in Miami, Trump was pursuing an entirely different conversation with the Kremlin.
“At this very moment, while our team is talking with the American team in Florida, the president of the United States is having a conversation with the Kremlin leader – the leader of this war, the leader of this aggression,” Zelensky stated. “And they reach an agreement under which America allows Russia to export diesel.”
For Ukraine, the decision risks undermining one of the West’s most critical tools for pressuring Putin to end the war.
‘Additional money for this war against us’
Trump defended the arrangement in a post on his social media platform, Truth Social, announcing that Russia had agreed to supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the US and global markets, with another 500,000 tons to follow in November and 1 million tons afterward.
“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” Trump wrote, adding that Russia would deliver another 3 million tons of diesel within a short period, depending on the operational condition of its refineries.
Combined with what Trump termed “total control of the Strait of Hormuz,” the US president claimed the agreement would rapidly lower domestic fuel costs.
Shortly after Trump’s announcement, the US Treasury Department issued General License 135, officially authorizing transactions involving the sale, delivery, offloading, and importation of Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The sudden authorization came just three weeks after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law on Sept. 18 – legislation explicitly designed to choke off Russia’s energy revenues and financial networks. Bipartisan US lawmakers had strongly urged Washington to fully implement the law ahead of its mid-October deadlines, warning that the Kremlin was exploiting loopholes to keep bankrolling its front lines.
Zelensky warned that the financial windfall from lifting these sanctions is impossible to separate from the violence on the ground.
“This is additional money, additional money for this war against us, without question,” the Ukrainian president said. “It only fuels Putin and gives him the opportunity to wage even more war.”
“And at this very moment, when we are talking about peace, America is allowing Russia to export diesel,” Zelensky continued. “I don’t know whether we’re talking about millions or billions. In any case, all of it goes toward the war against people, against Ukraine, against all of us.”
US fuel prices prioritized over sanctions pressure
The White House has framed the deal as a pragmatic response to severe domestic economic pressures. US diesel prices have recently climbed to an average of approximately $6.28 per gallon, squeezing truck drivers, agricultural supply chains, and American consumers.
However, energy analysts and European allies note that the initial shipment of 300,000 tons is modest compared to total US daily consumption, raising doubts about whether the deal can deliver the sweeping price relief Trump promised.
Furthermore, the decision risks severely fracturing the unified Western sanctions strategy.
For nearly five years, the US and its allies have sought to starve Moscow of the energy revenues required to pay military salaries, manufacture missiles, and sustain its occupation.
Allowing Russian diesel back into Western-regulated markets effectively rewards the Kremlin without securing any corresponding concession, such as a halt to attacks on Ukrainian civilians.
‘Gifts to Putin will not bring peace’
Zelensky reinforced his criticism in a separate statement on X, describing the sudden easing of energy sanctions as an investment in prolonging the war rather than ending it.
“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilised world,” Zelensky wrote.
In an interview with Axios, Zelensky was even more direct, calling the arrangement “not fair and not honest,” likening it to a birthday present for Putin, who turned 74 earlier this week.
Zelensky concluded his remarks to journalists by returning to what he characterized as the fundamentally unfair treatment of Ukraine’s negotiating team.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen,” Zelensky said. “And that is definitely unfair. It is definitely not how partners should behave.”
“And it is a weak decision. Unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners. Glory to Ukraine!”

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Russian tech giant Yandex’s data centers for a second straight day as new peace talks involving Kyiv, the U.S., and Europe get underway in Miami
articles.body:
Ukraine strikes Russian tech giant Yandex’s data centers for a second straight day as new peace talks involving Kyiv, the U.S., and Europe get underway in Miami
Ukrainian drones attacked Russia’s Kaluga region overnight into October 9, Governor Vladislav Shapsha said. He said Ukrainian forces struck infrastructure in Kaluga but gave no further details. Nine people were injured, five of whom were hospitalized.
Yandex later said its data center in Kaluga had come under drone attack. No employees were injured, but “several data center modules have been completely disabled.” The company warned that some Yandex services could experience disruptions.
This was the second attack on the Russian tech giant’s data centers in two days. Overnight into October 8, drones struck a data center in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region. A fire broke out, and the data center was shut down completely. Soon after the attack, users began reporting disruptions to Yandex services, media websites, and other services, including Avito, Ivi, Megafon, Russian Railways, and T-Bank.
Responding to the attacks, Yandex said its data centers were the company’s “iron heart” and that keeping them operational was “critical to services that have become part of people’s everyday lives.”
“We understand that for our users, clients, and partners, every outage disrupts plans and prevents them from doing things they normally do in their daily lives or at work. Yandex teams are doing everything they can, day and night, to keep services running and help those affected by the incident. This is our most important task right now, but unfortunately, it isn’t easy,” Yandex said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky briefly addressed the attack on Yandex on the evening of October 8: “You all know they [Russian forces] have struck our data centers and are still striking them. We responded. I can’t share all the details.”
Russia has regularly struck data centers in Ukraine in recent weeks. Since late September, Russian forces have damaged or destroyed data centers belonging to at least eight companies. Russia’s Defense Ministry has called these strikes a “forced digital detox.”
The peace process
Ukrainian representatives will meet with U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in the United States on October 9 and 10. The Ukrainian delegation has traveled to Miami, where the talks will take place. Its members include presidential chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, Davyd Arakhamia, who leads the Servant of the People parliamentary faction, and Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov. Reuters reported that Washington had invited national security advisers from the United Kingdom, France, and Germany, as well as representatives of NATO and the EU.
According to Axios, Kushner and Witkoff plan to present the Ukrainian delegation with “new ideas and proposals” for ending the Russia–Ukraine war. No details were given. The two presented the proposals to President Donald Trump at a meeting on October 8.
An Axios source said Witkoff and Kushner could travel to Moscow in October for further talks with Vladimir Putin.
Shortly before the Miami talks, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there were currently no prospects for a peaceful settlement of the Russia–Ukraine conflict. He said the war had reached a “strategic stalemate”: Russia continues to insist on full control of the Donbas, a condition Ukraine finds completely unacceptable.
Rubio said the situation could be resolved in only two ways: through a negotiated settlement or escalation by one or both sides.
In response, Zelensky said breaking the stalemate would require increasing economic pressure on Russia, allowing Ukraine to use Starlink for strikes on Russian territory, and refusing to reach agreements with Moscow on any future projects:
It would cost them nothing, absolutely nothing, to help Ukraine. And I’ve said frankly: Give us that. Help us defend our airspace and dominate it. Then Putin will come to the negotiating table. Why? Because he’ll lose everything. He’ll lose everything. Three months, two months — he’ll lose everything.
But instead, we’re waiting for the Chinese to develop their equivalent and hand it over to the Russians. So where’s the truth in that? Where’s the honesty? Where is any of it? What dead end? What dead end? This isn’t a dead end. It’s called unwillingness. It’s not a dead end.
In mid-September, Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure. In practice, however, that did not happen. Zelensky said Ukraine was ready to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if Russia agreed to stop striking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The Kremlin called an energy ceasefire “a very good idea.” Sources told The Kyiv Independent that Russia had demanded U.S. sanctions relief during talks on a possible energy ceasefire. It is unclear which sanctions were involved.
The war in photographs: the aftermath of a Russian strike on Zaporizhzhia
On the morning of October 9, Russian forces struck Zaporizhzhia with aerial bombs. Mykhailo Semikin, head of the Zaporizhzhia regional military administration, said six aerial bombs had been dropped on the city. Homes and cars were damaged. According to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service, a 50-year-old man was killed and 14 people were injured.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: In Russia, Missile Systems Research Institute and Center for Elimination of Ballistic Missiles Have Been Struck — General Staff
articles.body:
The Ukrainian Armed Forces struck the Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes and the Intercontinental Ballistic Missile Elimination Center in Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region.
This was reported on October 9 by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on its Facebook page.
The facility near the village of Dalne Konstantinovo-5 belongs to the V. P. Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes—a subsidiary of JSC Ground-Based Space Infrastructure Operation Center Facilities (TsENKI).
The company is engaged in the development and production of launch and technical complexes, refueling equipment, as well as ground-, air-, and sea-based missile and space complexes. This is stated on their official website.
Another facility reported as having been destroyed by the General Staff was the Intercontinental Ballistic Missile Elimination Center near the village of Surovatikha in the same region.
The center is involved in the disposal of missile weapons, as well as the production, preparation, storage, and transportation of rocket fuel. In addition, the facility maintains and repairs missile delivery systems.
The General Staff noted that the strike on this facility was aimed at weakening the Russian military-industrial complex’s capabilities to produce explosives and rocket fuel.
Gleb Nikitin, governor of the Nizhny Novgorod region, confirmed the nighttime drone attack on the region. According to him, infrastructure facilities were damaged by falling debris, but he described the damage as minor.
The Russian official also reported the death of a serviceman from the Bars-NN unit, who had participated in repelling the attack alongside forces from the Ministry of Defence of the Russian Federation and the National Guard of Russia.
According to reports from the Russian monitoring resource UAV Russia, drones were detected in several districts of the Nizhny Novgorod region on the night of October 9, specifically in the Sosnovsky and Kulebatsky districts. The threat was declared neutralized at 06:39.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that on October 9, Ukrainian drones attacked the Redkino Experimental Chemical Plant in Russia’s Tver region, which manufactures rocket fuel components.
The TsENKI is a Russian organization responsible for operating the ground-based infrastructure of the rocket and space industry. Its structure includes enterprises that develop launch complexes, work with rocket fuel components, and maintain the relevant equipment.
The Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes was established in 2010 through the merger of two design bureaus. Its predecessors participated in the creation of launch infrastructure for the Soviet R-7 intercontinental ballistic missile and rocket and space complexes.
The Intercontinental Ballistic Missile Elimination Center in the village of Surovatikha was established in 1993 on the basis of a missile neutralization and dismantlement station. Initially, its activities were related to the implementation of agreements on the reduction of strategic offensive weapons between Russia and the United States.
In 2009, the center became part of the JSC Ground-Based Space Infrastructure Operation Center Facilities (TsENKI). The organization’s 2018 report noted that, during the facility’s operation, 448 intercontinental ballistic missiles had been dismantled, and its activities also included work to extend the service life of missile systems.

articles.title: Putin and Trump hold phone talks – Kremlin
articles.body:
Putin and Trump hold ‘successful’ talks: Key details
Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump held a 90-minute phone conversation on Friday, discussing the Ukraine conflict, a major agreement on Russian diesel supplies, the crisis surrounding Iran, and prospects for broader cooperation between Moscow and Washington.
Trump described the exchange as “highly successful,” announcing that Russia had agreed to supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to American and global markets in an effort to ease soaring energy prices.
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said the conversation was friendly and substantive, revealing that Trump had rearranged his schedule to speak with Putin following the Russian leader’s 74th birthday.
Here are the key takeaways from the conversation, according to statements by both leaders and the Kremlin’s detailed readout.
Millions of tons of Russian diesel for the US
The most immediate result of the talks was a major energy agreement under which Russia will increase diesel exports to the US and global markets, potentially helping alleviate an international fuel shortage.
Trump announced that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons shortly thereafter. He also suggested that Russia could deliver an additional 3 million tons, depending on the condition of its refineries.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak subsequently confirmed that Moscow would begin lifting its diesel export restrictions ahead of schedule, reiterating the announced volumes and clarifying that exports could eventually reach 3 million tons per month, while assuring that Russia’s domestic market would remain fully supplied.
The US Treasury also issued a temporary sanctions waiver covering Russian diesel shipments until April 7, 2027.
Trump predicted that the agreement, together with Washington’s claimed control of the Strait of Hormuz, would bring diesel prices down rapidly, particularly benefiting American farmers, truckers and consumers.
Kiev ‘derailed’ peace talks
The Ukraine conflict dominated much of the discussion, with Putin briefing Trump on the situation along the front line and Moscow’s response to Ukrainian “terrorist strikes” on infrastructure and civilian targets deep inside Russian territory. The Russian leader stressed that Moscow retained the initiative and remained committed to its objectives, while expressing readiness for a lasting diplomatic settlement.
However, Putin said that Kiev had effectively sabotaged plans for the immediate resumption of trilateral negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States. During their previous conversation, the two leaders had discussed restarting the talks shortly after Russia’s State Duma elections. Ushakov said that Ukrainian drone attacks, including strikes targeting polling stations and election-related personnel, had fundamentally changed the situation.
Moscow would now reconsider when negotiations could resume, according to the Kremlin aide. Trump reportedly promised to convey Russia’s position to Ukrainian representatives meeting with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami.
Iran diplomacy ‘not exhausted’
Putin stressed that a negotiated settlement with Tehran remained possible, citing his October 8 meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan.
According to Ushakov, Putin noted that Washington and Tehran continued indirect contacts through Qatar despite their confrontational rhetoric.
Moscow also reiterated its offer to accept highly enriched Iranian uranium as a potential way out of the nuclear deadlock. Trump welcomed Russia’s involvement in diplomatic efforts to resolve the crisis, Ushakov added.
Melania’s humanitarian mission
Putin personally thanked First Lady Melania Trump for her efforts to reunite children separated from their families during the Ukraine conflict.
The leaders also discussed the humanitarian situation in the town of Aleshki in Russia’s Kherson Region, agreeing that Russian human rights official Yana Lantratova would maintain direct contact with Melania’s office.
Closer ties – and another summit?
The leaders expressed satisfaction with existing communication channels between their administrations, intelligence services and other government agencies, agreeing to maintain cooperation.
Putin emphasized that Moscow appreciated the attention Trump and his team continued to devote to relations with Russia despite Washington’s domestic and Middle Eastern priorities.
Asked whether the two presidents had agreed to meet in person, Ushakov said no specific summit had been discussed. However, he suggested that the upcoming APEC summit in China could provide an opportunity for another encounter if both leaders attended.
The Kremlin aide also declined to disclose whether Washington had offered any concessions in exchange for Russia’s agreement to supply diesel, suggesting that American officials might provide further clarification.
Birthday wishes and hockey diplomacy
The conversation was initially proposed by the American side as an opportunity for Trump to personally congratulate Putin on his October 7 birthday. According to Ushakov, Witkoff contacted the Kremlin that day to convey greetings from Trump, as well as personal wishes from himself and Kushner, who expressed hope of meeting the Russian leader again soon.
Officials subsequently arranged the call around Putin’s trip to Turkmenistan and the time difference between Moscow and Washington, with Trump postponing some previously scheduled engagements.
The US president opened the conversation with birthday wishes and greetings from Melania. The leaders also found time to discuss sports, with Trump praising Russian hockey star Alexander Ovechkin’s contribution to the game.

articles.title: Latvia’s Pro-Ukraine Landslide Hides a Weakness Putin Could Exploit
articles.body:
Latvia has just held what its own public broadcaster called “a bit of an embarrassing” election. This bashfulness from Latvia’s National Public Service Broadcaster, LSM, was because only 51.8% of eligible voters turned out, the lowest result since Latvia’s first parliamentary election in the modern era in 1993.
Yet those who did turn out handed Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs and his United List 35.3% of the vote and 42 of the 100 seats in the Saeima, Latvia’s parliament – the strongest result achieved by a single political force since Latvia regained independence.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Latvia has emerged from the election with an unusually strong government and an unusually disengaged electorate.
For most European democracies, that would primarily be a political problem. For Latvia, it is also a security problem.
Latvia is a NATO frontline state of just 1.8 million people, bordering both Russia and Belarus. Its grand strategy can be reduced to one overriding objective: make Latvia impossible to isolate.
Internationalize survival
Latvia cannot deter Russia through mass. It has to do it through connections. That means embedding NATO troops on Latvian soil, keeping the United States and Canada strategically invested in the Baltic region, and integrating more closely with Poland and the Nordic states.
It means spending close to 5% of GDP on defense, building fortifications along the eastern frontier, investing in drones and air defense, and reducing Russian economic and informational leverage.
Putin Rejects Peace Talks in Trump Call, Vows to Press War
Above all, it means supporting Ukraine. For Riga, Ukraine is both an ally and a forward school of national defense. The Ukrainian battlefield provides lessons in drones, electronic warfare, air defense and Russian tactics that Latvia hopes never to have to learn for itself.
Kulbergs has received a powerful mandate to continue this Atlanticist course. A likely coalition with the National Alliance and New Unity would control 59 seats. Support for Ukraine and NATO remains firmly anchored at the center of the Latvian government.
But Latvia’s defense strategy also depends on something NATO cannot provide: a cohesive and politically engaged society.
                                                                                                                                                                         Barely half Latvia’s electorate voted, raising uncomfortable questions for a national defence strategy built partly around participation and social cohesion. (Photo: PAP/Abaca)                             
The internal front line
Latvia follows an all-of-society approach to defense. Its National Security Concept is explicit that “the existence of the State of Latvia depends on a responsible attitude of all inhabitants of Latvia towards the State and its security.” It links national resilience to the readiness of society as a whole, while defining internal security as resting on a “cohesive civil society” whose citizens participate actively and are prepared to contribute to the defense of the state in a crisis.
Defense Minister Raivis Melnis put it clearly just over a week before the election: “The real first thing is resilience, which is people and country resilience.”
Then almost half of Latvia’s electorate stayed at home. Low turnout does not mean half the country would refuse to defend Latvia. But it does expose weakness in some of the social foundations on which Latvia itself says national resilience depends.
President Edgars Rinkēvičs has already drawn attention to the danger. “Disappointment and indifference are dangerous to the democratic foundations and future of our country,” he said after the result.
Participation was particularly weak in parts of Latgale, Latvia’s easternmost and most heavily Russian-speaking region. Turnout in Daugavpils, where Russian is dominant in everyday life, was just 46.55%. This takes us to the most sensitive part of Latvia’s security dilemma.
Russian-speaking does not mean pro-Russian
Almost a quarter of Latvia’s population is ethnically Russian, while Russian is spoken at home by a much larger share. That demographic legacy of the Soviet period has long made Latvia different from Lithuania and has placed questions of language, history and identity close to the center of national politics.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the temptation has been to view this population primarily through the lens of security.
The evidence is considerably more complicated. Former Latvian integration minister Nils Muižnieks said: “I do not think that we can talk about a fifth column in Latvia.”
Research among Russian-speaking Latvians also suggests that straightforward support for Moscow is a minority position. One major study found 55% supporting neither Russia nor Ukraine. Researcher Mārtiņš Kaprāns argues that this “neutrality cannot be reduced to apathy or ignorance.”
                                                                                                                                                                         Latvia’s parliament has emerged with a stronger governing majority, but record-low turnout raises questions about political engagement beyond its walls. (Photo by Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images)                             
The bigger problem appears to be alienation. Parts of Latvia’s Russian-speaking population have become detached from the country’s mainstream political and media environment. Some distrust Riga.
Some dislike policies reducing the public role of the Russian language. Some have become politically homeless following the collapse of Harmony, the party that once dominated Russian-speaking politics.
This election suggests that the two responses to that alienation are abstention and protest voting. Latvia First and Sovereign Power/Young Latvians, both considerably softer towards Moscow than the governing parties, will together control 32 seats.
That does not turn their voters into Kremlin loyalists. But from the perspective of national resilience, alienation is important.
The next stage of Latvian security
Russia does not need Latvia’s Russian speakers to become a fifth column. A population that distrusts state institutions, withdraws from politics or feels that the Latvian state belongs to somebody else already creates a seam Moscow can exploit.
Latvia therefore faces a difficult balancing act. It has good reason to restrict Russian influence, dismantle the remnants of Soviet political power and protect Latvian as the language of the state. At the same time, successful resilience ultimately requires Russian-speaking citizens to feel that they have ownership of that state too.
Latvia has spent years hardening its borders, strengthening its military and embedding itself so deeply inside NATO that Moscow could never confront it alone.
Kulbergs’s landslide gives him an unusually strong mandate to continue that work. The embarrassing part of this election is the reminder that Latvia’s next line of defense has to be built from citizens who believe strongly enough in the Latvian state to participate in it.
