articles.title: The more Putin escalates his attacks on Europe, the more Europe should support Ukraine | Timothy Garton Ash
articles.body:
Vladimir Putin is escalating both his full-scale war against Ukraine and his shadow war against the rest of Europe. His main purpose in the shadow one is to break European support for Ukraine so he can subjugate that country, something he regards as existential for Russia’s future and his own. While we in the rest of Europe must prepare as best we can to defend ourselves against every kind of hybrid attack, the central thrust of our response should be to redouble our support for Ukraine. Ukraine is his main target. It’s there, and only there, not in a contest of a thousand hybrid pinpricks, that Putin’s Russia can in a meaningful sense be defeated and deterred.
In a powerful new book, Warum Russland nicht aufhören wird (Why Russia Won’t Stop), the German historian Martin Schulze Wessel shows how Putin’s policy fits into a much older Russian tradition of territorial expansionism and striving for hegemony, combined with a religiously infused imperial ideology. He reminds us that in 2016 Putin said “Russia’s frontier ends nowhere” and in 2025, “wherever the boot of a Russian soldier steps, that is ours”. West Europeans, fondly imagining that we have consigned such brute territorial imperialism to the dustbin of history, tend to think there must be some other explanation (eg something we did “wrong”, like the eastward expansion of Nato). Finns, Estonians and Poles know better. Despite Russia’s weaknesses, the author concludes, it is “the most dangerous country in the world”. Some in Asia might question that large claim, but certainly Russia is the most dangerous country for Europe.
Schulze Wessel makes another simple but very pertinent point: Russia’s expansion was always facilitated by cooperation with other great powers and arrested when it faced equal and opposing powers. Since Donald Trump’s return to the White House last year, the United States has ceased to be the latter and has at times looked like the former. So now it’s Europe that is shouldering the burden of being the equal and opposing power. Europe (including the UK) has now given more aid to Ukraine than the US. Its combined economies are 10 times larger than Russia’s; Germany’s economy alone is twice the size.
And it’s Germany that’s now central to this European effort. Cumulatively, since the beginning of the full-scale war in 2022, Germany has been the biggest individual country donor apart from the US. According to the Kiel Institute’s Ukraine support tracker, it has given twice as much as Britain or France. As people in Kyiv and Odesa are daily pounded by Putin’s ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, it’s worth looking at the Kiel tracker’s figures for air defence systems. Germany has so far donated 19 of them, including five of the vital US-built Patriot air defence batteries – two more than the US itself has given.
In the first year of this war, I argued that Germany “has a unique historical responsibility to help defend a free and sovereign Ukraine”. At that time, I felt strongly that Germany was not yet doing what it should. Now, in the fifth year of a conflict that has already lasted longer than the first world war and shows no sign of ending, I can say without hesitation that it is. This is not just a matter of the numerical scale of its support for Ukraine and its own increased defence spending, which, on the latest projections from the German finance ministry, will reach €154bn (£130bn) in 2028 (Roughly the same as Russia’s total estimated military expenditure for this year).
It’s also a matter of political will. Chancellor Friedrich Merz has shown that will, and courage, by taking the train from Germany to Ukraine on the evening of 3 October, the 36th anniversary of German unification, with a strong delegation including defence industry leaders. The Russian bombardment of civilian targets in central Kyiv, including Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences and bridges across the Dnipro River, did not stop even though – or perhaps exactly because – Moscow knew the German leader would be there.
For a historian, there’s something very familiar here. Oh no, it’s Germany and Russia again! Yet each time is different. Historically, Germany is one of the powers that has done most to facilitate Russian expansion (just think of the 1939 Hitler-Stalin pact) but also most to threaten it. In the first world war, and even at the margins in the second, some Ukrainian nationalists saw in a conflict between Germany and Russia a chance for their independence. Instead, they got imperial Germany’s colonialism (and then German defeat) in the first case and Hitler’s genocidal fascism (and then German defeat) in the second.
Now, at last, Germany is genuinely engaged, at some cost and risk to itself, for the sovereignty of Ukraine. To anyone who knows this tangled history, there is something not just redemptive, but frankly inspiring in this sight: a democratic Germany playing a leading role in supporting an independent Ukraine’s bid to assume its proper place in a wider European community of free countries.
But for how long? And with how much support elsewhere in Europe? Precisely because Putin sees Germany’s centrality, it’s one of the main targets of his hybrid war, from explosive-laden drones at Leipzig airport that the German government has firmly attributed to Russia and assassination threats against defence industry bosses, all the way to covert political interference and disinformation. While Ukraine faces its most difficult winter yet, three closely connected things will be put to the test: Germany’s will to stay committed on the right side of history; the capacity of democracies to sustain the fight against a dictatorship (a perennial concern); and Europe’s ability to remain united in this cause.
A sceptic can point to many grounds for pessimism. Merz is unpopular at home. Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), the party currently making the running in German politics, would abandon Ukraine to Russia. In France, the National Rally’s presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, says her country can’t afford to go on giving so much to Ukraine. Solidarity with Ukraine is also crumbling on the right in Poland, with two smaller parties sounding frankly anti-Ukrainian. In one Italian opinion poll last month, more than half those asked were opposed to continued weapons deliveries to Kyiv.
In Brussels recently, I found a large audience seemingly stalwart in support of Ukraine – until, right at the end, our discussion turned to the issue of using the Russian frozen assets held in Belgium. Ah now, that’s a different matter … Yet with the terrible damage being inflicted on the Ukrainian economy, including its grain exports via the Black Sea, experts estimate that as much as €100bn of additional support for Kyiv may be needed in 2027 alone – and hard-pressed European taxpayers are in no mood to cough that up.
Putin believes decadent European democracies will crumble before the iron determination of an imperialist strongman. Our job is to prove him wrong.
- Timothy Garton Ash is a historian, political writer and Guardian columnist. His new book, Europe in 7½ Chapters, is published next week

articles.title: ‘The smell of death is everywhere’: Inside the humanitarian catastrophe unfolding in Russian-occupied Oleshky, where hundreds are trapped without food, electricity, or medicine
articles.body:
‘The smell of death is everywhere’: Inside the humanitarian catastrophe unfolding in Russian-occupied Oleshky, where hundreds are trapped without food, electricity, or medicine
Since 2022, residents of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region have lived under occupation. In 2023, the city was flooded after the Kakhovka dam was blown up: the flooding destroyed dozens of residential blocks and all of its infrastructure. In the fall of 2026, Oleshky found itself cut off. There’s a humanitarian catastrophe there: the city has no electricity, food, or medicine. Every way out is mined and blocked by Russian troops. Meduza spoke to people who have miraculously managed to stay in touch with those who remain in Oleshky. Here’s what they told us.
‘The harvest was so plentiful there was nowhere to put it’
“Oh, it smells amazing here!”
Svitlana (not her real name), a former resident of Oleshky who fled the city in 2022 because of the war, smiles as she recalls her garden — and the compliments her friend Nina used to pay it. Before the full-scale war, Nina used to bring her homemade milk every Thursday.
“I had [about a third of an acre] of land, and I planted peony bushes all along the perimeter. The scent was intoxicating!” Svitlana says. “Nina asked why I didn’t take the flowers to market. But how could I sell something so beautiful?”
Svitlana’s yard brimmed with flowers until autumn, and hers wasn’t the only one. “It was as if the townspeople were competing over whose front garden was more lavish. Oleshky bloomed and smelled wonderful.”
Svitlana calls the land she lived on for three decades “rodiucha,” which translates from Ukrainian as “fertile”:
Stick a branch in the ground and it will sprout. Everyone had everything: tomatoes, cucumbers, orchards… I grew 14 varieties of grapes, three varieties each of apricots and peaches. There was so much of a harvest that there was nowhere to put it: I sold some and canned the rest. I shared preserves with people displaced from Donbas — I’d send volunteers whole crates of it.
On weekends, Svitlana liked to spend time along the Kinska River, a left tributary of the Dnipro. The Kinska had a beach and good fishing spots, and from its pier you could catch a pleasure boat or a passenger ferry to Kherson, about 9 kilometers (5.6 miles) away by water.
Russian cell service in Oleshky, which has been under occupation since the first days of Russia’s invasion, operates with severe disruptions. But because the city is close to Kherson, Ukrainian mobile networks can still be picked up at random spots around town. That is how Svitlana stays in touch with her neighbors Olha and Dmytro (not their real names), the people closest to her who remain in Oleshky.
These days, Svitlana hears little from her neighbors. She says the constant risk of a drone strike keeps them in the basement most of the time. In the spring, Olha wrote to her on Viber: “We just need to survive.”
‘Every day I hear explosions over the phone’
Mykyta (not his real name), another resident who also fled the city in 2022, keeps in touch with Oleshky through Ukrainian mobile networks. He calls his mother, Tamara (not her real name), every day, and to reach him, she has to go out into the yard, find a signal, and stay put wherever she finds it.
Sometimes the call cuts off mid-sentence. “My mother runs from drones. She hears a sound in the sky and rushes straight into the house, where the signal disappears,” Mykyta explains. “Every day I hear explosions over the phone.”
Mykyta spent six months living under occupation: he didn’t want to leave right away, thinking “it would all be over quickly.” “But then [representatives of the occupation authorities] came to search my place and beat my legs so badly that I couldn’t walk normally for two months. That’s when I realized nothing was going to end quickly, and I left.”
Tamara and her husband, Borys (not his real name), stayed in Oleshky. According to Mykyta, his father refused outright to leave the city — he didn’t want to abandon the household. “Dad used to say, ‘Let’s just sit tight, maybe things will get better.’ Nothing got better. He got seriously ill, and that’s when my mother said they were staying — Dad wouldn’t have survived the trip. She’s already buried him.”
After her husband’s death, Tamara kept putting off leaving because she didn’t want to abandon her two dogs. But both dogs died this year, Mykyta says:
My mother tried hard: she wouldn’t cook anything extra for herself, she’d give it to them instead. But she had to feed them whatever she could. A lot of people in Oleshky now eat purslane — it’s this fatty grass. My mother added it to the dogs’ food. They ate tomatoes, cucumbers, honey, pasta — whatever supplies were left. I think that’s what did them in.
The humanitarian crisis in Oleshky began in 2023. After the Kakhovka dam was blown up, the city was flooded by 90%, and its infrastructure was severely damaged. Since then, there has been no electricity or gas.
Only people with their own wells have drinking water. But pumping water from a well requires a pump, running the pump without electricity requires a generator, and the generator needs fuel. The last fuel delivery to the city coincided with the final food supplies, in late spring 2026.
Kseniia Arkhipova, a police officer in Oleshky before the invasion, tells Meduza this. In 2022, during the occupation, she began volunteering to help local residents, which angered the pro-Russian authorities. After they detained her, she left her hometown for Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Since getting out of Oleshky, Arkhipova has coordinated help for her fellow residents remotely, helping deliver food and medicine, taking part in organizing evacuations, and keeping a list of people who have died in the city during the war. By August 30, she had confirmed 136 deaths since the start of the invasion.
As far as the volunteer knows, no one has managed to bring food into Oleshky since spring 2026: vehicles that have tried have come under fire and been forced to turn back.
The Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda has reported that by the end of summer it had become impossible to enter the city: Russian and Ukrainian drones clashed in the skies over Oleshky every day. The occupation administration itself accuses the Ukrainian military of blockading the city and claims that Ukrainian drones attack convoys carrying humanitarian aid.
Kseniia Arkhipova recalls:
In May and June, people in Oleshky still had supplies, then the harvest came in from their gardens: grapes, tomatoes, potatoes, zucchini. But the supplies ran out, and people started sounding the alarm — there’s no food. Mothers write to me: “Ksyusha, my child has nothing to eat, what do I do? He’s hungry all the time.” It’s like 1933 all over again, “wonderful Russian culture” in all its glory.
Kseniia is referring to the Holodomor, which killed nearly 4 million residents of the Ukrainian SSR. Ukraine’s official position, backed by 29 countries (Russia is not among them), holds that the Holodomor was a deliberate genocide of the Ukrainian people by the Soviet government.
Mykyta says that, just as in Soviet times, Ukrainians are dying of hunger because of Russia: “It doesn’t fit in my head that something like this could happen in this day and age. This is an actual Holodomor.”
In July, the occupation authorities in the Kherson region denied there was a humanitarian catastrophe. By August, however, they had acknowledged that Oleshky and nearby villages had no water or electricity, and that utility crews weren’t making repairs because of the shelling.
On September 21, Putin’s press secretary, Dmitry Peskov, called the situation in the Russian-occupied city “critical.” “The Kyiv regime is doing everything it can to hinder deliveries [of food and medicine]. Russian troops continue working to resolve the situation,” he said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has also addressed the crisis in Oleshky. In one of his evening addresses in May, he said: “The situation specifically in this part of the occupied territory is extremely difficult, and it’s very hard to carry out evacuations. It’s important that international organizations — everyone able to help with this — are engaged and take decisive action.”
‘Oleshky is closed off on all sides’
Residents of Oleshky have very few ways to get food: Ukrainian authorities say the city is under a complete blockade.
Tetiana Hasanenko, who heads the Oleshky city military administration from Ukrainian-controlled territory, said in comments to Ukrainska Pravda that Russian troops have mined every route out of Oleshky:
People have two options: either die from starvation, or come under drone or artillery fire and be killed. There is no third option.
At the same time, Yevhen Voronetskyi, a serviceman with the 34th Independent Marine Brigade “Borysfen” of the Ukrainian armed forces, told Ukrainska Pravda that Ukrainian troops have mined some routes out of Oleshky to prevent Russian forces from bringing in weapons. Voronetskyi said Ukraine’s military keeps the main road out of the city clear so civilians can leave, even helping people make their way along it and sometimes guiding them with drones along a relatively safe route.
In 2023, Russian forces mined the fields around the city out of fear of a Ukrainian military landing on the left bank of the Dnipro. There is no confirmation that the Russian army has continued mining the main roads around Oleshky. Each side blames the other.
Petro Andryushchenko, a former adviser to the mayor of Mariupol who now heads the Center for Occupation Studies, said in an interview with the Ukrainian outlet NV that Russian forces are using the city’s residents as human shields: “This is a real humanitarian catastrophe, and one created entirely by the Russians as cover for military operations.”
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine reported on June 25 that “thousands of civilians trapped in frontline communities in southern Ukraine are facing a deepening humanitarian crisis.”
Oleshky became a front-line city in the fall of 2022, when the Russian army, under pressure from Ukrainian forces, retreated from the right bank of the Dnipro and left Kherson. Since then, the occupation authorities say, Ukrainian attacks have hindered their efforts to rebuild Oleshky — including after the 2023 flooding — and to deliver food and medicine to the city.
As FPV drones became more common on the battlefield, Oleshky, like Kherson on the opposite bank, grew increasingly dangerous. The front line runs right between the two cities, along the river, and it takes drones only a few minutes to cross the Dnipro and reach a target.
But drones aren’t the only threat in the city and its surrounding area. The area around the city has been mined so heavily that by early 2026, entering or leaving it had become very difficult. That, said Tetiana Hasanenko, who is trying to stay in touch with the city’s residents, is precisely what led to the sharp deterioration of the situation in Oleshky.
Vegetable gardens in Oleshky have turned into a deadly obstacle course. Neighbors told Mykyta that the plot around his house, which he abandoned in 2022, is “littered with mines,” including antitank mines and “petal” mines.
According to Mykyta, the areas around the city are unsafe too: “The riverbanks were mined, and after the flooding [from the destruction of the Kakhovka dam], the water scattered those mines who knows where.”
“Oleshky is closed off on all sides,” Kseniia Arkhipova sums up. “There are about 1,500 people caught in this trap.” Since the start of the Russian invasion, the city’s population has shrunk nearly 15-fold: according to figures from the Oleshky city military administration, 22,000 people lived in Oleshky before 2022.
Some residents risk their lives to walk to Radensk, a nearby village, in search of food. Like Oleshky, it’s under Russian control. The roughly 20-kilometer (12-mile) route is extremely dangerous: the road is mined, and the open terrain is exposed to drone fire.
Some still manage to get food, which is sold at an improvised market in Oleshky. Mykyta learned the prices there from his mother: “I’m in shock. A sack of potatoes costs 7,000 rubles! A can of sprats costs 1,000 rubles, compared to 60 in Radensk.”
Mykyta says a friend of his mother’s advised her to turn to “some religious people.” He doesn’t know who they are, but he’s heard from his mother that they have more food than many other residents. Through these people, his mother Tamara was able to get “a couple of kilograms of buckwheat, some pasta, canned meat, oil, flour — a little of everything.”
Mykyta has been trying to arrange food deliveries to his mother through charitable organizations in nearby cities, but so far without success.
The Ukrainian military sometimes sends humanitarian cargo into the blockaded city. Since March, Ukrainian forces have used drones capable of carrying up to 10 kilograms (22 pounds) of cargo, dropping boxes of canned meat, flour, crackers, oil, and grains directly onto Oleshky.
But this isn’t regular supply, and not every resident gets a package. “A ten-kilo package is enough for one family for a week. And then what?” Kseniia Arkhipova adds.
On September 27, the Ukrainian military dropped its largest shipment of food into Oleshky to date, delivering about four tons (4.4 tons) of food at roughly 100 pre-selected locations. Arkhipova afterward received many grateful messages from locals, and she shows Meduza one of them: “A huge, huge thank you to the guys. God bless them, a deep bow to them!”
Overnight on October 4, the Ukrainian military carried out another operation delivering four tons (4.4 tons) of humanitarian aid to Oleshky by drone.
‘There were more than 200 people on the lists. But no evacuation ever happened.’
According to figures from Ukrainska Pravda, no evacuation of Oleshky has ever been officially organized in four years of occupation. In the spring, the occupation authorities promised for the first time to move Oleshky residents to safer towns. Hoping that would happen, Arkhipova, the volunteer, began coordinating people in a Telegram chat.
Svitlana, the Oleshky resident who left her blooming garden behind in 2022, followed Arkhipova’s messages in the chat. On March 5, she wrote to a neighbor: “Olechka, the question of evacuating Oleshky residents is being decided at the highest level. They’re compiling lists of people so they know exactly how many buses are needed.”
Kseniia recalls how “everyone hoped the Red Cross would come and evacuate everyone”:
The Russians started urging people: “Come to the hospital, sign up, leave your contact numbers. We need to know how many buses to send you. We need to count you — who’s bedridden, who isn’t.” There were more than 200 people on the lists. But no evacuation ever happened.
Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said, without specifying dates, that Kyiv had agreed on “clear mechanisms” for evacuation with Russia, backed by the International Red Cross. But Russia, he said, has stalled the process: “For a long time now, after the talks that were held, the Russian side has not confirmed its readiness to carry out a humanitarian mission to evacuate people.”
Kseniia Arkhipova said that by believing the rumors about the Red Cross and an organized evacuation, people missed their last real chance to leave: “Most of those 200 people are still in Oleshky. In the end, only 67 risked leaving on foot.”
Volunteers coordinate on-foot evacuations from Oleshky remotely, Kseniia says. They put together a plan based on information residents share with them whenever they manage to get in touch.
The last “window of opportunity” for evacuating on foot opened on September 10 and lasted about two weeks, Arkhipova said. That was when Russian troops cleared mines from a stretch of one of the roads leading out of the city.
The first thing residents do is make their way to nearby Radensk (also occupied by Russia). After making the trip, some are “completely unable to move,” Kseniia continues:
They arrive dirty, emaciated, with nothing. Sometimes they weigh less than 50 kilograms (110 pounds), just skin and bones. No clothes, no shoes, no money — no home. Recently an 87-year-old woman was brought out on a cart. When she saw bread, she took out a handkerchief, wrapped a crust in it, pressed it to her chest and said, “I won’t give it up, this is my bread.”
In Radensk, refugees from Oleshky are housed with volunteers willing to take them in, and “they just rest for a few days,” Kseniia says. Some are put up in empty, nonresidential spaces, like stores. Then those who are able make their way to free Ukrainian territory — through Russia and Europe. About 30 Oleshky residents have left the occupation since the start of September.
The volunteer says that among those who left, everyone who initially didn’t want to evacuate “regrets, without exception, staying stuck for so long.” “I yell at them: ‘I told you to leave a year ago, two years ago, three years ago!’ And they answer: ‘Ksyusha, it’s hard to leave everything behind. You’re young — you just turned around and left. We can’t do that.’”
Among those Arkhipova has helped leave are also refugees who for a long time didn’t believe they were really in danger. She said they decided to evacuate only after someone close to them had been killed.
After being rescued from occupation, Oleshky residents can count on support that Ukraine provides to evacuees and internally displaced persons (IDPs). ”[But] while they fill out the paperwork and wait for that measly 2,000 hryvnias [about 40 euros or 3,800 rubles], what are they supposed to do in the meantime?” Kseniia says.
From time to time, she manages to persuade Ukrainian charitable foundations and Russian antiwar organizations to help refugees from Oleshky.
The “window of opportunity” for evacuation has now closed again, Arkhipova says.
‘These people are in a cage’
Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s ombudsman, is convinced that an evacuation of Oleshky’s residents could realistically be carried out in a single day.
Kseniia agrees:
All that’s needed is to clear the road of mines and send in, roughly speaking, four big buses [into the city]. People will come out on their own, and those who can’t move will be wheeled out on carts. Loading everyone up and driving them out — the whole operation would take three hours! Why isn’t this being done? Because Russia can’t be negotiated with.
In late September, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha spoke about the crisis in Oleshky in an address to the UN and the International Red Cross. At Ukraine’s request, the OSCE called on Russia to give international organizations access to Oleshky, supply residents with food and medicine, and allow them to leave the city safely.
Vladimir Saldo, the Kremlin-appointed governor of the Russian-occupied part of the Kherson region, gave an interview to the television channel Vesti on September 28. Asked whether a full evacuation of Oleshky was possible and necessary, he said:
Of course such a possibility exists. But let’s try to understand the residents who are there. Taking them and forcibly removing them right now would probably be wrong and unfair. Those who wanted to leave have already left. There are no restrictions for anyone there.
Saldo then added: “We need to do everything so that they [the local residents] can get everything they need to live there: fuel, food, medicine, communications.”
Two days after Saldo’s interview aired, Kseniia Arkhipova learned that several Oleshky residents had again tried to walk to Radensk for food. She posted a notice in the city chat warning that four people had been injured by landmines along a certain route that day and urging anyone heading to Radensk to avoid that stretch of road:
Regardless of Saldo’s statements, many Oleshky residents genuinely don’t want to, or can’t, get out. For instance, Mykyta’s mother isn’t willing to abandon her home, he says: “She says if she leaves, everything will be looted. ‘And who needs us there [outside our hometown] anyway?’”
Kseniia Arkhipova also described the fear that residents still in Oleshky feel toward looters.
From her conversations with residents, she learned that Russian troops rotated through Oleshky around mid-September: “The ones who came in now are polite — they might come ask for food, [saying] ‘you leave us alone, and we’ll leave you alone,’” Kseniia recounts from her acquaintances’ stories. “But before that there were ones who took everything. Or they’d kick people out of their homes and onto the street because they had solar panels, which meant they had electricity.”
Among those who can’t leave the city are the people Arkhipova calls the “undocumented.” These are Oleshky residents whose Ukrainian passports and other documents were lost in the flooding after the Kakhovka dam was destroyed. They didn’t want to get Russian passports.
Now, to be evacuated from Oleshky, these people need at least some kind of passport: both the occupation authorities and border guards on the way to Ukrainian-controlled territory demand to see documents. Getting a Russian passport without other documents is very difficult: applicants first have to confirm their identity with the occupation authorities.
These bureaucratic hurdles come with additional checks, and the fighting makes moving between offices simply dangerous.
“I have acquaintances who have been trying to restore their documents for three years now,” Arkhipova says. “They have witnesses, they’re going through the courts, they’ve already gone around to every [office]. And they still won’t give them a passport.”
Without documents, Kseniia reasons, it’s impossible to cross any major checkpoint: “Not Novoazovsk, not Chonhar, not Armiansk will let them through. These people are in a cage.”
Kseniia calls other residents who remain in Oleshky the “low-mobility”: bedridden patients and elderly people who can’t be evacuated without special transport and an escort.
On top of that, Kseniia says, there are people in the city who are simply afraid of the filtration procedure at Russian checkpoints. According to Human Rights Watch’s observations, even civilians leaving occupied territory for areas under Ukrainian control often have to go through it — not just those entering Russia.
‘The smell of death is everywhere’
“Those who left after me say Oleshky is simply unrecognizable. The city is gone. There are no stores left, no post office,” Mykyta tells Meduza. “I look at photos myself, and I don’t recognize a lot of the places.”
Kseniia Arkhipova adds that in Oleshky, “people live in an isolated world”: “It’s worse than after the flooding [from the destruction of the Kakhovka dam]. There’s devastation and chaos in Oleshky. There’s no administration, no police. Cars don’t drive around — bicycles are the best you get.”
Arkhipova calls the hospital the “only intact island” in Oleshky. It used to give out food to those who were completely exhausted from malnutrition. But lately the facility “is operating on its last legs: there’s no medicine, no fuel — nothing.”
Mykyta also knows from his mother that there’s a medicine shortage in the city, and he recalls overhearing a Russian soldier say, back when he himself was still in Oleshky: “Why do you need medicine? Consider yourselves already dead.”
Still, Arkhipova says, the hospital can currently provide help: “There are doctors there who worked even before the war, even though they had chances to leave. They said, ‘I’m not going anywhere. What will people do without me?’ Recently an 11-year-old boy stepped on a ‘petal’ mine and lost his leg. If it weren’t for these surgeons, who would have performed the amputation? The child would have simply bled to death.”
The occupation authorities don’t allow burials for people killed in the fighting, the volunteer says. Novaya Gazeta reported that there is “no one to process” deaths in the city, but Arkhipova doubts that’s the real reason for the delay.
She says that people who die of natural causes are still being buried. “They [the occupation authorities] need a forensic medical examination so that a medical examiner will write: ‘These people were killed by the Ukrainian military,’” the volunteer explains. “And they need that so they can later pass that data on to the UN [and blame Ukraine]. That’s the scheme.”
The only way to bury those killed in the fighting, Kseniia says, is “quietly, in the garden.” But that’s dangerous: the occupation authorities consider these “spontaneous burials” illegal. “One girl buried a neighbor who was killed in a shelling attack in his own garden. They dragged her through the courts for two years afterward — had she killed him? They even came and dug up the body,” Arkhipova says. Meduza was unable to reach the Oleshky resident the volunteer describes.
Mykyta, whose father died under occupation, and Svitlana, whose husband, Ihor, also chose to stay in their hometown but then fell ill and died in the hospital, both confirm to Meduza that people who die of natural causes are allowed to be buried. Svitlana says that “by today’s standards” Ihor was buried “like a king.” She was able to send money to acquaintances in Oleshky, and they organized the ceremony.
“They reported everything to me: how they dug the grave, how a priest performed the burial service, how many wreaths they laid, what kind of cross they put up,” Svitlana recounts. “They buried my Ihor in not just one but two plastic bags, which was difficult because bags are in short supply there [at the hospital], and you have to sign for each one.”
Asked why her husband wasn’t buried in a coffin, Svitlana says: “There are no coffins left in Oleshky.” That’s what the acquaintance who organized the funeral told her. Svitlana believes it: there’s no way to bring new coffins into Oleshky, and getting wood from the forest is dangerous — it’s mined and exposed to drone fire.
Mykyta tells Meduza that his mother sometimes mentions acquaintances of hers who have been killed. “In March, a woman was killed — a strike hit a store while she was standing in line. Her husband hasn’t been able to retrieve the body since spring — they won’t give it to him,” Mykyta says, citing one example.
According to Kseniia Arkhipova, the morgue is “a small building not far from the hospital,” where bodies are “just stored.” “A body has been lying in a bag without refrigeration since January. What’s going to be left of it?” Arkhipova adds.
The Insider reported that the refrigerators in the morgue don’t work because there’s no fuel for the hospital generator. Tetiana Hasanenko, the head of the city military administration, said the morgue had effectively stopped functioning ever since the Kakhovka dam was destroyed. She said bodies have been stored in the hospital basement in recent months.
Sometimes, Meduza’s sources say, bodies are left lying right out in the street. “Russian [soldiers] lie on the roads for weeks, their own side doesn’t pick them up,” Mykyta says. “Dogs drag the bodies around. For my mother, these are just ordinary moments now — a dog tears off an arm or a leg and runs off.”
Kseniia Arkhipova also tells Meduza that stray dogs in Oleshky feed on human bodies. The Ukrainian news outlet Hromadske also reported that dogs dig up shallow graves in gardens and “drag off pieces of bodies,” while Ukrainska Pravda reported that bodies of not only Russian soldiers but also killed civilians lie in the city’s streets.
In the last days of September, Mykyta spoke with his mother again. Tamara told her son she had gone to see a doctor. “My mother says it’s hard to walk through the hospital,” Mykyta says. “The smell of death is everywhere.”
The Oleshky city military administration responded to Meduza’s request by referring to Tetiana Hasanenko’s previously published interviews. Meduza also sent a request to the occupation administration of the Kherson region but had not received a response at the time this story was published.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: Iran questions France’s nuclear double standards
articles.body:
Iran questions France’s nuclear double standards
TEHRAN— Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei has criticized 'France’s contradictory approach' to nuclear weapons, questioning why Paris considers its own nuclear deterrent essential to national security while insisting that Iran must never possess nuclear weapons, despite Tehran’s stated commitment to the peaceful use of nuclear energy.
In a post on X, Baqaei contrasted French President Emmanuel Macron’s remarks on the importance of military power and deterrence with his categorical opposition to Iran acquiring nuclear weapons.
During a test of a ballistic missile capable of carrying a nuclear warhead, Macron declared: “To be free, therefore, one must be feared, and to be feared, one must be powerful.”
Yet, as Baqaei noted, the French president has also insisted that Iran must never possess nuclear weapons, neither now nor in five or ten years.
The Iranian spokesperson argued that the central issue was not France’s possession of a nuclear deterrent, but the apparent double standard under which a rationale presented as essential to French security is treated as a threat when applied to Iran—even in discussions concerning a civilian nuclear program subject to international oversight.
Baqaei argued that the underlying problem was the desire of certain nuclear-armed powers to preserve their exclusive hold on strategic power and the authority to determine which countries may legitimately exercise it.
He said these powers seek to retain their own nuclear arsenals, presenting them as instruments of security and freedom, while invoking the prospect of a nuclear threat to justify restrictions on other countries, including those pursuing peaceful nuclear technology.
According to the Iranian diplomat, such an approach reflects a selective interpretation of security rather than a universal commitment to peace.
“A peace in which nuclear powers regard their own weapons as the guarantors of their freedom and security, but label the same logic a threat when invoked by others, is not true peace,” Baqaei wrote, arguing that this disparity amounted to a monopoly on power rooted in a sense of superiority.
Baqaei maintained that an international order that fails to recognize the equal right of all nations to security and peace risks reinforcing the dominance of a limited group of powerful states rather than safeguarding international stability.
His remarks placed the debate over Iran’s nuclear program within a broader question of consistency in international security policy: whether the principles invoked by nuclear-armed states to justify their own deterrence strategies should be applied fairly in their dealings with other countries.
Iran maintains that its nuclear program is intended for peaceful purposes and has repeatedly called for its nuclear activities to be assessed on the basis of international law and safeguards obligations.
Baqaei’s criticism thus challenged France to reconcile its stated commitment to preventing nuclear proliferation with its own reliance on nuclear weapons as instruments of deterrence, arguing that lasting peace cannot be built on a system in which security is treated as a privilege reserved for a select group of powers.

articles.title: Turkish F-16s help guard Latvia’s skies during election
articles.body:
- Turkish Air Force F-16s completed a short deployment to Latvia’s Lielvārde Air Base to support NATO air defense during Latvia’s parliamentary elections.
- Latvian Defense Minister Raivis Melnis visited the Turkish unit on Oct. 9 to thank it; Germany and Italy also sent jets.
Turkish Air Force F-16 fighter jets have completed a short deployment to Latvia’s Lielvārde Air Base, where they helped guard the country’s airspace around its parliamentary elections, Latvian Defense Minister Raivis Melnis said on Oct. 9.
Melnis visited the Turkish unit at the base on Friday to thank it for the deployment. The Latvian Ministry of Defense said the F-16s were in the country temporarily to support NATO’s Integrated Air and Missile Defence mission, the alliance’s standing system for protecting member states’ airspace. The ministry did not say how many jets took part, how long they stayed or whether they were scrambled to intercept anything during their stay. Photos released with the visit show F-16s from the Turkish Air Force’s 181st Squadron.
“I thank Türkiye for its responsiveness and quick action in making a significant contribution to strengthening the security of Latvia’s airspace. The presence of Turkish fighter jets in Lielvārde demonstrates NATO’s ability to react quickly and effectively move forces where they are needed. Close allied cooperation, mutual trust and readiness to act together are an essential prerequisite for the security of Latvia and NATO’s entire eastern flank,” said Melnis.
Latvia, like Estonia and Lithuania, has no fighter jets of its own. NATO has protected Baltic skies since 2004 through its Baltic Air Policing mission, which normally bases allied fighters at Šiauliai in Lithuania and Ämari in Estonia. Latvia usually does not host permanently stationed jets, so the ministry said the Turkish deployment also tested how quickly NATO can move aircraft into the country and whether Lielvārde is ready to receive and support allied air forces.
The Turkish F-16s were one of three allied contributions Melnis requested to protect Latvian airspace during the Oct. 3 election for the 15th Saeima, Latvia’s parliament. Germany sent four Eurofighter jets to Lielvārde for the vote, and Italy also contributed aircraft. Turkish F-16s had briefly visited the base in late August as well.
The deployments follow a series of drone incursions into Baltic airspace that Latvian officials link to Russia’s war against Ukraine. In June, French Rafale jets flying from Lithuania shot down a drone over eastern Latvia, the first time NATO jets downed a stray drone over the country. In August, an Italian Eurofighter shot down another drone that Latvia’s Defense Ministry said had entered Latvian airspace as a result of Russian electronic warfare.

articles.title: “Supplying Crimea is turning into a nightmare”: Ukrainian drones hit Russian trucks 770 times in September, and winter will make it worse, analyst says
articles.body:
- Ukraine's "middle strikes" on Russian logistics haven't let up
- Ukrainian drones hit Russian trucks 770 times in September
- A shift to protected convoys hasn't reduced the truck losses
Ukraine's campaign of so-called "middle strikes" targeting Russian supply lines isn't generating the same headlines it did back in the spring, when the campaign was intensifying.
But that doesn't mean Ukrainian units aren't launching thousands of drones a month and blowing up a lot of Russian trucks. Indeed, the pace of Ukrainian strikes, concentrated along the main supply routes threading through occupied southern Ukraine into occupied Crimea, has leveled off without ever really decreasing since an early summer surge.
It's evident Ukraine's middle-strike campaign "didn't stop and wasn't slowed down," noted French mapper Clément Molin, one of the most important observers of the counterlogistics campaign.
For September, Molin tallied 770 confirmed drone strikes on Russian trucks in the logistical zone 10 km beyond the line of contact. That's up from 630 strikes in August, 656 in July, and 586 in June, the month the campaign really got underway. There were just 214 strikes in May and at most a few dozen in each of the previous three months.
Whether Ukrainian troops can take advantage of the Russians' weakening logistics anytime soon is less evident.
Since June, the Ukrainians have hit around 700 Russian trucks a month that analysts can confirm with video and photographic evidence. There are undoubtedly many more damaged and destroyed trucks that left no digital evidence.
There are thousands of Russian trucks on the road in Ukraine every day, so hitting 700 of them in a month won't immediately strangle Russian logistics. But that accumulating destruction does strain Russian logistics—and terrify the truck drivers who are in the drone crosshairs. "Russian drivers post videos on a daily basis, showing how dangerous a ride in southern Ukraine is getting," Molin wrote.
What's remarkable is that the counterlogistics campaign hasn't faltered even as the Russians have adapted. Early on, Russian trucks mostly traveled alone and without protection, making them fairly easy picking for a bevy of Ukrainian middle-strike drone types including the Hornet, the B-2, the RAM 2X, the Chaklun, and various high-endurance first-person-view quadcopters.
The drones ride along Ukraine's overlapping command and control systems, which include Starlink satellite terminals (some dangling from balloons) as well as mesh radio networks. Many of the drones have built-in AI for autonomously detecting and homing in on trucks in the final seconds of flight.
Convoy operations
Reeling from the truck strikes, the Russians adapted this spring. Commanders began requiring all trucks to travel in convoys including mobile fire support groups, analysis group Tochnyi reported in May, citing Dmytro Putiata, a retired command post battle captain from the Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces 20th Brigade "K2."
Trending Now
Today the Russian convoys have a standard structure, according to Molin. "Convoys usually gather three to five trucks and two to three air-defense trucks." Combined with radio jamming gear that's increasingly common on both the supply trucks and the gun trucks, that's seemingly a lot of protection.
But the drones target the gun trucks, too, peeling back the protection in order to expose the supply trucks to follow-on attacks. In that way, the Ukrainians have sustained their attacks on the supply trucks despite the increase in mobile air defense activity along the most important supply routes.
And it's going to get worse for the Russians as fall wears into winter. "Supplying Crimea is turning into a nightmare and the arrival of winter and more difficult conditions will not help," Molin wrote.
There will be less foliage on the trees lining the roads, and thus less cover from Ukrainian surveillance. Moreover, Molin pointed out, "it will be more difficult to go off-road" and avoid the big paved roads that are the main drone kill zones.
Russian logistics are under pressure, and that pressure is only increasing. Ultimately, the Ukrainians aim to starve Russian forces in Crimea. Strikes on cargo ships plying the Black Sea prevent the Russians from simply shifting the logistics off the coast. Meanwhile, strikes on overland logistics "may lead to substantial softening of front-line positions," Tochnyi noted in May.
Softening those front-line positions to the point of melting away could facilitate what Tochnyi described as "eventual breakthrough operations" in occupied southern Ukraine.
It's not inconceivable. Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps recently proved, by way of its successful Operation Vivaldi, that local Ukrainian counteroffensives are possible.
But that doesn't mean they're easy. To win, the 3rd Army Corps had to carefully husband its forces and meticulously prepare the battlefield under conditions of strict secrecy before attacking. That same kind of preparation is underway along the supply lines into Crimea, but it's unclear whether local Ukrainian forces have enough combat power in reserve to shift from defense to offense and exploit Russia's deepening supply woes.
At least not yet.
Read Also
- Armored assaults aren’t dead. Robots got the credit, but it was Ukrainian infantry in armored trucks that reversed a year of Russian gains near Lyman
- Ukraine fired its first FP-7 ballistic missile in combat. Its maker says next version will do what Ukraine needed since 2022
- Ukraine keeps finding ways to replace its MiG-29s. It’s running out of MiG-29s to find

articles.title: Zelensky and Kiev mayor trade blame over Russian strikes
articles.body:
Zelensky and Kiev mayor trade blame over Russian strikes
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky has slammed Kiev city authorities for an “almost complete failure” to protect the capital’s critical infrastructure from Russian attacks, escalating his longstanding feud with Mayor Vitaly Klitschko, who blames central government corruption.
In a social media post on Friday, Zelensky reported “extensive damage” to power grids following Russian strikes and criticized delays in strengthening infrastructure defenses across Ukraine, singling out Kiev for failing to take the necessary precautions.
His remarks came a day after Klitschko urged residents to consider temporarily leaving the capital, warning that the city was in “survival mode” as winter approaches.
In an interview with AFP on Thursday, Klitschko said Kiev was stockpiling food, drinking water and fuel. He urged residents with friends or relatives outside the capital to consider staying with them temporarily. However, he ruled out a full evacuation.
The mayor issued a similar warning in January, when a severe energy crisis left thousands of residential buildings without heating in freezing temperatures. The appeal sparked a public confrontation with Zelensky, who accused city authorities of failing to prepare adequately.
Speaking to AFP, Klitschko again blamed some of the shortcomings in Kiev’s winter preparations on Zelensky’s government. Rejecting accusations that city officials had fallen behind, he argued that “finding scapegoats won’t make people warmer.”
In a separate interview with Germany’s Bild published on Wednesday, Klitschko criticized corruption scandals linked to Zelensky’s administration, warning that wartime graft was “a real poison” for Ukraine.
The dispute comes amid escalating long-range strikes between Russia and Ukraine. Last week, Zelensky pledged to intensify attacks on Russian oil refineries, prompting Moscow to announce expanded strikes on Ukrainian military and defense-industrial facilities and supporting infrastructure, including in Kiev.
Moscow has said its strikes are in retaliation for Ukrainian drone and missile attacks on civilian targets inside Russia. According to Russian Foreign Ministry Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik, 29 people, including two children, were killed in such attacks in the week ending October 4.
Klitschko warned that even extensive preparations might prove insufficient if the capital’s air defenses failed to repel further strikes.
Zelensky acknowledged a “big deficit” in air defenses on Thursday, appealing to Western backers for more interceptor missiles ahead of winter. Multiple media reports have linked shortages of Patriot interceptors in US and allied stockpiles to the US-Israeli war with Iran.

articles.title: ‘This is not how partners behave’: Zelensky furious over Trump's Russia deal
articles.body:
Russia announced Saturday that it was beginning to lift domestic restrictions on diesel exports following U.S. President Donald Trump's announcement Friday of an agreement to purchase Russian diesel, marking a significant policy reversal after years of American pressure on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
Axios reported overnight, citing a U.S. official familiar with the matter, that Trump decided to pursue the agreement with Russia after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky ignored repeated American requests for Kyiv to stop attacking Russian oil refineries.
Kyiv appeared unwilling to comply with Trump's demands even after the agreement. Ukraine launched an overnight attack on Russia involving some 500 drones, according to the report, including a strike on an oil facility in the Rostov region.
The American official criticized Zelensky, saying he was misreading the situation and that continued Ukrainian attacks on refineries were undermining the trust the Ukrainian president had built with Trump over the past six months.
Zelensky sharply criticized the U.S.-Russia agreement Friday, accusing Washington of exploiting negotiations with the Ukrainian delegation as cover for its own dealings with Moscow.
"I believe our team is simply being used as cover. This is certainly not fair and not how partners should treat each other," Zelensky said.
Ukrainian media reports noted that officials in Kyiv doubted the agreement would achieve Trump's objective of lowering global fuel prices. They nevertheless acknowledged that the deal itself weakened Ukraine's negotiating position.
Russian petroleum exports have been restricted by both international sanctions and domestic export bans imposed after Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities disrupted production and caused fuel shortages inside Russia.
Now, according to Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees the country's energy sector, Moscow is beginning to lift those restrictions ahead of schedule.
Trump announced on his Truth Social platform that he had reached the agreement during a phone conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The two leaders had been expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia.
Instead, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and an additional 1 million tons shortly afterward. Russia would then supply another 3 million tons within a relatively short period, he added.
Warm exchanges between Trump and Putin
Senior Kremlin adviser Yuri Ushakov described the conversation to Russia's state-run RIA Novosti news agency.
"The conversation lasted an hour and a half, and neither side wanted to be the first to hang up," Ushakov said. He added that Trump had expressed his willingness to continue speaking with Putin that evening, overnight and the following day.
Putin's economic adviser Kirill Dmitriev, meanwhile, posted several messages on social media thanking Trump for the agreement. One of the posts consisted of a single word: "Diesel."
Ushakov and Kremlin-aligned media sought to portray the agreement as evidence of a new phase in relations between Moscow and Washington, arguing that it demonstrated Russia could no longer be considered internationally isolated.
Describing the personal exchanges between the two presidents, Ushakov said Trump had warmly congratulated Putin on his 74th birthday earlier in the week. Trump wished Putin success and conveyed greetings from first lady Melania Trump, Ushakov said.
"Vladimir Putin thanked his American counterpart for the congratulations and warm words," the senior Russian official said, adding that Moscow appreciated the attention Trump and his team were devoting to dialogue with Russia despite domestic U.S. issues and developments in the Middle East.
On the ground, however, Russian attacks deep inside Ukraine continued to exact a heavy toll on civilians.
Overnight, Moscow launched a missile attack on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia. According to Ukrainian media reports, at least seven people were killed when a residential building suffered a direct hit. Local authorities said another 14 people were missing.

articles.title: Putin Rejects Peace Talks in Trump Call, Vows to Press War
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin rejected the resumption of peace negotiations and reaffirmed Moscow’s intention to continue the war against Ukraine until all Kremlin objectives are fulfilled during a telephone conversation with US President Donald Trump, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told Russian state media.
According to Ushakov, Putin made it clear during the exchange that Russia will sustain combat operations without diplomatic concessions.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Putin made it clear that Moscow will continue hostilities until it achieves all stated goals,” Ushakov said.
The Kremlin aide claimed that Trump initiated the call to extend warm birthday greetings to the Russian leader, wishing him success and passing along regards from First Lady Melania Trump.
In response, however, Putin reiterated Russia’s unyielding terms regarding Ukraine, dismissing prospects for an early negotiated settlement.
Ushakov added that Putin accused Ukraine of attempting to disrupt elections in Russia and asserted that Ukrainian resistance is futile, claiming Russian forces hold the operational initiative across the front lines.
Ushakov further claimed that following the discussion, Trump instructed American officials to relay the diplomatic “signals” received from the Kremlin directly to the Ukrainian government.
Hardline stance despite diplomatic overtures
Putin’s refusal to consider peace talks comes despite intensive diplomatic maneuvering by Washington to initiate a negotiating framework ahead of winter.
Easing Diesel Sanctions Shows Weakness to Putin, Sybiha Says
On Friday, Oct. 9, high-level multilateral consultations convened by the US in Miami – bringing together US special envoy Steve Witkoff, Ukrainian negotiators, and representatives from Britain, France, Germany, the European Commission, and NATO – concluded after a six-hour session without a announced breakthrough.
While Witkoff characterized the dialogue as constructive, European and Ukrainian officials expressed skepticism regarding Moscow’s willingness to engage in substantive de-escalation.
Putin’s uncompromising posture in the phone call also aligns with public warnings issued by Ukrainian leaders.
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned on Friday that concessions to Moscow project Western weakness, asserting that Putin interprets economic and diplomatic overtures as appeasement rather than incentives for peace.
The Trump diesel pact
The phone call and Putin’s subsequent rebuff unfolded alongside controversy surrounding Trump’s announcement of a bilateral commercial agreement permitting Russian petroleum shipments into American and global markets.
Trump announced that Russia agreed to supply over 300,000 metric tons of diesel fuel immediately, with 500,000 tons scheduled for November and 1 million tons thereafter, potentially scaling up to 3 million tons depending on refinery operations.
Trump argued that the deliveries, combined with what he termed “total control of the Strait of Hormuz,” would curb fuel costs for American consumers and global markets amid energy market volatility fueled by the US-Israeli conflict with Iran.
Shortly after the announcement, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary general license authorizing the sale and import of Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The sanctions waiver was enacted just three weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on Sept. 18, which was designed to expand statutory penalties across Russia’s energy, banking, and defense sectors.
Hours before the license was issued, President Volodymyr Zelensky had directly appealed to visiting US lawmakers to strictly enforce statutory sanctions as a vital tool to compel Moscow to negotiate.
The sanctions relief granted Moscow an economic accommodation it had sought since July, when Russia imposed an export ban on domestic diesel following successful Ukrainian drone strikes that damaged major Russian refining facilities.
Trump had previously urged Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, attributing elevated diesel benchmarks to Ukrainian interdiction operations rather than the Middle Eastern conflict.

articles.title: Trump's diesel agreement with Putin accused of contradicting Russia sanctions law
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's Friday announcement that Russia will supply diesel fuel to the global market marked an apparent pivot from recent efforts to pressure Moscow to end the Ukraine war by targeting Russian energy exports.
Trump claimed the move, unveiled with less than a month left in an affordability-focused midterm election, would swiftly bring down record-high diesel prices.
But commentators and critics were quick to highlight contradictions between the new policy and prior efforts by the U.S. to clamp down on Russian oil sales.
Those efforts most recently included the enactment of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, empowering Trump to impose tariffs up to 100% on the top purchasers of Russian crude oil or gas, among other restrictions. Trump signed the bill into law just three weeks ago.
"Congress just passed a law giving Trump the power to impose new tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil & gas," Scott Lincicome, vice president of the libertarian Cato Institute, said on X after Trump's Friday announcement.
"Can America tariff America?" he quipped.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., a member of the Senate Ukraine Caucus, accused Trump's latest move of being "directly contrary to Congress's intent in our bipartisan sanctions bill."
Peter Harrell, visiting scholar at Georgetown University Law Center's Institute of International Economic Law, in an X post said that the relaxation of Russian diesel restrictions "pretty much proves the point that the Graham Russia Bill was not going to force the Trump Administration to increase economic pressure on Moscow."
Some of the criticism crossed party lines.
"Through the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, we gave the president significant authorities and leverage against China and Russia to bring Putin's war to an end with a negotiated settlement," Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, said in an X post. "Unfortunately, while I understand the desire to bring down diesel prices, I am concerned the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil will only fund the Kremlin's war machine—emboldening more violence and destruction, as we have seen in recent days," McCaul said.
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's questions about the diesel agreement with Russia.
Less than a year earlier, the Trump administration slapped sanctions on multiple Russian oil companies in response to what it called "Russia's lack of serious commitment to a peace process to end the war in Ukraine."
Trump also had previously slammed NATO allies for continuing to buy Russian oil. In a September 2025 Truth Social post, he wrote, "the purchase of Russian Oil, by some, has been shocking! It greatly weakens your negotiating position, and bargaining power, over Russia."
Later that month, Trump again harangued world leaders for doing business with Russia.
"They're funding the war against themselves. Who the hell ever heard of that one?" he said in a speech at the United Nations General Assembly. "They can't be doing what they're doing. They're buying oil and gas from Russia while they're fighting Russia."
Trump announced the diesel deal in a Truth Social post Friday afternoon after what he described as a "highly successful discussion" with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Under the agreement, Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, then another 500,000 tons in November, followed by 1 million tons "immediately thereafter" and 3 million more depending on refinery conditions, Trump wrote.
The Treasury Department soon after said that Trump directed the Office of Foreign Assets Control to immediately issue a "temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market." OFAC specified that the sanctioned transactions will be authorized for about six months, until April 7.
Russia seemed to celebrate the move. "Russia-US cooperation on diesel and energy will benefit the world," an X account associated with Putin's economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev said in response to the announcement.
But Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whose military has started targeting Russian oil refineries, said in a searing statement that the U.S. easing sanctions on Moscow "plays into Russia's hands."
"Any easing of sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious weakness," Zelenskyy said. "Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged."
"We count on America's fair support for our defense of life, for our defense of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia," he said.
"A strong one, not a weak one," he added.
Trump thanked Putin later Friday afternoon for enabling "massive amounts of oil" to come to the U.S.
"We need oil for the world, and this is diesel, which is what we need, so we're very happy to get it," Trump told reporters before heading to Syracuse, New York.
The Trump administration has previously eased some Russian energy sanctions temporarily, though more narrowly than Friday's announcement.
Earlier this year, in an attempt to stabilize markets after the start of the Iran war, the Trump administration issued limited, 30-day waivers allowing countries to buy sanctioned Russian oil that was already in transit.
But some interpreted the latest move as a more significant step.
"It looks like Trump cut a deal with the devil," Jeremy Siegel, professor emeritus of finance at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, told CNBC's "Closing Bell" Friday afternoon.
"It's not a permanent solution at all. It's sort of a short-term Band Aid," Siegel said. "And cutting back on or eliminating sanctions on Russia for the invasion in Ukraine, I think, is a very unfortunate consequence."

articles.title: Trump envoys discuss ‘winter preparedness’ with Kiev and its European NATO backers
articles.body:
Trump envoys discuss ‘winter preparedness’ with Kiev and its European NATO backers
US President Donald Trump’s top envoys have begun two days of negotiations with Ukrainian and European representatives in Miami, focusing on preparations for the coming winter and potential ways to de-escalate the Ukraine conflict on terms that would be acceptable to Moscow.
US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff described Friday’s discussions as “constructive,” saying American representatives had discussed prospects for a “lasting peace” with Kiev and its most hawkish European backers, including Britain, France and Germany, as well as officials from the European Commission and NATO.
The talks covered “near-term measures related to winter preparedness,” including energy resilience and grain exports, as well as longer-term security guarantees, post-war reconstruction and Ukraine’s potential accession to the EU, according to Witkoff.
“The exchange was productive and helped identify areas for further exploration ahead of the United States’ next engagement with Russia,” he wrote on X.
Today, representatives from the United States, the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine, and NATO met in Miami and held constructive discussions on potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace. The discussions covered a broad range of issues, including near-term measures related to winter preparedness (energy resilience, grains exports), security guarantees, as well as longer-term arrangements for Ukraine’s and Europe’s security to prevent future conflicts, and support Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction and economic prosperity, including EU accession. The exchange was productive and helped identify areas for further exploration ahead of the United States’ next engagement with Russia. Participants reaffirmed their shared commitment to continuing diplomatic efforts toward a sustainable peace that strengthens security and creates opportunities for lasting stability and prosperity.
— Special Envoy Steve Witkoff (@SEPeaceMissions) October 9, 2026
The negotiations were scheduled to continue on Saturday, and no concrete agreements or breakthroughs have been announced so far.
The US delegation is led by Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, while Kiev is represented by Vladimir Zelensky’s chief of staff, Kirill Budanov, foreign intelligence chief Rustem Umerov, deputy chief of staff Sergey Kislitsa and senior lawmaker David Arakhamia.
The European delegation reportedly includes Bjoern Seibert, chief of staff to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, and national security advisers from Britain, France and Germany. NATO is represented by Geoffrey van Leeuwen, chief of staff to Secretary General Mark Rutte, according to European media reports.
The talks follow reports that Witkoff and Kushner were preparing to present “new ideas and proposals” aimed at breaking the diplomatic deadlock. According to Axios, the pair could travel to Moscow later this month for further talks with Putin.
One proposal under consideration reportedly involves a partial ceasefire covering strikes on energy infrastructure, amid growing anxiety among Kiev’s European backers over the economic and energy consequences of the conflict.
“They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop,” a US source previously told AFP.
The Miami meeting also coincided with a 90-minute phone conversation between Trump and Putin on Friday, during which the leaders discussed Ukraine, Iran and a major agreement to resume Russian diesel supplies to American and global markets.
Zelensky lashed out at Trump, effectively accusing Washington of stabbing Kiev in the back by striking a separate diesel deal with Moscow. Zelensky branded the move “a weak decision by strong partners” and accused the US of using talks with the Ukrainian delegation in Miami as a “smokescreen” while negotiating with Putin behind Kiev’s back.
Trump has repeatedly pressed Zelensky to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, blaming them for worsening a global diesel shortage and driving up fuel prices for American consumers. According to Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, Trump promised Putin that he would convey Moscow’s position to the Ukrainian delegation in Florida.

articles.title: ‘We’re being used as a front,’ Zelensky says of Trump’s diesel deal with Putin
articles.body:
Russia and the U.S. have agreed on a deal to supply Russian diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets. President Donald Trump announced the agreement on the evening of October 9 after a phone call with Vladimir Putin. Trump called the talks “highly successful.” Putin confirmed that Russia is ready to supply oil and petroleum products to the U.S. and global markets.
The U.S. said it is easing sanctions on Russian diesel. The Treasury Department has already issued a temporary license allowing sales of Russian diesel on the global market through April 7, 2027, despite U.S. sanctions. Washington previously eased sanctions on Russian oil temporarily because of a market crisis caused by the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran.
Russia has also begun lifting restrictions on diesel exports, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said. Sanctions and domestic export bans restrict exports of Russian oil and petroleum products worldwide. A ban on diesel and marine fuel exports by producers, for example, remains in effect through the end of October. Russia imposed it amid Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and a domestic fuel crisis caused by Ukrainian attacks over the summer.
Trump said the two sides agreed on the “immediate” delivery of more than 300,000 metric tons of Russian diesel. Russia will supply another 500,000 metric tons in November, followed by an additional million metric tons. Novak said Russia is ready to supply additional diesel to the U.S. market as early as October. Exports are also expected to rise in November and December as refineries resume operations after repairs.
Ukraine criticized the diesel deal between Moscow and Washington. President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on social media that any easing of sanctions on Russia without agreements on de-escalation shows “obvious weakness.” “Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis,” he said.
The deal comes as talks on ending the war resume. A Ukrainian delegation is reportedly meeting with U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami on October 9 and 10. Reuters reported that the national security advisers of the U.K., France, and Germany, along with representatives of NATO and the EU, were invited to the talks. Axios reported that the U.S. negotiators plan to present the Ukrainian delegation with “new ideas and proposals” and then discuss them with Russia. No details of the proposals were given. “I think our team is simply being used as a front. That’s certainly dishonest, and it’s certainly no way to treat a partner,” Zelensky told reporters after the U.S. announced the diesel deal.
Russian authorities asked the U.S. to lift sanctions as part of talks on an “energy truce,” sources told The Kyiv Independent on the eve of the diesel deal. Officials in Kyiv said Ukraine was ready to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if Russia agreed to stop striking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Trump, who is under pressure over rising U.S. fuel prices ahead of the congressional midterm elections, has repeatedly demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil facilities. He said the attacks were causing global fuel shortages and price increases.
Putin rejected the idea of an “energy truce” with Kyiv on October 2. Speaking at the Valdai forum, he said stopping the strikes alone would not solve the problem of high diesel prices in the U.S. and around the world unless sanctions on Russia were lifted.
