articles.title: Trump Makes Deal With Putin On Diesel Exports. Ukraine Calls It A 'Gift'
articles.body:
WASHINGTON -- US President Donald Trump said he reached an agreement with President Vladimir Putin to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports, a move Ukraine immediately criticized as a "gift" to the Kremlin.
Seeking to contain soaring energy prices, Trump said in a social media post on October 9 that the two leaders agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and another million after that.
The move will see prices "COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" Trump wrote.
Diesel futures fell about 4 percent after the announcement but remained more than 110 percent higher than at the start of the year. Brent crude traded at around $104 a barrel, down just 0.3 percent on the day.
The decision came as Ukrainian, US, and European officials held talks in Miami aimed at ending Russia’s war against Ukraine. The discussions concluded without a breakthrough.
The waiver drew critical comments from Kyiv to lawmakers in Washington, who warned that easing restrictions could provide Moscow with additional revenue to sustain its war against Ukraine.
It also raised questions about US policy toward Russia following Trump’s recent signing of legislation intended to tighten sanctions against countries supporting Moscow’s energy trade.
"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote in a post on social media.
"Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis."
To enable the flow of diesel, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary general license authorizing the sale, delivery, and import of Russian-origin diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
Trump said that after the initial flows, Russia would supply a further 3 million tons “within a short period of time.”
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow was ready to increase supplies in October, with exports expected to rise in November and December as refineries resume operations after maintenance.
Diesel prices have climbed since the United States and Israel launched air strikes on Iran in February, sparking a conflict that is now in its eighth month.
Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing prices higher and urged Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian energy facilities.
“The problem I have with Ukraine and Russia is that, you know, a lot of the diesel comes … from Russia, and the Russia plants are being hit by Ukraine,” Trump told reporters recently.
Ukrainian officials have said they are prepared to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if Moscow halted its recent barrage of strikes on Ukraine’s energy and other civilian infrastructure installations.
As Ukraine’s negotiating team was in Florida, Zelenskyy also questioned the purpose of the Miami talks while Washington was allowing Russia to earn money from fuel exports.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen,” he said.
Earlier on October 9, Zelenskyy welcomed a bipartisan delegation of US senators to Kyiv and called for stronger pressure on Moscow.
Meanwhile, on Capitol Hill, the waiver for Russia drew the ire of several lawmakers.
“It surely looks bad. The president has always had a moral blindness when it comes to Putin. Propping up Russia’s war economy is terrible,” Republican Representative Don Bacon told RFE/RL.
Democrat Senator Richard Blumenthal, a co-author of the bipartisan Russia sanctions legislation, called the decision an embarrassment, arguing that it would benefit Russia and China while undermining congressional efforts to pressure Moscow.
“This poorly concealed attempt to mitigate the havoc caused by Trump’s illegal war in Iran will only benefit the Chinese & Russian economies & lead to the slaughter of more innocents in Ukraine,” he wrote on social media.
Blumenthal called the agreement “a stain on our nation’s character” and said it ran counter to Congress’s intent in its recent passing of a sanctions bill.
He also warned US companies considering purchases of Russian fuel: “Congress is watching.”
Daniel Fried, a former US diplomat and sanctions expert, also criticized the timing of the waiver.
“General License allowing sale of Russian diesel, proceeds of which support Russia’s war against Ukraine. Not a promising start to the imminent talks on ending the war,” Fried said in a social media post.
Kerri Bitsoff, a former senior Treasury Department official who worked at the Office of Foreign Assets Control, said the move showed Trump was prioritizing the Iran conflict and its economic consequences over pressure on Russia.
“The Russia legislation put the onus, and the ability to act, in President Trump's hands,” Bitsoff told RFE/RL.
“Today's diesel license shows Trump is prioritizing the Iran conflict over pressure on Russia, and he likely doesn't intend to use a lot of the authorities in the bill,” she said.
Ukrainian sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said the waiver could also undermine Trump’s argument that Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries were the main driver of rising diesel prices.
“If limiting diesel sanctions on Russia provides market relief then it’s clear the primary impact to the global diesel market was the Iran conflict and blockade, not Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, which would have had a secondary impact,” Vlasiuk told RFE/RL. “It lines up with price timelines.”
The decision also raises questions about the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022, which prohibits Russian oil imports into the United States unless the president certifies that Russia has agreed to withdraw from Ukraine, recognized Ukrainian sovereignty, and poses no threat to NATO.
Supplied materials from officials on the decision does not establish how that provision applies to the new license.
The Miami discussions, initially expected to last two days, concluded on Friday, October 9, according to US envoy Steve Witkoff.
Representatives from the United States, the E3 group of European countries, the European Commission, Ukraine, and NATO held “constructive discussions” on ways to de-escalate and end the war before winter.
Witkoff said the agenda included winter preparedness, energy resilience, grain exports, security guarantees, longer-term security arrangements for Ukraine and Europe, and support for Ukraine’s postwar reconstruction and eventual European Union accession.
“The exchange was productive and helped identify areas for further exploration ahead of the United States’ next engagement with Russia,” he wrote on social media.
The Kremlin said Trump and Putin had also discussed prospects for resolving the war during their phone call, alongside the situation surrounding Iran and other bilateral issues.

articles.title: Michigan Senate debate: El-Sayed, Rogers spar over Iran, Israel
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Michigan Senate debate: El-Sayed and Rogers spar over Iran and Israel
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers traded barbs on Thursday over Iran and Israel during their first televised debate in the race for Michigan’s open Senate seat, ahead of November’s US midterm elections.
Held in Grand Rapids, Michigan, the debate opened with both candidates being asked whether they would support a pause on the federal petrol tax amid rising fuel prices linked to the war with Iran.
Fuel prices have surged since US-Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February triggered the conflict, adding to concerns over the cost of living among American voters.
Both candidates backed a pause on the federal petrol tax before turning to their respective positions on the war.
Rogers, who initially supported the US offensive against Iran, has since called for the months-long conflict to end.
The Republican Senate candidate reiterated that position during the debate, as did El-Sayed, who has repeatedly criticised the Trump administration over its handling of the war.
The Democrat also blamed the administration for Iran’s decision to close the Strait of Hormuz, a critical international trade route.
“This is what happens when you start wars you never should be fighting,” El-Sayed said.
“We literally taught the Iranian regime that they have a choke on the Strait of Hormuz, and now we’re living in that reality.”
Although Rogers agreed that “we need [the war] to come to an end”, he defended the military campaign, arguing that US attacks had set Iran’s uranium enrichment programme back by “twenty years”.
His remarks echoed claims by the Trump administration that military action was necessary to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.
Tehran has repeatedly denied US and Israeli accusations that it is seeking to develop nuclear weapons.
The Islamic Republic maintains that its nuclear programme is peaceful, while insisting that it will not compromise on its civilian nuclear activities or make structural concessions without the lifting of US economic sanctions.
El-Sayed criticised Rogers for his support of the war and for defending the Trump administration, accusing him of changing his position for political reasons rather than out of concern for Americans’ financial circumstances.
"The reason he’s flip-flopping has nothing to do with policy, has nothing to do with your costs. Has everything to do with his sagging poll numbers,” El-Sayed said.
He added moments later: “Weak, cowardly, won’t stand up until his poll numbers drop.”
El-Sayed and Rogers clash over Israel
During the debate, El-Sayed faced questions over his criticism of Israel’s genocidal military campaign in Gaza, following his recent refusal to say whether he considers Israel or Iran a greater threat to the US in an interview with US cable news network NewsNation.
The candidates hold opposing positions on US military assistance to Israel, which has received more US foreign aid cumulatively than any other country since the Second World War.
Rogers reaffirmed his support for continued US aid to Israel, while El-Sayed called for an end to military assistance, arguing that American taxpayers’ money should instead be directed towards domestic priorities such as education and healthcare.
“He wants unconditional support for a foreign government,” El-Sayed said of Rogers. “I want unconditional support for kids in our schools, unconditional support for our healthcare, childcare.”
The Democrat also blamed Israel for drawing the US into military action against Iran.
“I don’t want to be pushed into war by Israel, and I don’t want to be in war with Iran,” El-Sayed said.
Rogers, meanwhile, argued that Israel had “the right to defend itself in a very difficult neighbourhood”, reiterating his support for the country.
“Is there anything Israel could do that would lose your support?” debate moderator Rick Albin asked.
“Listen, if they’re talking about using nuclear weapons, they would definitely lose my support,” Rogers replied.
Rogers targets El-Sayed over Muslim identity
Beyond their disagreements over foreign policy, the candidates repeatedly traded personal insults.
El-Sayed described his Republican rival as “weak”, “cowardly” and a “sock puppet for the Trump administration”. Rogers, in turn, called his opponent a “glitchy AI chatbot” who was running a “con” and would “say anything to win”.
The pair also challenged each other over campaign donations and their personal finances.
El-Sayed lambasted Rogers over a waterfront property he owns in Florida, while Rogers pointed to a rental property owned by El-Sayed’s wife in the United Arab Emirates.
According to Albin, the candidates continued arguing even when the cameras were off. The moderator repeatedly urged them to maintain order, telling them to “work with me” and adding: “I appreciate your passion, but please, let's try to keep this orderly.”
The debate also covered the trade dispute with Canada, immigration, healthcare, and the cost of living.
However, some of Rogers’ attacks arguably fixated on El-Sayed’s Muslim faith and alleged associations with extremist groups.
El-Sayed has repeatedly faced Islamophobic attacks on the campaign trail, with Trump leading attacks on the Democrat, including labelling him as an “extremist, terrorist sympathizer”.
Trump also claimed his history “goes back to the days of the Jihad” in a post on Truth Social.
During the debate, a discussion about healthcare led Rogers to claim that El-Sayed had “taken money from individuals on his campaign who openly support Hamas, Hezbollah, al-Qaeda”.
The former US congressman also challenged El-Sayed over his opposition to surveillance cameras operated by Flock Safety, arguing that the technology had helped apprehend people suspected of terrorism.
Rogers then suggested that El-Sayed’s concerns about the cameras warranted further scrutiny.
“Why would that bother you?” Rogers asked. “Well, if you have somebody in your family that might be on the terrorism watch list...”
El-Sayed interrupted, challenging Rogers to make explicit the implication he appeared to be suggesting.
“Are you going to go ahead and say that I’m a – go ahead and say it,” El-Sayed said. “You’ve been tiptoeing about it the whole time. Just say it. Just say it. Go ahead and say it.”
The exchange comes amid repeated attacks on El-Sayed’s Arab and Muslim identity during his campaign, highlighting wider concerns about Islamophobia directed at Muslim and Arab candidates in US politics.
If elected, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim member of the US Senate.
Michigan Senate race could shape control of Congress
A CBS News poll published earlier this week showed El-Sayed leading Rogers by 45.6 per cent to 41.4 per cent, with a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points.
The race is among those expected to help determine which party controls the Senate following the midterm elections.
The elections will shape the final two years of Trump’s presidential term, with Republicans facing the prospect of losing their current hold on Congress amid the president’s declining popularity and the fallout from the war on Iran.
Trump himself has been holding numerous rallies to potentially reverse the party’s political fortunes.

articles.title: Trump lifted Russian fuel ban after Zelensky rejected his demands – Axios
articles.body:
Trump lifted Russian fuel ban after Zelensky rejected his demands – Axios
US President Donald Trump has approved a temporary waiver of sanctions on Russian fuel exports. The move came after Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky ignored multiple requests to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries, Axios has reported, citing a US official with direct knowledge of the matter.
Trump has persistently blamed Ukraine, and Zelensky personally, for exacerbating the global fuel crisis, accusing authorities in Kiev of deliberately targeting Russian refining facilities and driving up prices for American consumers. Despite repeated warnings from Washington, the Ukrainian leader pledged earlier this month to ramp up the long-range strikes.
“The attacks on the refineries cause pain in Russia, but it causes pain for the US, too,” the US official told the news outlet.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly warned Ukrainian negotiators during eight hours of talks in Miami earlier this week that Trump planned to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin and lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
A Ukrainian official told Axios that Witkoff and Kushner threatened to cut off US intelligence sharing with Kiev if it continued to ignore Trump’s requests to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, but the US official denied that any such threat had been made.
The media outlet cited the official as saying that the dispute over the diesel deal emerged as the US mediators conducted constructive talks on ending the conflict with Ukrainian and European diplomats. The negotiations reportedly focused on finalizing security guarantees for Ukraine from the US, Europe, and NATO, as well as new territorial proposals.
The official added that Witkoff and Kushner had presented postwar plans covering Ukraine’s reconstruction, military funding, and budget deficits, while participants discussed Kiev’s potential EU accession, its future relationship with NATO, and a possible postwar security framework between Europe and Russia.
Trump and Putin held a phone call on Friday, shortly after which the US Treasury Department announced a temporary waiver of sanctions on Russian fuel trade, allowing diesel to be sold, delivered, and exported, including into the US, until at least April 7, 2027.
Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the US and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and a million tons thereafter, with up to three million additional tons available “within a short period of time.”
The Kremlin said Moscow was ready to supply oil and petroleum products to global markets, adding that this would benefit the world economy. Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak also confirmed that Russia would lift diesel export restrictions ahead of schedule, with the process to begin “immediately.”
Russia had previously extended restrictions on diesel, ship fuel, and gas oil exports until October 31 to stabilize the domestic market amid seasonal demand from the harvest. Fuel producers are barred from exporting until October 31, while fuel resellers face a ban until January 31, 2027. Gasoline exports are also prohibited until the end of January.

articles.title: Ukrainian journalists say Austria detained them “like terrorists”: prosecutor says suspicion unsubstantiated
articles.body:
Austrian police detained Ukrainian investigative journalist Mykhailo Tkach and cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko in Vienna yesterday, on 8 October. Both were later released, but the circumstances of their detention remain unclear, and the prosecutor’s office said suspicion against them had not been substantiated so far.
The detention lasted more than 12 hours, the first time Tkach had been held that long while on a reporting assignment abroad. The case unfolded alongside a separate Austrian espionage investigation involving two men suspected of working for Ukraine’s military intelligence. Authorities have not said whether the cases are connected.
Tkach describes detention
In a video published by Ukrainska Pravda, Tkach said seven people wearing masks and carrying weapons approached their car at a traffic light about 3–5 kilometers from central Vienna, broke its windows, and pointed weapons at them.
He said the people did not identify themselves or explain their actions. The journalists were pulled from the car, forced face down onto the road, searched, and had their hands taped behind their backs, according to Tkach. He said he initially thought they were being kidnapped because he did not see identification or have time to notice police markings. He realized they were police only after seeing police vehicles.
“As I felt it, they detained us like terrorists,” Tkach said.
He added that people shouted and pointed weapons, and there was no communication. He said one person put a knee on his neck and shouted at him to be quiet. He also saw glass from the broken window fly into Bondarenko’s face.
In a second report, Ukrainska Pravda said Tkach’s account of a document presented to him listed three allegations: espionage in the interests of Ukrainian military intelligence, participation in a criminal organization, and, as far as he remembered, causing harm to Austria. He said investigators did not explain the evidence behind the allegations.
Vienna prosecutor’s office spokesperson Nina Bussek told the Austrian Press Agency (APA) that suspicion against the two journalists had arisen during other investigations but had not been substantiated. She said it currently appeared that the suspicion was not holding up. Austrian officials have not publicly addressed Tkach’s account of the force used.
Diplomatic response and calls for an investigation
Tkach and Bondarenko were in Vienna on an assignment to find Ruslan Kravchenko, Ukraine’s former prosecutor general, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Kravchenko was dismissed on 15 September amid an investigation by Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office into alleged protection of fraudulent call centers. He denied involvement. Der Standard reported that it remained unclear whether the journalists’ detention was connected to their reporting on him.
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi confirmed Tkach’s release and said the Ukrainian consul had requested access to him, according to NV. Musaieva said Bondarenko had been injured and hospitalized.
A statement signed by Ukrainian media and civil society organizations, including Euromaidan Press, called for an immediate, transparent, and independent investigation of law enforcement’s actions. The signatories also demanded an independent review of the force used, the return of seized equipment, and necessary medical and legal assistance.
Separate espionage investigation
Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner confirmed the arrests of four Ukrainians, according to ORF. The two men detained on 5 October were placed in pretrial detention until 21 October on suspicion of secret intelligence activity against Austria. APA reported that they were suspected employees of Ukraine’s military intelligence service. Both deny the allegations.

articles.title: Russia Kills Three Ukrainian Children Hours After Trump Hands Putin a Multimillion-Ton Diesel Lifeline
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Kills Three Ukrainian Children Hours After Trump Hands Putin a Multimillion-Ton Diesel Lifeline
As Washington moves to reopen the door to Russian energy exports, Moscow continues its deadly assault on Ukraine, striking residential buildings and launching waves of drones across the country.
Russian forces killed at least seven civilians, including three children, in an attack on the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on October 10—just hours after US President Donald Trump announced a major agreement with Vladimir Putin involving millions of tons of Russian diesel fuel.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Zaporizhzhia regional authorities on October 10, Russian strikes hit residential buildings across the city. A direct hit caused part of a five-story apartment building to collapse, leaving residents trapped beneath the rubble.
Three children were among the seven people killed, while at least 10 others were injured, including another child. Two victims remained in critical condition as rescuers continued searching for survivors.
The deadly assault came less than a day after Trump described his conversation with Putin as “highly successful” and announced a deal on Russian diesel exports despite US sanctions intended to restrict Moscow’s war revenues.
The attack was part of a broader Russian aerial assault involving 160 drones, including 110 jet-powered drones. According to Ukraine’s Air Force on October 10, Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 117 drones, including 82 jet-powered aircraft.
Russian strikes were recorded at 14 locations, while falling debris was reported at another 10. Air defenses were also activated around Lviv and Ivano-Frankivsk in western Ukraine. At least seven people were confirmed killed in Zaporizhzhia, while a final nationwide death toll had not yet been established.
On October 9, Trump announced that Putin had agreed to supply more than 300,000 metric tons of Russian diesel immediately, followed by another 500,000 tons in November, 1 million tons afterward, and potentially an additional 3 million tons.
The announced shipments would total more than 4.8 million metric tons. The US Treasury Department subsequently issued a temporary license easing sanctions on Russian diesel exports for six months, allowing additional shipments to international markets.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the agreement, warning that easing sanctions would strengthen Russia rather than bring an end to the war.
“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will repay the diesel with further terror and perfidy,” Zelenskyy wrote, arguing that renewed Russian petroleum exports would help prolong Moscow’s military campaign.

articles.title: Ukraine Vows to Keep Striking Russian Refineries Despite Trump Deal – FT
articles.body:
Ukraine intends to press ahead with long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries despite a bilateral agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel to US and international markets, the Financial Times reported.
A senior Ukrainian official dismissed US calls to halt operations against Moscow’s energy infrastructure, signaling that Kyiv will not adjust its asymmetric targeting strategy.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We will burn [Russian] refineries,” the senior official told the Financial Times.
The vow comes as energy market analysts question Moscow’s physical ability to fulfill the commercial commitments announced by the White House, citing extensive degradation across the Russian petrochemical sector caused by repeated Ukrainian interdiction operations.
According to data cited by the Financial Times, Russian refineries are currently operating at approximately 60 percent of their installed capacity due to operational halts, emergency repairs, and equipment deficits resulting from Ukrainian strikes.
“The biggest question for me is: where are they going to get the diesel from?” said Michelle Brouhard, head of policy and geopolitical risk at energy intelligence firm Kpler. “Russia does not have an export problem. It has a refining problem.”
Russian refining deficit
Industry data highlights the extent of the contraction across Russia’s downstream petroleum sector over the past year.
Russia Exploits School Knife Attacks for Disinformation
Prior to 2025, Russia exported an average of 2.6 million metric tons of diesel fuel per month by sea, according to Kpler records.
However, maritime shipments fell precipitously throughout 2026 as successive Ukrainian drone waves damaged primary distillation units, cracking facilities, and storage hubs across European Russia and western Siberia.
With domestic refining capacity constrained, the Kremlin enacted strict restrictions on petroleum product outflows in July, effectively prohibiting domestic diesel exports to prevent localized fuel deficits and inflation within the Russian domestic market.
Outside rare exceptional consignments, seaborne diesel exports have effectively ceased.
The Financial Times also noted that the US has historically accounted for a negligible share of Russian refined petroleum consumption.
Washington has not imported Russian diesel fuel since July 2022, following early sanctions enacted in response to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. During periods when American importers did purchase Russian diesel, volumes averaged approximately 77,000 metric tons per month, peaking at 210,000 metric tons in January 2022.
The Trump diesel pact
The dispute over refining strikes follows Trump’s announcement on Truth Social that Moscow had agreed to supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter.
Trump indicated that deliveries could scale up to 3 million tons within a short timeframe, though he acknowledged that shipments would depend on the condition of Russian refineries.
The US president claimed that the bilateral deal, alongside US naval operations in the Strait of Hormuz, would quickly alleviate fuel costs for American consumers and global markets amid volatility fueled by the US-Israeli conflict with Iran.
Following Trump’s announcement, the US Treasury Department issued a general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The regulatory exemption was granted only three weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on Sept. 18, which aimed to expand statutory penalties across Russia’s energy, banking, and defense sectors.
The sanctions waiver granted Moscow an economic accommodation it had sought since its July export ban, when Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov asserted that Russian fuel could ease international benchmarks only if granted unrestricted market access.
Trump has repeatedly urged Ukrainian officials to suspend strikes on Russian petroleum facilities, attributing high diesel benchmarks to Ukrainian interdiction rather than shipping disruptions in the Middle East.

articles.title: How life has changed in a Moscow suburb where Ukrainian drones hit the same apartment building twice
articles.body:
How life has changed in a Moscow suburb where Ukrainian drones hit the same apartment building twice
On September 20, 2026, Ukraine launched another large-scale drone attack on the Moscow region. One drone hit a high-rise apartment building in Kotelniki, southeast of Moscow. Another had struck the same building in June. Neither strike killed anyone, but the attacks badly frightened many people in the neighborhood. Reporters from Bereg, a cooperative of independent journalists, visited the Novye Kotelniki residential complex to see how repairs were progressing after the two attacks and how residents had responded. Meduza is translating their report in full.
‘People were shaking, children were crying, older people’s blood pressure was shooting up’
Drivers struggle to find parking in this densely populated neighborhood in Kotelniki, outside Moscow. Shoppers wait in short lines at grocery store checkouts. It’s a warm, sunny weekend day, yet the courtyard of the Novye Kotelniki residential complex is unusually empty.
On September 20, a Ukrainian drone struck one of the complex’s high-rise buildings for the second time. The first strike came on June 18, 2026. The drone crashed into almost the same spot on the courtyard side, in the upper third of the building, and exploded.
A black scorch mark stands out against the beige-and-brown exterior, with a hole at its center. All that remains of the balconies on floors 19–22 is twisted metal and rebar. Some of the facade tiles have broken off.
The few residents walking in the courtyard occasionally look up at the building and whisper to one another. Many decline to tell Bereg how the constant drone alerts have changed their lives. “What is there to say?” says a woman of about 40 in a black hijab, waving off the question, though she had just been discussing that very subject with a friend.
Olga, a blonde woman in a trench coat, comes out of a neighboring building with her two-year-old daughter. She says this is their first walk in the courtyard since the recent attack.
This time, she says, the property management company quickly cleared the broken glass and other debris from the courtyard. But she’s still scared: “You never know, she could pick up a piece of glass or something. You’re more scared for her than for yourself.”
On the day of the attack, Olga woke to explosions at four in the morning. She woke her husband. At first, he thought she was imagining things, but then he heard the explosions, too. Deciding it wasn’t safe to stay in their apartment, they carried their sleeping daughter downstairs to the ground floor, where neighbors had already gathered.
Olga stayed in the lobby until eight in the morning. Throughout that time, she could hear explosions outside. “It was a nightmare: People were shaking, children were crying, older people’s blood pressure was shooting up, and we were all looking for medicine for them,” she tells Bereg. “You feel like you’re in a war zone, and you can’t believe this is happening to you.”
Olga missed the summer attack — her family was away. Perhaps that’s why, unlike many of her neighbors, she hadn’t put a “go bag” with documents, medicine, and other essentials in her entryway. Before the September attacks, she had felt less anxious than others. Afterward, she no longer felt safe.
Still, her family’s daily routine hasn’t changed. She and her husband decided against moving their bed farther from the windows, figuring it wouldn’t save them. “Look at the size of that hole,” she says, gesturing toward the damaged high-rise.
“You keep thinking: God, what if it happens again tomorrow?” Olga says. “I was on sedatives for two days. I definitely don’t feel safe here. I’m stressed every day.”
Her family is considering moving, but unless the attacks become more frequent — “not once or twice, but practically every day” — she and her husband are unlikely to “seriously start looking into it.” Olga hopes things will “get back to normal” because “they [the Ukrainians] have already hit what they wanted to hit, and now they’ll calm down.” She means the Moscow oil refinery, the Ukrainian military’s target. But the high-rise stood in the path of the drones flying toward it.
A few things help Olga manage her anxiety: She’s become even more absorbed in caring for her child and stopped reading the news, although she used to scroll through neighborhood chats even at night. “There’s so much noise now, so many planted stories, so much fake news,” she says. “Even the [real] news — there’s so much of it. You watch all this, and the whole situation keeps playing over in your head. What for?”
Ruslan, who lives in the same complex as Olga, takes the opposite approach: He tries to read all the news. He says the drone attacks don’t make him anxious.
“I knew there’d be an attack — the elections and all that,” Ruslan says. He says the neighborhood has only been quiet for the last few days. Before that, neighbors often heard air defenses in action at night and early in the morning.
On September 20, Ruslan and his family counted “at least 40 explosions.” “We could see flashes in the sky from our window — almost like the ones over Israel!” he says excitedly. “There were about 10 a minute at one point.” He saw the drone crash into the neighboring building. He and his family were about to head out into the stairwell when they heard a loud noise outside the window and red light flooded the apartment.
Like Olga, Ruslan doesn’t have a “go bag,” and he says he won’t be getting one. He sees no need, because “our air defenses have gotten better at their job.” “Yeah, there are screwups. Unfortunately, they can’t intercept everything. But overall, our guys are doing their job, and they’re doing it well,” Ruslan says. “Every day on my way home from work, I see the air defense systems changing locations.”
He tells Bereg he believes there won’t be any more strikes on the neighborhood because they’re no longer worth it for Ukraine: “They launched so many, and the results were really poor. They understand it’s a waste of money.”
With a smirk, Ruslan recalls wondering during the first attack whether the target might have been the apartment building rather than the refinery — “maybe some general lives here.” But he quickly dismissed the idea: First, it was a large-scale attack, and second, “what general would live here?”
Ruslan believes Moscow and its immediate surroundings are now “very well protected” and that the authorities should focus on deploying air defense systems in other regions. That’s his only complaint about the security measures. “I think our government will take care of us, and everything will be fine. Our army will handle it,” he says. “Maybe I’m not that well informed, or maybe I’m too optimistic. But I think everything really is fine.”
The toll of Ukraine’s October attacks on the Moscow region
The next large-scale attack on the Moscow region came overnight on October 6. It struck communities northwest of Moscow, damaging private homes and nonresidential buildings in settlements in the Solnechnogorsk, Volokolamsk, Istra, and Domodedovo districts. Ukrainian Telegram channels that monitor attacks and the Russian outlet Astra also reported a fire at the Volodarskaya oil depot, southeast of Moscow. The Ukrainian strikes and Russian air defense operations killed two people and injured nine.
Ruslan’s school-age daughter looks at him admiringly. They chuckle together as they recall a neighbor who panicked during the latest attack. “Run, run, we’re under attack!” Ruslan says, imitating her, though he quickly adds that “everybody’s different.”
His daughter says that after the summer attack, one of her classmates transferred to another school — her family had decided to move. “They were renting [their apartment]. Maybe if we rented here instead of owning, we’d feel better about moving, too,” Ruslan says. “Plus, we’ve got a mortgage here — where are we gonna go?”
‘I’ll be working to pay the rent. I’m just scared to live here.’
A man in a black jacket, probably an employee of the property management company, walks through the courtyard with a ring of keys. He unlocks a door marked “Shelter” leading to the basement, looks inside, locks it again, and moves on to the next building. Each of the complex’s more than 20 high-rises has a shelter.
Residents of Novye Kotelniki say the management company told them the basements are kept locked because they contain “technical equipment that the engineers are responsible for.” In the event of a real threat, residents are to call the dispatch office. A staff member will then come during the attack and unlock the basement door. The company promises this will happen quickly.
But on September 20, residents of some buildings complained in the neighborhood Telegram chat that they hadn’t been able to get into the basements until after seven in the morning, although the large-scale attack began at four.
Signs reading “Shelter” have been hung at the basement entrances, but the management company has done little to equip the rooms, residents say. Some have benches; others don’t even have those, leaving people to sit on the concrete or stand.
Aleksandra, a resident in her mid-40s, is smoking near the entrance to one shelter. Asked how she feels about the increasingly frequent attacks, she says emphatically: “It’s really bad, really bad!”
Aleksandra lives in the building that drones have struck twice. Or rather, she used to — after the recent strike, she realized she was afraid to stay in her apartment. “As they say, what happens once might never happen again, but what happens a second time…” she says.
Aleksandra was home during both attacks. On June 18, she and her husband woke to repeated explosions and began getting ready to go to the shelter. As she was tying her sneakers, a drone crashed into the building. “I hear this huge bang — and plaster starts falling down in our apartment!” she tells Bereg. “I opened the door, and there was already smoke in the stairwell. We didn’t know if we’d be able to get downstairs.”
No one opened the shelter, and neighbors crowded onto the ground floor. “It all ended around eight, and that’s when they opened the basement,” Aleksandra says indignantly. “Well, what’s the point of going down there once it’s all over?”
On the day of the second drone strike, Aleksandra again heard “a lot of activity” as explosions kept going off. First, she went out onto the communal balcony to take a look. From there, she could see several fires near the Moscow oil refinery, the Mega shopping mall, and the Sadovod market. She was horrified. “I wake my husband up: ‘Get up, there’s a real war out there — everything’s burning, everything’s in flames!’” she says.
To reach the stairs, Aleksandra and her husband had to pass through the communal balcony. As soon as they opened its door, there was a loud explosion, and a wave of heat hit them. “I knew it had hit the building,” she says. “Something went bang, and things started falling.”
As we talk in the courtyard, there’s a crash in the distance, quiet but distinct. Aleksandra flinches and abruptly turns toward the sound.
“I think something fell at the construction site.”
“I react like that all the time now [to sudden noises],” Aleksandra says. “My nerves are completely shot. I went a week without proper sleep, even with Novo-Passit, glycine, and things to calm me down. I’d sleep for two hours, then be awake again.”
On September 20, Aleksandra and her husband waited for the explosions to stop, went back up to their apartment, packed everything they needed, and left for their dacha. They’re staying there temporarily but return to their apartment in Novye Kotelniki every few days.
“We’re living out of bags: one in the car, one at the dacha, and one here. We come back, wash up, do the laundry, hang it up, and head back out,” Aleksandra says. “We try to get everything done as fast as we can. They’ve just posted [on Telegram channels] again that apparently another large-scale attack is expected. Who knows?”
But they can’t stay at the dacha for long: It has almost no amenities, and the trip to work takes three hours. Driving every day proved too expensive, so they switched to public transportation.
Aleksandra took out a mortgage to buy her apartment. She has no other home and no relatives who can take her in. Now she’ll have to pay both her mortgage and the rent on a new place in a safer neighborhood. “I’ll be working to pay the rent. What else can I do?” she says with a sigh. “I don’t know what I’ll eat, but I’m just scared to live here.”
“Looking at the windows, I could tell that lots of people had left — almost no one was still here,” she says. “Today we packed up a bunch of bags and took a heater. And everyone coming toward us had bags, too. People are leaving, and no one wants to come back.”
‘I thought the same place wouldn’t get hit twice. Turns out it doesn’t work that way here.’
Far fewer people go into the high-rise hit by the two drone attacks than into the other buildings. Many residents emerge carrying large bags — clearly, they’re leaving for a long time.
The lobby has two entrances: one from the courtyard, the other from the road. The courtyard entrance is now cordoned off with barriers wrapped in red and white tape. The concierge warns that residents can’t leave through that door, either. A chair braces it shut from inside, and a sign on it reads: “No entry! Risk of death!” It doesn’t explain the danger.
Another notice asks residents not to use the elevators between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. so they can be available to “construction workers repairing the building.” Residents ignore the request, and there are no workers in sight.
Residents say that for the first few days after the attack, the elevators ran only in the evenings. Those with apartments on the upper floors of the 25-story building had to take the stairs or enter through the neighboring stairwell, use the elevator there, and cross the roof to reach their own building. The management company temporarily opened access to the roof for that purpose. The elevators are now running, and access to the roof has been closed off again.
On many floors, boxes and bags of belongings are scattered about, along with plastic-wrapped crates of toys, black bags of construction debris, window frames, packages of building materials, and parts from household appliances.
The smell of smoke still lingers on the fifth and sixth floors. On September 20, burning debris landed on a windowsill and started a fire. On the upper floors, it smells of burned plastic.
The 21st floor suffered the worst damage. Workers had to remove the front panels from one elevator and the structure surrounding the shaft opening. A padlocked grille has replaced the door separating the elevator lobby from the apartments. The apartment the drone struck is on this floor.
Georgy, whose name has been changed, was home in a neighboring apartment at the time. He and his wife, Yelena, whose name has also been changed, were about to head downstairs when he heard an unusual humming sound from the direction of the balcony. “I go over to the balcony and realize it [the drone] is getting closer, but I can’t see it. I can’t figure out where it’s coming from,” he tells Bereg. “I look down — and there it is, coming from the direction of the quarry, heading straight at me.”
Georgy managed to shout to Yelena to run. He didn’t have time to get out of the way himself. The drone hit the neighboring apartment and exploded. The blast wave and a hail of fragments hit him.
His arms and legs were badly cut. Bleeding heavily, he got dressed and pulled on his sneakers. His wife retrieved their cat, which had hidden under the bathtub. They grabbed a bag of documents and jewelry they had prepared in advance and ran downstairs.
“If it had flown just a little higher, that would’ve been it — we wouldn’t be talking now,” Georgy says, visibly shaken as he looks at his bandaged wrists. “The explosion was unreal. I’d never experienced anything like it in my life. I wouldn’t wish that on anyone.”
The couple went to the home of friends who lived nearby. From their friends’ window, Georgy saw an ambulance arrive at the complex. He went over to the medics himself for first aid and to have them “record [him] as one of the injured.” A few hours later, the couple returned to their apartment for belongings, then went back to their friends’ home. After that, they went to Yelena’s relatives’ home, where they’re now staying.
Georgy shows photos of the wrecked apartment on his phone. The stretch ceilings have melted. The windows and balcony are gone, and everything is covered in soot. Furniture and appliances have toppled over, and fragments and pieces of the walls are scattered everywhere. After what he’s been through, Georgy tries to avoid going to Novye Kotelniki unless he absolutely has to. He arranged to meet Bereg’s reporter at a shopping mall in Moscow.
“I thought the same place wouldn’t get hit twice. Turns out it doesn’t work that way here,” Georgy says. It wasn’t until several days later, he says, that he fully realized “what could have happened.” It’s been hard to cope with. The other day, he went to get a haircut, and the buzzing of the clippers made him uneasy.
“I barely slept for three nights. I asked my doctor to prescribe something to calm me down, but it’s still pretty tough,” Georgy says. “It’s okay, we’re strong, we’ll get through it. I think time heals.”
Moscow regional authorities are working out how to repair the apartment and pay compensation, but Georgy is avoiding those subjects for now. Over the past week, he’s had to return to the apartment several times to let in specialists who are to assess the damage from the attack, as well as local administration representatives and officers from the Investigative Committee, Russia’s criminal investigation agency. Those visits convinced him that he could no longer live in the complex, even if the building were fully repaired.
“When you go back there, you start shaking — the atmosphere’s different, the aura’s different,” he says. “I’ve developed a phobia of the place, so I want to get everything sorted out as soon as possible and put this nightmare behind me.”
Georgy’s neighbors are collecting signatures for a petition to the management company and the authorities. They’re demanding additional protection for the building that drones have now hit twice.
“It feels unfair that they can’t keep our homes or our lives safe. You don’t feel very safe in your own capital,” Georgy says.
He believes the air defenses can’t handle the number of drones flying toward Moscow. He sees only one way to guarantee an end to the attacks:
It wouldn’t hurt to end this military operation. One decision — and it would all be over.

articles.title: Seeing Systems unveils Reaver drone carrier
articles.body:
A British company has launched an uncrewed vessel designed to carry, launch and recover as many as a hundred strike drones, controlled with the boat itself through a single command and control layer, the Apex Europe conference in London heard on Wednesday.
Matthew Le Maitre, chief technology officer at Seeing Systems, introduced the vessel at the end of a capability presentation. “Today, I am proud to announce that Seeing Systems stands ready to meet the challenge posed by this new paradigm,” he said. “Apex, please meet Reaver.”
Reaver 101 combines the strike power of UAVs with the endurance of an uncrewed surface vessel, and one command and control layer covers both sea and air for the whole mission. Maximum range is 2,000 nautical miles, it operates far from shore without a support ship, and it moves by road or inside a C-17 to wherever it is needed.
The four payload fits shown covered littoral strike against targets ashore, anti-surface strike against enemy vessels at sea, reconnaissance drones pushed out ahead of the force, and offshore air defence using interceptors against one-way attack drones. Reconfiguration is quick. “When the threat changes, the payload changes. The vessel does not,” Mr Le Maitre said.
“An adversary has no way of knowing which Reaver is doing which job, so every one of them has to be treated as an all-capable threat,” he said. “That is the decisive advantage of autonomous mass. It forces the enemy to solve thousands of problems at once.”
“Mass on its own is a useful advantage,” he said, “but it only becomes truly decisive if it can be controlled effectively. A thousand platforms that each need their own crew are not mass, they’re a manpower problem.” Autonomy allows one team to set the vessels’ routes and the drones’ tasks from a single interface.
The waters a Reaver would fight in will be jammed, spoofed and hostile. Navigation continues when GPS is denied, using inertial dead reckoning cross-checked against radar, and when communications degrade the system steps down through defined levels of autonomy so the mission continues until the link is restored.
The vessel carries its own autonomous deployment and retrieval system, designed and built by the company, which launches drones while the boat is under way and recovers them for reuse. “Recovery capability is what turns a single strike into a sustained operation,” Mr Le Maitre said, adding that the system has already launched and recovered drones at sea in trials.
Open architecture and standard drone protocols allow new airframes and sensors to be integrated without redesigning the vessel. Production runs on live lines in the United Kingdom, the hull from a partner that has already delivered uncrewed boats to the Royal Navy, and the drones from the company’s own lines. “The capital ship takes a decade to build. Reaver’s production lines are already running,” he said.
Mr Le Maitre built the case for the vessel on the cost of the ships it is meant to supplement. “For centuries, navies have measured their power by the size of their capital ships, and since the Second World War, the aircraft carrier has been the capital ship around which the rest of the fleet has been built,” he said. “Capital is a highly relevant word here. In today’s money, each of the Royal Navy’s two Queen Elizabeth class carriers would cost close to 4.6 billion pounds.”
“Now they are undoubtedly extraordinarily capable ships, but these vessels are so important to the Royal Navy that they also represent an extraordinary target. Our adversaries know that, and they plan accordingly. Protecting them effectively is now one of the hardest problems the fleet faces.”
Ukraine and the Middle East have exposed an asymmetry that upends the warfighting conventions of this century, in his account, and cheap mass-produced uncrewed systems are overwhelming platforms that used to dominate. Improvements in AI targeting and swarming will make those weapons more lethal over time, and efficiencies in mass production will make them cheaper.
“Iran has been severely disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz for over seven months, despite the US Navy committing three carrier strike groups to the region,” he said. “They’ve achieved this via a combination of drones, mines, small boats and USVs.” Iran managed it with a degraded green water navy and an air force heavily damaged by joint American and Israeli strikes.
“Just as Ukraine proved on land, Iran is proving at sea that the new asymmetry can be leveraged to frustrate a much stronger military adversary,” he said.
The arithmetic he showed sets one carrier against 4,600 fully armed Reavers. Each is designed to carry up to 100 Havoc strike drones carrying a two kilogram high explosive payload apiece, which across the fleet comes to 460,000 strike drones and more than 900 tonnes of warheads.
“An adversary facing an aircraft carrier has one rather large target to find and eliminate,” he said. “An adversary facing a comparable Reaver fleet has 4,600 targets to contend with.” Losing one costs a fraction of a per cent of the force, in his account, and “the rest of the force keeps fighting.”
The capital ship made sense while manpower was the limit on fielding mass, he argued, and autonomy has removed that limit.
“The Royal Navy has already announced its strategic shift to a hybrid navy,” he said. “We believe that Reaver will be an integral part of that new navy. Reaver will be ready to defend the UK as we move into a more uncertain world.”

articles.title: Ukrainian drone destroys Pantsir on Russian ‘Flakturm’
articles.body:
- The SBU’s Alpha unit released footage of a drone destroying a Russian Pantsir air defense system mounted on a “Flakturm”-style air defense tower.
- The SBU did not disclose the location, date or drone type used in the strike.
A Ukrainian drone has destroyed a Russian Pantsir air defense system on top of a “Flakturm,” one of the purpose-built anti-aircraft towers Russia has been putting up to stop Ukrainian drones, according to new footage released by the Security Service of Ukraine’s Alpha special operations unit.
The video shows the strike on the elevated platform, which Russia built to raise the air defense system above trees and terrain. The Security Service of Ukraine, known as the SBU, did not say where or when the strike took place, what type of drone was used, or whether the tower itself was destroyed along with the Pantsir.
The towers are widely nicknamed Flakturms after the Flaktürme, the massive concrete anti-aircraft towers Nazi Germany built to defend Berlin, Hamburg and Vienna from Allied bombers during World War II. Russia’s use of them became public in September 2023, when state television channel Russia-24 broadcast footage of Pantsir systems mounted on metal towers around Moscow.
Russia places air defense systems on these raised platforms to give their radars a clearer view of low-flying drones and to extend the distance at which they can spot targets. Ground-based radars have trouble seeing small drones that fly close to the ground or behind obstacles, and lifting the system several meters higher helps the radar look over them. The tradeoff is that a tower cannot move. Once its position is known, Ukrainian drone units can plan precision strikes against a target that will still be there when the drone arrives.
The Pantsir is a truck-mounted short-range air defense system that combines a radar, surface-to-air missiles and twin 30 mm cannons. It is one of the main systems Russia uses to shoot down drones and cruise missiles, and Ukrainian forces have made it a priority target. SBU head Vasyl Malyuk said in late 2025 that Ukraine had destroyed 48% of Russia’s Pantsir systems since the start of that year, adding that Russia builds about 30 a year, fewer than Ukraine was destroying.
The strike adds to a series of Ukrainian attacks on Russian air defenses this month. Ukraine’s General Staff said its forces hit another Pantsir-S1 near Kudepsta in Russia’s Krasnodar region on Oct. 8 and into Oct. 9, and Ukrainian FP-2 strike drones destroyed a Pantsir-S2 earlier in October, according to footage published online.

articles.title: Zelensky Warns Against Easing Russia Sanctions as US Authorizes Russian Diesel Sales Through 2027
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump announced in a post on Truth Social Media that Russia agreed to supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the US and global markets. Another 500,000 tons would follow in November and 1 million tons after that.
“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” Trump wrote, adding that Russia would then deliver 3 million tons of diesel within a short time, depending on the condition of its diesel refineries.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Combined with what he called a “total control of the Strait of Hormuz,” the deal would quickly bring down diesel prices for Americans and the rest of the world, Trump claimed.
Shortly after, the US Treasury Department authorized the sale and import of Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The new license came only three weeks after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law on Sept. 18, appearing to completely disregard the bill intended to target Russia’s energy and defense industries, as well as networks close to Putin.
Hours before the license was issued, President Volodymyr Zelensky appealed to the visiting US lawmakers to enforce the law, as it remains crucial for ending the war.
The move also gives Moscow something it had openly demanded. In late September, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russian diesel could flood international markets – but only if it reached them without sanctions or restrictions.
Sybiha Presses WTO Chief on Black Sea Shipping, Remote Audits
Since July, Russia has banned nearly all of its diesel exports, after Ukrainian drone strikes managed to halt a large share of its refining capacity.
Meanwhile, Trump has repeatedly pressed Kyiv to ease those strikes, pinning the blame on Ukraine for record diesel prices instead of the US-Iran war.
Zelensky warns against sanctions relief
Zelensky argued that easing sanctions on Russia without a clear and durable de-escalation agreement would be a sign of weakness that benefits Moscow. “In my view, this is a weak decision,” he said.
The Ukrainian president appeared to respond directly to Trump’s announcement. “Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged,” he said.
Zelensky also pointed to the EU’s decision to delist two Russian oligarchs – Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman – both closely connected to Putin and the Kremlin’s war effort.
Since that move, he said, Russian strikes and terror of civilians have only intensified.
When the US lawmakers asked what it would take to end the war, Zelensky listed three conditions:
- enforcement of sanctions under the law championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham
- support for Ukraine in protecting lives
- and sustained pressure on Russia over the war.
De-escalation offered – again
Zelensky reiterated that Kyiv is prepared to take de-escalation steps that match Russia’s own, and that the American negotiating team is aware of this position.
Zelensky framed Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian refineries and other oil facilities as a response to Moscow’s years-long campaign against Ukraine’s power grid. Halting them, he said, would depend on Russia ending its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Moscow, however, has repeatedly rejected such arrangements. In the very few times it had agreed to a ceasefire, it failed to honor it, with attacks resuming immediately.
The president stressed that any easing of the conflict must be reciprocal rather than one-sided, and pointed to Russia’s results on the battlefield. In his view, Russia is relying on strikes against civilians to make up for its failure to reach its military goals.
This year, he said, Russian forces are weaker on the front line than at any earlier point in the war.
“That is exactly why Putin relies on terror. That is exactly why he relies on attempts at backroom deals on one or another easing of pressure on Russia, to buy more time and more opportunities for war.”

articles.title: US, Ukrainians, Europeans discuss 'new ideas' to end war
articles.body:
US, Europe and Ukraine hold 'constructive discussions' on joint plan to end war
US, Ukrainian and European negotiators held talks in Miami on Friday to seek a common proposal to end the war in Ukraine, as President Donald Trump's decision to ease restrictions on Russian fuel drew criticism from lawmakers and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
US, Ukrainian and European officials met in Miami on Friday in a renewed diplomatic push to end Russia's war in Ukraine, with Washington seeking a way out of the dangerous stalemate.
The talks were overshadowed by US President Donald Trump's announcement of a deal with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to boost diesel supplies, underscoring how the conflict has become entwined with soaring energy prices.
Read moreTrump strikes diesel deal with Putin, reversing years of pressure on Russia over Ukraine war
US envoy Steve Witkoff posted to X after the meeting that the "constructive discussions" tackled "potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace".
Witkoff said the meeting included "the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO".
The discussions covered energy resilience, grain exports, security guarantees and "longer-term arrangements for Ukraine's and Europe's security to prevent future conflict", Witkoff said.
He also noted the "productive" exchange discussed supporting Ukraine's post-war reconstruction and economic prosperity, including EU accession.
Witkoff did not say if the parties would meet on Saturday as originally planned.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned on Thursday that the conflict had reached a potentially explosive impasse, with the failure to reach a negotiated settlement raising the risk of further escalation.
"The other way that stalemates end is through escalation," Rubio told reporters in Lisbon, warning that the conflict could spread to neighboring NATO countries.
"We do not believe that there is a military solution to this conflict," he added.
Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for surging fuel prices, although the US-Israeli war with Iran has been the principal disruptor of global energy supplies.
Following a telephone call with Putin on Friday, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets, with another 500,000 tons to follow in November.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The US Treasury Department said it was issuing a temporary license to allow Russian diesel to flow to global markets. It was not immediately clear whether Trump and Putin had discussed Ukraine during their call.
New proposals
The Miami meeting follows visits to Moscow and Kyiv last month by Witkoff, a longtime Trump confidant, and Kushner, the president's son-in-law, as Washington seeks to revive negotiations that have yielded little progress.
US negotiators have since been developing fresh proposals with Russian and Ukrainian officials, a source familiar with the discussions told AFP.
With winter approaching, the prospect of continued fighting and attacks on vital infrastructure has added urgency to the search for a settlement.
The renewed diplomacy comes against a backdrop of deadly Russian attacks, including a strike on buses in the frontline Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk that killed 30 people.
Territorial deadlock
Trump's repeated attempts to broker an end to the war have foundered over Moscow's sweeping territorial demands, particularly its insistence on controlling all of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, including areas still held by Kyiv.
Zelensky has rejected surrendering Ukrainian-held territory, warning that Russia could use it as a springboard for another attack.
Russia, which launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, now occupies roughly one-fifth of Ukrainian territory.
European officials have expressed concern over high energy costs and the wider economic consequences of the conflict, according to the US sources.
Witkoff and Kushner briefed the president on their latest proposals on Thursday at a meeting also attended by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other senior officials, Axios reported.
The US administration hopes to make diplomatic headway before November's midterm elections, with Washington also seeking to arrange broader talks involving Russia and Ukraine later this month.
The Kremlin has signaled that such three-way negotiations could resume in October, although no date has been announced.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

articles.title: Ukraine’s ADF down 117 out of 160 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine overnight
articles.body:
Ukraine’s ADF down 117 out of 160 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine overnight
As reported by Ukrinform, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this on Telegram.
Starting at 18:00 on October 9, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with 160 strike UAVs, including Shahed-type drones (110 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parodiya-type decoy drones launched from the areas of Oryol, Kursk, Shatalovo, Millerovo and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in the temporarily occupied Crimea.
The air assault was repelled by Ukrainian fighter aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire teams of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 9:00 on Saturday, October 10, air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 117 drones.
Hits were recorded at 14 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 10 locations.
The attack is ongoing, with several enemy drones still in Ukrainian airspace.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky discussed with a U.S. congressional delegation the implementation of Senator Lindsey Graham’s legislation and the acceleration of licensing for the production of missiles for Patriot systems.

articles.title: ‘Obvious weakness’: Zelenskyy slams Trump’s Russian diesel deal, warns it could prolong war
articles.body:
Zelenskyy calls Russia sanctions relief without de-escalation deal ‘obvious weakness’
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday (local time) warned that easing sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement would be an “obvious weakness” that could prolong the war by allowing Moscow to continue selling petroleum products.In a post on X, Zelenskyy said peace could not be achieved through weakness and called for stronger sanctions, continued support for Ukraine and sustained pressure on Moscow to end the war.
"Peace never comes through weakness. Today, representatives of the US Congress were in Kyiv – a bipartisan delegation – and I am grateful to them for visiting Ukraine at such a difficult time. They asked: what is needed to end the war? The answer must be strong. There must be sanctions under the Lindsey Graham bill, there must be support for Ukraine in protecting lives, and there must be pressure on Russia for its war. And today, there was a conversation between the leaders of America and Russia. A conversation that leads to something different," he wrote.
Referring to the diesel announcement, Zelenskyy said, “Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world.
Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.""Recently, there was a European decision to lift sanctions on Russian oligarchs. Since then, Russian strikes and the torment of people have only increased," he added.Citing recent Russian attacks across Ukraine, Zelenskyy said, "This past week alone, there was a brutal Russian missile strike on a residential building in Pryluky, aerial bombs were dropped on Kramatorsk – on ordinary city buses – and there have been constant attacks on Kyiv’s energy infrastructure and on the life-sustaining infrastructure in Dnipro, Kharkiv, Odesa, and our other cities. Dozens of people have been killed and hundreds wounded."He alleged that Russia was resorting to such attacks because it was struggling to achieve its objectives on the battlefield. "The Russians are compensating for their inability to achieve their objectives on the battlefield with this kind of terror. This year, Russia is weaker on the battlefield than at any other point in the war. That is why Putin is relying on terror. That is why he is relying on attempts to strike backroom deals to secure some form of pressure relief for Russia, in order to buy more time and more opportunities for war," he further said.Zelenskyy said Ukraine was prepared to take reciprocal steps towards de-escalation, adding that the American team was aware of Kyiv’s position."Ukraine is ready to take symmetrical de-escalatory steps, and the American team knows our position. Our strikes on Russian oil refineries and other oil facilities are a response to Russia’s years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine’s energy sector. Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure. This is the kind of agreement we are proposing to America, and we believe the United States has enough power to achieve such a compromise," he said.
Zelenskyy’s remarks came after US President Donald Trump spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin and announced a deal to secure diesel supplies from Russia, marking a shift in Washington’s pressure on Moscow over the war in Ukraine as the US seeks to address rising fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections.In a social media post on Friday, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”. He added that Russia would deliver another 3 million tonnes “within a short period of time”.The announcement came just a month after Trump signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law aimed at curbing Moscow’s oil and gas revenues, which help fund its war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Zelensky discusses Graham Act, anti-ballistic missile production with U.S. congressional delegation
articles.body:
Zelensky discusses Graham Act, anti-ballistic missile production with U.S. congressional delegation
President Zelensky announced this on Facebook, according to Ukrinform.
“I am grateful to the U.S. congressional delegation – Roger Wicker, Senator Kevin Cramer, Congressman Marc Veasey, and Congressman Dan Crenshaw – for being here with our people today amid virtually nonstop Russian attacks. Russia is not getting what it wants on the battlefield and is trying to make up for it through escalation,” Zelensky said.
According to him, an air raid alert remained in effect throughout the meeting in Kyiv because of the threat posed by jet-powered Shahed drones. The President stressed that in Kyiv alone, since the beginning of this month, Russian forces have damaged two schools with such drones and struck bridges, energy facilities and other critical infrastructure.
“We can only protect ourselves from this terror by working together, and we discussed how the United States can help save lives. Of course, we expect the Lindsey Graham Act to be implemented. This is a matter of political will, and it is now important to show leadership and fully cut off the financial flows sustaining Russia’s war machine,” Zelensky emphasized.
The sides also discussed other necessary steps, including accelerating licensing for the production of missiles for Patriot systems.
“Ukraine is ready not only to produce ballistic missile interceptors for its own needs, but also to strengthen the United States and its allies through joint production,” Zelensky stressed.
He thanked the United States for its unwavering support.
As Ukrinform reported, a bipartisan U.S. congressional delegation in Kyiv expressed support for expanding Ukraine’s access to Starlink capabilities and coverage.

articles.title: Child Killed, 2 Injured in Drone Strike Near Nikopol
articles.body:
An 11-year-old boy was killed and two other children were injured on Saturday, Oct. 10, when Russian forces dropped an explosive munition from an unmanned aerial vehicle in the Nikopol district of Dnipropetrovsk region, regional authorities reported.
Head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration Oleksandr Hanzha confirmed the casualties on his official Telegram channel, stating that the attack took place in the Pokrovska territorial community.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“An 11-year-old boy was killed as a result of an enemy attack in the Nikopol district,” Hanzha said. “The Russians dropped a munition from a drone in the Pokrovska community. Two more children were wounded – a 12-year-old boy and a 10-year-old girl.”
Hanzha stated that both surviving children were transported to a medical facility, where doctors are administering emergency medical assistance.
The Nikopol district, located across the Dnipro River from the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, faces daily Russian artillery shelling, loitering munition attacks, and tactical drone drops targeting civilian areas and municipal infrastructure.
Daylight drone and ballistic barrages across central Ukraine
The fatal drone drop in the Pokrovska community formed part of a wave of Russian strikes targeting non-combatants and civilian settlements across central and eastern Ukraine on Saturday.
In Kyiv, Russian forces conducted a daylight ballistic missile strike on the northern Obolonskyi district, hitting a restaurant building, sparking a major blaze, and scattering missile debris across an adjacent residential courtyard.
Major Drone Attack Paralyzes Moscow Airports, Flights Delayed
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed that the number of casualties from the capital’s restaurant strike rose to six, with five victims hospitalized and one treated on-site by emergency medical crews.
The ballistic barrage followed morning waves of turbojet loitering munitions that damaged electrical distribution nodes in Kyiv region, temporarily shutting down all three lines of the capital’s metro network, paralyzing electric surface transit, and cutting off municipal water supplies.
Climbing casualties in southern urban centers
Concurrently, emergency responders in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia continued recovering victims following a Russian guided aerial bomb (KAB) strike launched at 4:48 a.m. local time on Saturday.
The strike directly hit a five-story residential building and damaged 26 homes across the Shevchenkivskyi and Voznesenivskyi districts.
While initial morning assessments indicated four fatalities, the State Emergency Service and regional military authorities confirmed that the death toll surged to 17, including three children, as rescue brigades cleared collapsed masonry and searched for trapped residents beneath the rubble.
Another 16 civilians, including two children, sustained injuries.
