articles.title: Saudi Arabia will never break Yemen’s resistance: Ansarallah leader
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia will never break Yemen’s resistance: Ansarallah leader
TEHRAN — Speaking on the tenth anniversary of the Saudi airstrike on Sanaa’s Great Hall, Ansarallah leader Sayyed Abdul-Malik al-Houthi declared Thursday that Riyadh’s decade-long war to subjugate Yemen has collapsed into a strategic failure.
The October 2016 massacre, which left roughly 1,000 mourners dead or wounded inside a crowded funeral hall, remains a stark monument to Saudi war crimes carried out with direct American support.
The Ansarallah leader emphasized that every governorate across Yemen has suffered identical atrocities, with civilian homes, markets, and schools systematically targeted in a failed effort to force submission.
Al-Houthi dismantled the Saudi monarchy’s religious posturing, arguing that its claim to guard Islam’s holiest sanctuaries rings hollow.
The sword emblazoned on the Saudi flag has never drawn blood in defense of Muslims, he observed, but has consistently served Zionist and American ambitions to fragment the region and isolate the Resistance Front.
The address coincided with a sharp escalation on the ground.
On Thursday, the Yemeni Armed Forces shot down a Saudi-operated Turkish Bayraktar Akinci drone over Taiz and launched a ballistic missile strike at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, disrupting flight operations and triggering widespread alarms.
Parallel missile strikes hit Saudi troop concentrations at the Qa’wah camp near Ras al-Ara and positions along the Bab al-Mandab approach, inflicting dozens of casualties and detonating enemy ammunition depots.
Addressing regional governments, al-Houthi issued a direct warning to Qatar regarding its renewed political and media alignment with Saudi policies.
He reminded leadership in Doha that its previous involvement in the coalition against Yemen did not prevent Riyadh and Bahrain’s Al Khalifa regime from plotting regime change in Qatar and imposing a suffocating blockade.
Assisting Saudi Arabia now, the Ansarallah leader cautioned, makes Doha complicit in war crimes while exposing it once again to betrayal by its alleged allies.
Al-Houthi affirmed that Yemeni forces hold full operational authority to strike enemy assets across the Red Sea and Arabian Sea from any point in the country.
Rebuffing Western media claims, he placed full blame for maritime instability on Saudi and American militarization around Bab al-Mandab.

articles.title: ‘Nuclear weapons not routine instruments of statecraft’: India’s warning to Pakistan at UN
articles.body:
‘India will not bow to nuclear blackmail’: New Delhi hits back at Pakistan at UN (Anmol Sher Singh Bedi)
NEW DELHI: India on Friday warned Pakistan against using nuclear weapons as a tool of political pressure, asserting that New Delhi would not bow to nuclear blackmail and that any terrorist attack against the country would invite a fitting response.Exercising its Right of Reply at the United Nations General Assembly's First Committee, which deals with disarmament and international security, India said nuclear weapons must not be treated as “routine instruments of statecraft”.Senior Adviser (Disarmament) at India's Permanent Mission to the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva, Anmol Sher Singh Bedi, delivered the response following remarks by Pakistan on Jammu and Kashmir.
“Jammu and Kashmir is an integral and inalienable part of India,” Bedi said, rejecting Pakistan's claims over the region.He said India's military capabilities were defensive in nature and shaped by its security environment, rather than directed against any particular country.“We heard concerns about escalation. These are legitimate concerns. However, these are best judged by conduct over time. Nuclear weapons must not be treated as routine instruments of statecraft,” Bedi said.
He warned that relying on the threat of nuclear weapons to shield activities below the threshold of conventional warfare could increase the risk of escalation rather than promote restraint.“A posture that relies on nuclear overhang to limit the consequences of subconventional activity raises the risk of escalation and not the prospect of restraint,” he said.Bedi also outlined what he described as a recurring pattern in regional crises, involving provocation, denial of responsibility and subsequent appeals for restraint after a response.“Where those in power are neither elected by people nor accountable to them, their decisions carry no risk and impose no cost for those who take them. That is how crisis becomes an instrument of power. That is how instability becomes useful, and that is how the cycle keeps on repeating,” he said.
India reiterates three red lines
India said its position on terrorism and national security remained clear, identifying three principles that would guide its response to threats.“First, any terrorist attack against India will receive a fitting response. Second, India will not bow to nuclear blackmail. Third, India will make no distinction between those who sponsor terrorism and those who mastermind it,” Bedi said.He said India's actions in May 2025 followed a “grave provocation” and were undertaken in self-defence after the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir, in which 26 civilians, mostly tourists, were killed.“These actions were measured, targeted, and designed to be non-escalatory,” Bedi said.India launched Operation Sindoor on May 7, 2025, targeting what it described as terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir in retaliation for the Pahalgam attack. The Resistance Front, a proxy of Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba, was linked to the attack.Bedi also stressed that the use of non-state actors by a country did not absolve it of responsibility for their actions.“The use of force by states under the garb of non-state actors does not erase the state's responsibility. India's right of self-defense remains intact,” he said.
India raises Indus Waters Treaty, nuclear proliferation
India also referred to the Indus Waters Treaty, arguing that the agreement depended on mutual trust and cooperation between the two countries.“A state cannot undermine those foundations of trust and cooperation and at the same time insist that the privileges flowing from the relationship remain untouched,” Bedi said.Following the Pahalgam attack, India announced that the treaty would be held in abeyance until Pakistan credibly and irrevocably ended its support for cross-border and other forms of terrorism.On nuclear proliferation, Bedi invoked the legacy of Pakistani nuclear scientist Abdul Qadeer Khan and the international proliferation network associated with him, which supplied nuclear equipment and expertise to countries seeking to develop nuclear weapons.
The network contributed to international concerns that led to United Nations Security Council Resolution 1540, adopted in 2004, which requires states to prevent the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and their means of delivery to non-state actors.“This is relevant in the context of demands for unquestioned nuclear cooperation and transfer of advanced weapons and military capabilities. We urge all states and all responsible suppliers to exercise the highest degree of vigilance, not because of India, but for their own security,” Bedi said.
Ayush Pandey is a journalist at The Times of India, covering breaking news, politics, defence, and major legal and policy developments across India and the world. His reporting focuses on elections, national security, and institutional affairs, tracking the decisions and conflicts that shape public life. He specialises in sharp explainers and in-depth feature stories that go beyond headlines to decode political shifts, defence strategy, geopolitical flashpoints, and changing public sentiment. His work combines speed, clarity, and depth for a fast-moving digital audience.

articles.title: Trump strikes deal for over 4.8 million tons of Russian diesel despite sanctions
articles.body:
President Donald Trump announced Friday that he had reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin for more than 4.8 million tons of Russian diesel, a dramatic shift in U.S. policy toward Moscow as Washington seeks to ease soaring fuel prices ahead of the November midterm elections.
The announcement came just weeks after Trump signed sweeping sanctions legislation targeting Russia's energy sector over its war in Ukraine, raising questions about Washington's commitment to maintaining economic pressure on the Kremlin.
Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons shortly afterward. An additional 3 million tons would be delivered within a relatively short period, he said.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote on social media.
Shortly after the announcement, the U.S. Treasury Department issued a temporary license easing sanctions on Russian diesel exports. The authorization allows Russian diesel loaded onto tankers as of Friday to be supplied to global markets without triggering U.S. sanctions until April 2027.
The White House did not immediately clarify who would pay for the shipments, when the fuel would become available or whether deliveries scheduled for November would arrive before the November 3 elections.
The agreement comes as the war in Iran continues to disrupt global energy markets. According to AAA, the average price of diesel in the United States reached $6.23 per gallon Friday, after hitting a record $6.52 on September 22.
Zelensky: ‘Gifts to Putin will not bring peace’
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky sharply condemned the agreement, warning that increased Russian energy revenues would help Moscow finance its continued war against Ukraine.
"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilised world," Zelensky wrote on X.
"Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis," he added.
The Kremlin said the Trump-Putin phone call focused on prospects for resolving the war in Ukraine and also addressed developments in Iran.
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev welcomed the agreement, saying cooperation between Moscow and Washington on diesel and energy would benefit the world.
The announcement also drew criticism from Democrats. Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called the decision "infuriating" and accused Trump of undermining sanctions intended to weaken Russia's war economy.
The latest Treasury authorization follows several temporary exemptions granted to Russian energy shipments since the outbreak of the Iran war. However, it marks a more substantial relaxation of restrictions, extending beyond the shorter waivers previously issued.
For Moscow, the agreement offers an opportunity to expand energy revenues despite Western sanctions. For Kyiv, it represents a potentially damaging reversal of efforts to constrain Russia's ability to finance its invasion.

articles.title: Ukraine and Finland condemn Trump’s deal to import Russian diesel
articles.body:
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo has condemned an agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel to American and global markets, describing the decision as a major disappointment.
Speaking to Finnish broadcaster Yle on Saturday, Orpo questioned whether the agreement would have any significant effect on fuel prices, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Washington of providing financial support to Russia during its war against Ukraine.
The agreement, announced by Trump on Friday, provides for Russia to deliver more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by another 500,000 tonnes in November and one million tonnes thereafter.
Trump also announced plans for an additional three million tonnes, depending on the condition of Russian refineries damaged by Ukrainian attacks.
The US Treasury subsequently issued a temporary licence permitting imports of Russian diesel until 7 April 2027, easing sanctions introduced to restrict Moscow's energy revenues.
Orpo told Yle's Ykkösaamu programme that the announcement was a "terrible disappointment", although he stressed that the agreed quantities represented only a fraction of US diesel consumption.
He also questioned whether Russia would fulfil the deliveries and said he did not expect the agreement to have much impact on American or global markets.
Zelenskyy described the agreement as a gift to Putin and "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".
"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Zelenskyy wrote on X, warning that Russia would repay the diesel with further attacks.
The announcement coincided with talks between Ukrainian, European and American representatives in Miami aimed at ending the war.
Trump defended the arrangement as necessary to reduce fuel costs following disruptions caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran, which began in February.
According to figures from the American Automobile Association reported by Reuters, average US diesel prices reached $6.28 per gallon on Thursday, approximately 70% above their level before the conflict.
Diesel prices have become a concern for the administration ahead of the 3 November congressional elections, particularly because of their effect on farming, transport and consumer costs.
The agreement also attracted criticism from American lawmakers. Republican congressman Don Bacon called for stronger sanctions against Russia rather than measures that would increase Moscow's revenues.
Energy specialists questioned the potential benefits for consumers.
In an interview with Finnish newspaper Ilta-Sanomat, Hanna Kalenoja, a transport specialist at the Finland Chamber of Commerce, said the agreement would primarily redirect existing Russian diesel exports rather than increase global supplies.
Russia has continued exporting diesel despite production disruptions caused by Ukrainian strikes on its refineries.
Kalenoja explained that the agreement would determine whether available Russian fuel reached the United States and its allies instead of Asian markets, where much of it has previously been sold.
She told IS that Finnish motorists were unlikely to see meaningful reductions in diesel prices as a result of the agreement.
Clayton Seigle, an energy strategist at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, also questioned the potential price benefits, telling the Associated Press that the agreement would provide Russia with additional export revenue without substantially reducing diesel costs in the United States or Europe.
Seigle said Russia was seeking buyers for its summer-grade diesel as domestic demand shifted towards winter and Arctic fuel grades.
Kalenoja identified Washington's willingness to ease sanctions on Russia in response to energy costs as a concern for Europe, where governments have maintained restrictions on Russian energy imports.
Meanwhile, the Finnish government continues discussing measures to help households and businesses facing higher fuel prices.
Orpo told Yle that proposals include tax changes, commuting deductions and support for professional drivers, but ministers have yet to agree on a package.
The prime minister also announced plans to propose ending tourist visas for Russian citizens across Europe at next week's European Council meeting, citing concerns about possible Russian sabotage operations.
HT

articles.title: ‘Obvious weakness’: Zelenskyy criticizes Trump-Putin diesel deal over lack of de-escalation
articles.body:
Burç Eruygur
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Friday that easing sanctions on Russia without a de-escalation deal would be an "obvious weakness," following a diesel supply agreement announced by US President Donald Trump after talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
In a statement on US social media platform X, Zelenskyy said he had received a bipartisan delegation from the US Congress in Kyiv earlier Friday.
He said he called for stronger sanctions and increased pressure on Russia, as well as further support for Ukraine.
"And today, there was a conversation between the leaders of America and Russia. A conversation that leads to something different," Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian president argued that Russia's recent increase in airstrikes against Ukraine was intended to compensate for Moscow's "inability to achieve their objectives on the battlefield."
He accused Moscow of attempting to "strike backroom deals to secure some form of pressure relief for Russia, in order to buy more time and more opportunities for war."
"Any easing of sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious weakness," Zelenskyy said. 
'Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in war'
Zelenskyy reaffirmed Kyiv's readiness to take reciprocal steps toward de-escalation with Moscow.
He said Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and other facilities were a response to Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy," Zelenskyy said.
"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis," he added.
Zelenskyy's remarks followed Trump's announcement of what he described as a "highly successful discussion" with Putin.
Trump said on his Truth Social platform that the talks resulted in an agreement for Russia to "immediately supply" more than 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to US and global markets.
According to Trump, Russia would provide another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."
He added that another 3 million tons would be delivered "within a short period," depending on the condition of Russian diesel refineries.

articles.title: Easing Diesel Sanctions Shows Weakness to Putin, Sybiha Says

Easing sanctions on Russian petroleum products will neither stabilize global energy benchmarks nor accelerate a negotiated peace in Ukraine, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned on Friday, Oct. 9.
Responding to Washington’s decision to facilitate imports of Russian diesel, Sybiha argued that the move projects Western weakness to the Kremlin, asserting that only a comprehensive, mutually enforced energy ceasefire – backed by allied deterrence – can genuinely lower global fuel prices.

articles.title: Putin Touts 90% Dollar-Free CIS Trade as Russia Sidesteps Western Sanctions
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin used a summit of former Soviet republics in Turkmenistan on Friday, Oct. 9, to promote what Moscow sees as a financial lifeline against Western sanctions – claiming that 90% of Russia’s trade settlements with Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries now take place in national currencies rather than dollars or euros.
The announcement highlights how the Kremlin is using its post-Soviet economic networks to reduce reliance on Western financial systems while sustaining trade during its war against Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A $110 billion trade network beyond the dollar
Speaking at the summit in Avaza, a resort on Turkmenistan’s Caspian coast, Putin said Russian trade with CIS countries exceeded $110 billion in 2025 and continued growing in 2026.
He praised the development of a “stable financial infrastructure” independent of foreign influence, arguing that it allowed economic cooperation to continue despite outside pressure.
“It allows us to deepen economic cooperation regardless of foreign influence,” Putin said.
The shift toward national currencies has become increasingly important for Russia since Western governments imposed sweeping financial restrictions following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Putin also urged CIS members to remove remaining obstacles to regional commerce.
“Barriers should be lifted,” he said.
How former Soviet trade routes help Russia evade sanctions
The risks extend beyond the currencies used to settle transactions.
Trump Says He and Putin Have Cut Diesel Deal, Zelensky Accuses Washington of ‘Weakness’
Western governments have repeatedly identified Central Asia and the South Caucasus as potential routes for restricted goods entering Russia through third countries.
The researchers identified two methods: rerouting sanctioned products through neighboring countries and misreporting the destinations of shipments passing through Russia.
They estimated that these channels offset roughly one-third of the decline in direct European exports to Russia in restricted product categories during 2022–23.
The goods involved included industrial equipment and dual-use products with potential military applications.
A shrinking club of former Soviet republics
The economic figures contrast with the steady erosion of the CIS’s political influence.
Established in December 1991 following the collapse of the Soviet Union, the organization was designed to preserve cooperation among newly independent republics.
Georgia formally withdrew in 2009 following Russia’s invasion the previous year.
Ukraine, one of the CIS’s founding states, gradually dismantled its participation after Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014 and accelerated its withdrawal from remaining agreements following the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Moldova has also moved toward a definitive break.
Armenia, meanwhile, has increasingly diversified its security and diplomatic relationships after years of dependence on Moscow.
Across Central Asia, governments are expanding economic cooperation with China, the European Union and Turkey while maintaining important commercial ties with Russia.
For Putin, however, the CIS remains a platform to demonstrate that Moscow retains regional influence despite its confrontation with Ukraine and the West.
Iran joins the gathering
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian attended the summit as a special guest, reflecting Moscow’s growing cooperation with another government facing extensive Western sanctions.
Putin and Pezeshkian met separately on Thursday, Oct. 8, discussing bilateral relations and the ongoing conflict involving Iran.
Pezeshkian thanked Moscow for opposing what he described as US unilateralism, while Putin offered Russian assistance in efforts to resolve the Middle East conflict.
Russia and Iran have expanded military and economic cooperation since Moscow invaded Ukraine, with Iranian-designed drones becoming an important part of Russia’s attacks.
The next CIS summit will take place in Bukhara, Uzbekistan, in October 2027, with Azerbaijan serving as co-chair before assuming the presidency and hosting the summit in 2028.
Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko welcomed Azerbaijan’s decision as a “historic moment” and expressed hope that Armenia would follow in 2029 – despite Yerevan’s growing distance from Moscow.

articles.body:
Zelensky: Ukraine faces particular threat of further Russian missile strikes in coming days
According to Ukrinform, Zelensky announced this on Facebook.
"It was right during Russia's ballistic attack on Kyiv today that we spoke with the President of France. Thank you, Emmanuel, for your support," Zelensky said.
He noted that additional air defense packages were clearly needed and that Ukraine was working with all its partners to secure the necessary decisions.

The two leaders also discussed the challenges posed by the easing of sanctions on petroleum products.
"The Russians must feel that they will have no capacity left to prolong the war. We are coordinating substantively and preparing meetings. Thank you, France!" Zelensky stressed.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Ukraine's air defense forces intercepted some of the ballistic missiles Russia used to attack Kyiv during the day on October 10.
Photo: Office of the President of Ukraine

articles.title: Montenegro to deport Russian pro-Kremlin war blogger and founder of Rybar propaganda project Mikhail Zvinchuk
articles.body:
Montenegrin authorities are set to deport Mikhail Zvinchuk, founder of the Russian pro-war propaganda project Rybar. Zvinchuk’s wife, Valeria, and three of the project’s employees, are also on the deportation list, local outlet Vijesti reported, citing Montenegro’s Police Directorate. Bosnian investigative journalists found that Zvinchuk entered Montenegro from Bosnia and Herzegovina after flying there from Germany.
News of the detention of Zvinchuk, his wife, and other Rybar staff emerged earlier in the day on Oct. 9. Vijesti identified the other detainees as Sergei Belous, Pavel Lekatorchuk, and Kira Doroshenko. All five individuals have now been ordered to leave Montenegro, with law enforcement authorities saying the decision was made on the basis of national and internal security grounds.
According to Montenegrin police, Zvinchuk, his wife, and Rybar employees entered the country two days earlier. They stayed in the town of Risan on the Bay of Kotor, where they were ultimately detained. Officers seized cameras, a GoPro, a filming drone, and mobile phones from the group.
Bosnian investigative outlet Detektor found that Zvinchuk and his team entered Montenegro from Bosnia and Herzegovina. They arrived in Sarajevo on Oct. 2 on a flight from Germany. While Zvinchuk, his wife, and Rybar employees were in the country, elections were taking place in Bosnia. Bosnia’s Security Ministry has not yet commented on the information.
On Oct. 6, Rybar published a video roundup for the Solovyov Live program that was filmed in Bosnia. The following day, Oct. 7, the Rybar team entered Montenegro by land.
Zvinchuk later boasted that he had entered Montenegro despite the sanctions and travel ban levied against him. In a post on social media, Zvinchuk said Montenegro was the 26th country he had visited and described how he entered the country:
“Remember: even if you are under sanctions, like me, even if you have a travel ban, like me, even if you are traveling to a country that has pledged, out of solidarity, to enforce that travel ban, as in my case ... THERE IS A WAY!”
Zvinchuk added that travelers like him could always run into “an idiot border guard who turns out all your pockets but forgets to check the database.”
On Oct. 8, prior to his arrest, Zvinchuk again appeared on the Russian propaganda channel Solovyov Live, where he claimed that “Montenegro is in tears because visas are being introduced for Russian tourists.”
Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajić confirmed Zvinchuk’s detention in a post on X earlier today:
“The message following today's successful action in which the head of the information network ‘Rybar’ was apprehended is clear: out institutions are doing their job, Montenegro is protecting its interests, and no one will jeopardize our European future.”
Rybar founder Mikhail Zvinchuk, a former employee of the Russian Defense Ministry’s press service, is under EU and UK sanctions. The EU’s sanctions justification says he is part of a working group created by Vladimir Putin to coordinate Russia’s mobilization efforts in support of the ongoing war against Ukraine. Rybar’s main Telegram channel has more than 1.5 million subscribers.
In 2024, the United States offered a reward of up to $10 million for information about people working on the project, which it said used social media to "sow discord, promote social division, stoke partisan and racial discord, and encourage hate and violence in the United States.” The U.S. State Department also listed Zvinchuk as being involved in attempts to influence the U.S. electoral process.
In February 2026, OpenAI blocked a network of accounts linked to Rybar. The project’s team had used ChatGPT as a content farm to generate social media and blog posts in Russian, English, and Spanish.
In September, Czech police detained and questioned Russian nationals Vitaly Chashchukhin and Igor Dolmatov, whom journalists from local outlet Seznam Zprávy had earlier lured to a meeting in Prague and secretly recorded discussing their work for the Rybar project. After questioning, both were ordered to leave the Czech Republic within three days as undesirable persons.
Chashchukhin and Dolmatov are known to live in Germany, where Chashchukhin performs work for sanctioned Russian media outlets Izvestia, Channel Five, and REN TV. In his reports, he portrays Germany as a country in economic decline, claiming its only hope for prosperity requires a halt to arms supplies for Ukraine and a return to the purchase of cheap energy from Russia.
Zvinchuk’s detention drew reactions from Russian government officials including Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov and ex-president Dmitry Medvedev, and also from media outlets, bloggers, and pro-war channels. Ivan Filippov, a propaganda researcher and author of the Telegram channel “All Quiet on the Zzzzzestern Front,” told the independent outlet Vot Tak that many commentators — regardless of their views — were asking why a sanctioned Russian propagandist who was aware of the risks had traveled to a NATO country that is seeking EU membership:
“Some people are expressing sympathy, but looking at the reactions now, the dominant question is why he went there in the first place. The pro-war “Z”-community is genuinely stunned. [Head of RT] Margarita Simonyan believed he would be extradited to Ukraine,” Filippov said.
Montenegro joined NATO in 2017 and is seeking to join the EU after adopting the euro in 2002 and applying for membership in the bloc in 2008. It imposed sanctions on Russia after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The government recently approved plans to end visa-free travel for Russian citizens starting from Nov. 1, as Montenegro aligns its visa policy with the European Union ahead of a possible accession by 2028. Local media reported this spring that around 14,000 of the 21,000 Russians registered in Montenegro had left after the government announced plans to introduce visa requirements.
“Montenegro’s accession as the 28th member state by 2028 is within reach,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said at an EU-Western Balkans summit in June.

articles.title: China denies report of reciprocal nuclear site visits with US
articles.body:
Faisal Mahmud
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
China on Friday denied a report that Beijing and Washington had discussed reciprocal visits to nuclear facilities, with further talks reportedly planned in the coming months.
"The relevant report is not true," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a regular news conference in Beijing, according to an official transcript of the briefing.
The denial came after CNN reported, citing sources familiar with the matter, that China and the US had discussed possible reciprocal visits to nuclear sites.
According to an earlier CNN report, preliminary discussions covered possible visits to US Department of Energy laboratories and corresponding Chinese research centers, alongside potential access to nuclear test sites.
The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), in its June report, estimated that China possessed 620 nuclear warheads as of January 2026, compared with more than 5,000 held by the US, including retired warheads.
According to SIPRI, the world's nine nuclear-armed nations possessed an estimated 12,187 warheads, including 190 held by India, 170 by Pakistan, 90 by Israel and 60 by North Korea. Russia and the US together accounted for nearly 86% of the global inventory.
SIPRI said China was expanding its nuclear arsenal faster than any other country, while Washington and Moscow continued extensive nuclear modernization programs.
The developments follow the expiration of the New START nuclear arms reduction treaty between Washington and Moscow in February.

articles.title: Zelenskyy after speaking with Macron: threat of missile strikes remains particularly high in coming days
articles.body:
Zelenskyy after speaking with Macron: threat of missile strikes remains particularly high in coming days
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has discussed the challenges posed by the US easing sanctions on Russian oil products with French President Emmanuel Macron.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter); European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy noted that he and Macron spoke as Russia was carrying out a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv on Saturday.
Quote: "The need for additional air defence packages for Ukraine is evident, and we are working with all our partners to secure the necessary decisions. Unfortunately, the threat of further missile strikes remains particularly high in the coming days."
Details: Zelenskyy said it is important to step up pressure on Russia in response and that bold, joint steps must be taken.
Quote: "We discussed the challenges posed by the easing of sanctions on oil products. The Russians must feel that they will have no capacity left to prolong the war. We are coordinating substantively and preparing meetings."
Background:
- US President Donald Trump said the previous day that he had spoken with Putin and reached an agreement with him on supplies of Russian diesel fuel to the US and global markets.
- The Finnish prime minister has called the agreement a "terrible disappointment".
- Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal has described the US president's decision as a major mistake and called for increased support for Ukraine to help it "turn Russian oil refineries into ruins".

articles.title: Drones strike oil-loading terminal in Rostov, triggering major fire – videos
articles.body:
Drones strike oil-loading terminal in Rostov, triggering major fire – videos
Drones attacked the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Refinery oil-loading terminal in Russia's Rostov Oblast on the night of 9-10 October, triggering a major fire at the site.
Source: Russian media outlet Astra; monitoring Telegram channels; Rostov Oblast Governor Yuri Slyusar
Details: Judging by photos and videos posted by eyewitnesses, a large fire broke out in Rostov-on-Don following a series of powerful explosions.
Slyusar confirmed the fire and said air defence forces were responding. He wrote that "more than 50 UAVs have been shot down since yesterday evening".
He also said that the drone attack had damaged a railway bridge. As a result, "train services in both directions have been suspended".
The targeted facility handles the transshipment of petroleum products for export and is involved in supplying fuel to the Russian military. It also generates foreign-currency revenue that helps finance Russia's war against Ukraine. The terminal has a design capacity of approximately 2.5 million tonnes a year.
Background:
- On 9 July, Ukraine's defence forces and the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine confirmed a successful drone strike on the oil-loading terminal near Bataysk in Rostov Oblast, which caused a fire.
- In September, Ukrainian forces conducted further airstrikes on the production facilities at the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Refinery in Rostov Oblast.

articles.title: Zelensky slams Trump’s ‘weak decision’
articles.body:
Zelensky slams Trump’s ‘weak decision’
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky has lashed out at US President Donald Trump over his decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, accusing Washington of striking a deal with Moscow behind Kiev’s back.
Zelensky described the move as “definitely unfair,” “definitely not partner-like” and “a weak decision by strong partners,” effectively portraying it as a stab in the back just as Ukrainian negotiators and Kiev’s European backers were meeting American officials to discuss a potential peace settlement in Miami.
In a voice memo sent to Western journalists on Friday, Zelensky suggested Trump had used talks with Ukrainian negotiators as a “smokescreen” while pursuing a separate agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“You know, it looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible,” he told Axios in a separate phone interview, referring to the Russian leader’s 74th birthday earlier this week.
Q: Zelenskyy said you're weak because of the Putin deal. He just criticized you TRUMP: Who said that? Q: Zelenskyy. He said you're weak TRUMP: Okay. *walks away* https://t.co/niHd2ynoVP
— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) October 9, 2026
Trump initially ignored journalists’ questions about Zelensky calling him “weak” but later brushed aside the criticism, defending the agreement as necessary to ease soaring fuel prices.
Reporter: President Zelensky said that this is a weak move by a strong partner that will only prolong the war. Trump: We need oil for the world and this is diesel, which is what we need. So we're very happy to get it. https://t.co/8clgGPbJvv
— Faytuks Network (@FaytuksNetwork) October 9, 2026
“We need oil for the world and this is diesel, which is what we need. So we’re very happy to get it,” the US president said.
Earlier on Friday, Trump announced that following a “successful discussion” with Putin, Moscow had agreed to immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to American and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November, another million tons shortly thereafter, and potentially 3 million additional tons depending on refinery capacity.
The US Treasury subsequently issued a six-month sanctions waiver allowing Russian diesel exports, as Washington seeks to contain a global fuel shortage exacerbated by the US-Israeli war on Iran and Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Trump has repeatedly blamed Kiev – and Zelensky personally – for worsening the global fuel crisis, accusing Ukraine of deliberately knocking out Russian refining capacity and driving up prices for American consumers.
During a visit to Ireland last month, Trump directly demanded that Zelensky halt the strikes. “Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia… Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world,” he said.
Trump doubled down earlier this week, arguing that the main driver of soaring US fuel prices was no longer the disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, but Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has similarly linked the strikes to a broader global “energy shock.”
Despite Washington’s repeated warnings, Zelensky pledged last weekend to intensify long-range strikes on Russian oil facilities. A senior Ukrainian official told the Financial Times on Friday that Kiev would ignore Washington’s deal with Moscow and “will burn their refineries.”
Frustrstion and anger in Kyiv tonight over Trump's diesel deal with Putin. Zelenskyy blasts Trump, calling the move "weak." A senior Ukrainian official tells me Kyiv will continue its long-range drone strikes on Russia's energy facilities "We will burn their refineries."
— Christopher Miller (@ChristopherJM) October 9, 2026
The fuel shortage has become an increasingly pressing domestic issue for Trump ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. US diesel prices surged to record highs above $6.50 per gallon in September, with prices in California exceeding $8 in some areas.
Putin confirmed following Friday’s conversation that Russia was prepared to supply oil and petroleum products to American and global markets, expressing confidence that the move would have a positive effect on the world economy.

articles.title: Ukrainian producer that neutralized more than 7,000 drones over 100 square kilometers in year, plays enemy in Pentagon contest, and gets invitation to continue
articles.body:
A Ukrainian company has played the enemy in a Pentagon drone contest, and the US liked what it saw. Phantom Defense, a Ukrainian defense-tech firm, was one of three companies whose systems built the counter-drone environment for Gauntlet II, the second stage of the US military’s Drone Dominance program, and has been invited to take part further, Defender Media reports.
Drone Dominance is the Pentagon’s four-phase effort to field cheap attack drones fast, a roughly $1 billion program to buy more than 200,000 low-cost attack drones by 2027. Phantom Defense brought a system that was already proven at home, where in one city it neutralized more than 7,000 enemy drones over an area of more than 100 square kilometers in a year, the company says.
Rather than enter a drone of its own, Phantom Defense supplied the resistance that the American drones had to fly through. Its setup paired the Specter PRO, L, X, and XL jammers with the Streamhunter video-interception tool and a command-and-control layer that detected and classified targets, coordinated the countermeasures, and confirmed the kills. The jammers suppressed drones and held up in heat and rain, it adds.
The arrangement lets American developers fly their drones under live electronic attack rather than calm conditions, recreating a battlefield where a drone’s performance swings with the jamming around it, according to the company.
One map to run the whole fight
At the center sits Phantom Defense’s C2 system, Kupol, which integrates separate tools into a single ecosystem on a shared map. It lets crews run electronic warfare remotely, without driving out to a position, and ties in sensors, interceptor drones, and turrets, the company says.
Kupol reads the terrain and a drone database to propose the best way to take down a target, then logs each mission automatically so its recommendations sharpen over time.
The high-power Specter PRO station, built to shield positions, critical infrastructure, and cities, serves as the hardware anchor.
An invitation, not yet a contract
Previously, Ukraine’s battle-tested drone makers also took part in Drone Dominance. However, they didn’t succeed in it, though some of their technology competed under Western partners. The program bars direct purchases from Ukrainian firms, which must set up a US legal entity to bid.

articles.title: Trump says he reached a deal with Putin to supply Russian diesel to U.S. and global markets, breaking with years of American sanctions policy
articles.body:
Trump says he’s reached a deal with Putin to supply Russian diesel to U.S. and global markets. Zelensky calls it ‘an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.’
U.S. President Donald Trump said he had reached a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel fuel to U.S. and global markets. Trump said they reached the agreement during “highly successful” talks by phone.
Russia agreed to supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel fuel to U.S. and global markets as soon as possible, Trump said. It will supply another 500,000 metric tons in November and 1 million metric tons “immediately thereafter.”
“Based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries,” Moscow could also supply another 3 million metric tons of diesel “within a short period of time,” Trump said.
Trump’s announcement came as the U.S. Treasury Department issued a temporary license allowing Russian diesel fuel to be supplied to the global market until April 7, 2027.
“Thanks to our total control of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump said.
In a response on social media, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the diesel deal “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”:
Exports of Russian oil and petroleum products to countries around the world are restricted by sanctions and Russia’s own export bans. For example, a ban on producers exporting diesel fuel, marine fuel, and gas oil remains in effect until the end of October.
Sources told Interfax on October 6 that Russian authorities were considering partially lifting the ban on diesel exports for some producers that month.
Ukraine has also been striking Russian oil refineries. These attacks caused a fuel crisis in Russia during the summer of 2026. Donald Trump has repeatedly urged Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil facilities. According to Trump, the strikes are causing a global fuel shortage and driving up prices.

articles.title: Record 20 Russian officers killed in Ukrainian strikes on headquarters in Donetsk, monitors say
articles.body:
Record 20 Russian officers killed in Ukrainian strikes on headquarters in Donetsk, monitors say
Ukrainian missile strikes on Russian army command posts in Donetsk on Aug. 26 killed more Russian officers than in any other single attack during the war, independent monitors claim.
Mediazona, an independent Russian outlet that tracks Russian military deaths in collaboration with the BBC Russian Service, identified 20 officers killed in the attack.
Each of the dead Russian officers was identified by name, age, and rank by Mediazona. Seven colonels, six lieutenant colonels, five majors, one captain, and one senior lieutenant were killed in the strikes, which hit the headquarters of the Central Military District and the 41st Combined Arms Army in occupied Donetsk.
According to Mediazona, 18 of the Russian officers died immediately in the missile strike, while two succumbed to their injuries.
Denis Pushilin, the head of the Russian illegal occupation administration in Donetsk Oblast, confirmed in a post on Telegram that Ukraine had launched an attack on targets in Donetsk on Aug. 26, claiming that Anglo-French "Storm Shadow" air-launched cruise missiles were used, and that eight civilians were injured.
Mediazona also identified two other instances of "mass casualties" amongst staff officers of the 41st Combined Arms Army, according to their research, eight officers were killed on Aug. 4, with an additional four killed on Sept 8, 2025.
At least 276,113 Russian soldiers have been killed in Ukraine since 2022, according to Mediazona, which tracks individuals killed by searching through obituaries, posts on Russian social media networks, and leaked Russian databases.

articles.title: Iran's IRGC strikes tanker and threatens to target vessels beyond Hormuz
articles.body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard warned that vessels “violating” its designated routes would be pursued and "punished" anywhere in the region, as maritime agencies reported two further strikes on commercial ships in the Persian Gulf.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed responsibility on Friday for setting an oil tanker ablaze in the Strait of Hormuz and threatened to pursue vessels it deems in violation beyond the strait and across the wider region, as maritime security agencies reported two further strikes on commercial ships in the Persian Gulf.
The IRGC Navy said it targeted the engine room and propulsion system of the MV Sun Shine, a tanker belonging to the company Natwit, after the vessel attempted to use what it described as an unauthorised route through the strait's southern section. The attack caused a fire on board.
In a statement, the IRGC warned that action against "violating" vessels would no longer be confined to the Strait of Hormuz and that any ship using what it deems unauthorised routes would be pursued and "punished" anywhere in the region.
Companies it accuses of co-operating with the US would be sanctioned and all their vessels targeted, it added.
The IRGC laid blame for the incidents in the strait on the US military, accusing Washington of interfering in the decisions of shipping and insurance companies and paying "large bribes" to induce compliance.
"Direct responsibility for these incidents and the escalation of tensions in maritime transport in the region lies with the aggressive US army," the statement said.
Tehran's Friday prayer leader separately told his weekly sermon that the strait would remain closed until Iran's conditions were fully met.
Hojjatoleslam Mohammad Javad Ali-Akbari said Iran had set out "seven conditions" and would decide its next steps once they were met, adding that military readiness had improved, weak points had been addressed, and Iran's strategy had shifted from defence to offence.
Iran has said it controls the Strait of Hormuz and will not permit military forces from hostile countries in the area, vowing to respond "decisively" to any attempt to disrupt its management of the strait.
Lanes clear, CENTCOM says
US Central Command said on Friday it had cleared the strait's main shipping lanes, removed naval mines from principal transit routes, and declared them open to all vessels not in violation of US maritime sanctions against Iran.
Thousands of commercial ships had passed through safely as a result, CENTCOM said.
The competing claims came as the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre reported that an LPG carrier was struck by unknown projectiles on Friday morning, 13 nautical miles west of Al-Jazira in the United Arab Emirates, causing a major fire that was later brought under control.
UKMTO had reported the previous day that an oil tanker north of Qatari waters was struck by several projectiles resulting in casualties, in the first such attack in six months.
In a separate incident on Thursday, the maritime intelligence company Vanguard reported that a tanker had caught fire roughly 40 kilometres off Fujairah in the Gulf of Oman, identifying the vessel as probably the Dalkut, sailing under the Marshall Islands flag.
At least 12 attacks, attempted attacks or harassment incidents targeting oil tankers and gas carriers were recorded in the strait between 28 September and 5 October, the highest weekly figure since the war began on 28 February, according to media reports.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments normally pass, has been effectively closed since the outbreak of the war, following Iranian missile and drone strikes on commercial vessels and a US Navy blockade of Iranian ports.
The latest data indicate that oil exports from other countries in the region, excluding Iran, have returned to pre-war levels in recent days.

articles.title: Trump announces Russian diesel deal amid soaring US fuel prices
articles.body:
Trump announces Russian diesel deal amid soaring US fuel prices
Russia to supply 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by 1.5 million more, as prices soar amid the Iran war.
United States President Donald Trump said that Russia has agreed to supply 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to global markets amid discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the American and global marketplace, another 500,000 tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 tons immediately thereafter,” Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform.
The president added that Russia would deliver an additional 3 million tonnes of fuel “within a short period of time”. He said that the country would supply 500,000 tonnes in November.
An envoy for Russian President Vladimir Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, praised cooperation between Russia and the United States on diesel and energy in a post on X shortly after.
“Russia-US cooperation on diesel and energy will benefit the world,” Dmitriev wrote on X.
Putin-Trump call
The Kremlin said Putin told Trump in a phone call on Friday that Russia was ready “to supply oil” to the US and world markets.
“The Russian side reaffirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and world markets,” the Kremlin said regarding the talks.
The Kremlin said the call between Putin and Trump, which lasted an hour and half, covered large-scale economic initiatives, including Russian fuel supplies.
The read-out from Moscow said Trump welcomed Russia’s involvement in efforts to settle the war with Iran.
Earlier this week, Putin met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan and told him Russia would “do everything” to help end the war, Russian news agencies reported.
In a call on Wednesday, Putin told Pezeshkian that Moscow was prepared to mediate, according to Iran’s IRNA news agency.
Putin told Trump that Russia would consider when to resume peace talks, the Kremlin said. It added that both leaders were interested in taking part in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China in November.
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Trump warmly congratulated Putin on his birthday during the call and wished him success and wellbeing.
Petrol price pressures
The deal comes despite Ukrainian air strikes, which have taken more than half of the country’s oil refining capacity offline, according to claims made by Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence on Sunday.
The latest announcement comes a week after the G7 countries agreed to release 100 million barrels amid pressure from the White House.
The move also comes as prices of diesel, used in agriculture, heating homes and trucking goods, are near record highs ahead of the November 3 congressional elections that will determine control of Congress.
Diesel prices have been elevated in recent months but have started to decline. The average price for a gallon is $6.27 ($1.66 per litre), according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. That’s down $0.10 from this time last week, but up $5.94 from this time one month ago.
Diesel prices, which can drive inflation, are up 70 percent since the US and Israel’s war on Iran began this year, despite two high-profile recent moves by Trump to boost supplies of the fuel: pressuring allies to release emergency reserves and expanding access to tax-exempt red-dyed diesel, which is normally used for farm equipment.
The wars in Iran and Ukraine have triggered an unprecedented global fuel supply crunch.

articles.title: Drone attack on Erbil renews Kurdish fears over Iran War fallout
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Drone attack on Erbil camp renews Kurdish fears over Iran War fallout
Two explosive-laden drones targeted a camp housing Iranian Kurdish refugees near Erbil on Thursday night, raising fresh concerns about security in Iraq's Kurdistan Region following the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces and their air defence systems.
The Kurdistan Region's Counter-Terrorism Service said the attack took place at 22:19 local time in the Kawergosk area of Khabat district, west of Erbil, the regional capital. No casualties were reported.
Local reports said the drones caused material damage near the site, although other accounts suggested they had crashed in an uninhabited area. The extent of the damage remains unclear, and no group has claimed responsibility.
The attack follows more than a month of relative calm in Erbil and has renewed concerns over the region's vulnerability to drone strikes, particularly after US-led coalition forces withdrew their air defence systems at the end of September.
Kurdish officials have repeatedly called for stronger air defences and greater coordination with the federal government in Baghdad, which holds primary responsibility for protecting Iraqi airspace.
A captain in the Kurdish Peshmerga forces told The New Arab that the latest attack highlighted the urgent need for air defence systems capable of intercepting drones, a role previously carried out by the international coalition.
"The renewed attacks make it necessary to accelerate the provision of air defence systems capable of dealing with drones," the officer said, speaking on condition of anonymity. He added that surveillance and interception measures alone could not provide sufficient protection without dedicated defensive capabilities.
The officer suggested the attack could be linked to Iran, citing the nature of targets struck in previous incidents. However, there has been no official confirmation of responsibility for Thursday's attack.
The Kurdistan Region has faced repeated drone and missile attacks in recent months amid escalating tensions involving Iran, the United States and Israel. Iranian Kurdish opposition groups and associated refugee camps have been among the targets.
Earlier attacks have also affected areas of Erbil and Sulaimaniyah provinces, with Kurdish security authorities reporting the interception of drones targeting civilian and military sites. Some strikes blamed on Iran have killed members of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups based in northern Iraq.
The latest incident comes shortly after the US-led coalition completed its military withdrawal from Iraq under an agreement reached between Baghdad and Washington in 2024.
Coalition forces previously operated air defence systems in the Kurdistan Region that intercepted incoming drones and missiles. Kurdish political and military leaders had warned before the withdrawal that removing those systems without providing replacements would leave the region exposed to further attacks.
The Kurdistan Regional Government has argued that its airspace forms part of Iraq's national airspace and that the federal government must take responsibility for its protection.
Ali al-Harki, a member of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), told The New Arab that the renewed attacks threatened civilians and placed further pressure on the region's security arrangements.
"There is an urgent need for Baghdad to assert its authority over Iraqi airspace and take security measures to prevent further attacks," he said.
"Kurdistan's security is part of Iraq's security, and the Baghdad government cannot distance itself from the responsibility it must assume for protecting the country's airspace."
The attack has also raised concerns about the safety of refugee families living in camps across the region, particularly those associated with Iranian Kurdish opposition groups that have previously been targeted.
Those concerns have grown following the departure of US forces and their defensive equipment from Erbil, which has left regional authorities seeking alternative arrangements to protect civilian areas and critical infrastructure.
With the perpetrators of Thursday's attack still unidentified, Kurdish officials are pressing Baghdad to strengthen air defence capabilities and improve coordination between the Iraqi military and the Peshmerga to prevent further strikes.

articles.title: Finland to deliver F-16 ammunition to Ukraine in coming days – Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukraine will receive ammunition for F-16 fighter jets in the coming days as part of the assistance package to help protect Ukrainian skies from Finland, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced following a conversation with Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
"We'll receive ammunition for our F-16s in the coming days. This is what's currently enabling us to shoot down jet-powered," Zelenskyy wrote on the social network X.
He said that he briefed Stubb on the latest Russian strikes. The sides also discussed a new challenge: additional revenue for Russia from petroleum product exports, which can be used to finance further Russian aggression.
"We're preparing meetings and coordinating steps that can be useful under the current circumstances," Zelenskyy said.
The President of Ukraine thanked Stubb for support and underlined the importance that we continue working together to protect people and limit Russia's ability to wage this horrific war.

articles.title: Putin tells Trump Russia would 'supply oil' to US, global markets; Zelenskyy slams deal
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has said his country was ready to "supply oil" to the US and world markets during his phone call with US counterpart Donald Trump, the Kremlin said.
Trump announced earlier on Friday that the Russian leader had agreed to release diesel fuel to the US and world markets.
"The Russian side reaffirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and world markets," the Kremlin said in its account of the talks between the leaders.
Russian deputy prime minister in charge of energy Alexander Novak said Moscow was ready to supply the American market with 300,000 tonnes of diesel from October, 500,000 tonnes in November and one million tonnes in December, matching the terms outlined earlier by Trump.
"In the long run, this volume could reach three million tons per month," he told Russian news agencies.
'Unworthy of our partners'
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy immediately slammed the offer.
"It is certainly not honest, it is certainly unworthy of our partners, and it is, in my view, a weak decision," he told reporters.
He said this would mean "extra money for the Russian war" against Ukraine, adding that "it only fuels Putin and gives him the opportunity to wage an even more intense war."
He said the Ukrainian team meeting with Trump's envoys in Florida on Friday and Saturday had "simply served as a front" for this agreement with Moscow.
According to the Kremlin, Putin and Trump also discussed the "settlement of the Ukrainian crisis, the situation surrounding Iran, as well as various aspects of bilateral relations", during their call.
Shortly after Trump's call with Putin, the US Treasury Department said on X that its Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) was "immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28, prompting Tehran to respond with missile and drone attacks across the region and effectively close the Strait of Hormuz.
The conflict has continued for more than seven months, driving up global energy prices as commercial oil traffic through the strategic waterway has effectively halted.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June after Pakistan and Qatar mediated to halt hostilities and pave the way for negotiations.
Implementation of the agreement has since stalled amid disagreements, including over security and navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Wicker Rejects Territorial Concessions to End War in Ukraine
articles.body:
US Senator Roger Wicker, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said on Friday, Oct. 9, that he cannot envision an end to the war in Ukraine that involves Kyiv ceding sovereign territory seized by Russia.
Speaking at a press conference in Kyiv, the senior Republican lawmaker affirmed that Russian President Vladimir Putin will not succeed in defeating the Ukrainian people, even as Moscow seeks to weaponize the upcoming winter to break civilian resilience, Interfax-Ukraine reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Vladimir Putin will not be able to defeat the Ukrainian people this year or next year. If we allow it, he can make the lives of Ukrainians miserable, and I think that is precisely what he wants,” Wicker told reporters, as reported by Interfax-Ukraine.
Wicker noted that Ukraine faces another challenging winter following severe Russian infrastructure bombardments over the past year. He warned that Russian forces are deliberately expanding targeting parameters beyond electricity and district heating networks to include water supply systems.
“We do not know how difficult the conditions will be, but the Russian dictator’s goal is to make people’s lives miserable,” Wicker said. “In addition to blackouts and the lack of heating and electricity, we understand that Vladimir Putin also aims to strike the water supply system to further compound people’s suffering.”
The senator stressed that while Ukrainians do not seek prolonged hardship, they remain determined to resist Russian aggression.
Putin Touts 90% Dollar-Free CIS Trade as Russia Sidesteps Western Sanctions
“Given the events of recent years and current circumstances, I do not see an end to the war that involves the Ukrainian people giving up their sovereign territory seized as a result of an invasion that violates international law,” Wicker said.
Trump diesel pact
Wicker’s rejection of territorial concessions coincides with growing scrutiny in Kyiv and European capitals over Washington’s diplomatic posture toward Moscow.
On Friday, Oct. 9, US-led peace talks held in Miami – bringing together US, Ukrainian, and European officials alongside representatives of Britain, France, Germany, the European Commission, and NATO – concluded after a single six-hour session without a announced breakthrough.
US special envoy Steve Witkoff characterized the discussions as constructive, noting that delegates examined avenues to de-escalate and conclude the conflict ahead of winter.
However, the Miami consultations were overshadowed by US President Donald Trump’s announcement of an agreement with Putin to permit Russian diesel shipments to American and global markets.
Trump confirmed that Russia would supply over 300,000 metric tons of diesel immediately, followed by another 500,000 tons in November, prompting the US Treasury Department to issue a temporary sanctions waiver.
President Volodymyr Zelensky and lawmakers from both parties in Washington criticized the transaction, warning that easing economic restrictions and purchasing Russian petroleum products provides fresh financial revenue for Moscow’s war apparatus while peace delegations were actively negotiating.

articles.title: ‘Medieval’ and ‘disturbing’: US plan to livestream execution elicits global condemnation
articles.body:
The US is facing worldwide condemnation over a “barbaric” plan to execute a disabled man by firing squad and livestream it to the public, with critics comparing the Trump administration to dictatorships in Iran and Afghanistan.
The Pentagon confirmed on Thursday that the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at a military base at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, would be livestreamed on 3 December.
The United Nations’ office of the high commissioner for human rights warned on Friday that broadcasting the killing would amount to a public execution and “breach the absolute prohibition of torture”.
The plan also drew opprobrium from politicians, religious leaders and human rights advocates in the US and abroad. Hillary Clinton, the former US secretary of state, wrote on social media: “A barbaric idea, beneath our dignity as a country. Push back on this.”
Yassamin Ansari, the first Iranian American Democrat elected to the US Congress, posted: “In Trump’s America, we’re doing public executions now. WTF. This is what happens under brutal dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan. It’s all part of Trump’s authoritarian takeover of the United States.”
Britain, which abolished the death penalty in the 1960s, moved to distance itself from the execution. Bridget Phillipson, the UK’s equalities minister and Labour party chair, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that she found the concept “rather disturbing”.
Phillipson stressed that the decision was a matter for the US government, adding: “They are a close ally. Does that mean that we support everything the US government does? No.”
Under US military law, a president must approve an execution by firing squad. Trump did so on the recommendation of his defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, according to the Pentagon.
JD Vance – a practicing Catholic – told reporters on Friday he wouldn’t watch the livestreamed execution of Hasan, but stopped short of criticizing the administration’s decision.
When asked how his Christian beliefs influence his view of the public execution, Vance dismissed controversy about the manner of execution and appeared to question whether the livestream will happen.
“Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope the people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” the US vice-president told reporters. “That said, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it.”
Hegseth gleefully confirmed the livestream plan after previously saying that the execution would be public. Speaking to the conservative broadcaster Real America’s Voice, he said people should be able to watch because they need to understand that there were “serious consequences” for such crimes.
Asked whether Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”
Now 56, Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 after being convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. Twelve of those killed and 30 of the wounded were soldiers.
The former army psychiatrist opened fire with a handgun at a medical facility at Fort Hood on 5 November 2009 as soldiers waited for medical checks before deployment. He was shot by a police officer during his arrest and left partly paralysed, and now uses a wheelchair.
The execution is expected to be the first by firing squad carried out by the US military since 1945, when army private Eddie Slovik was executed for desertion during the second world war. The last US military execution of any kind took place in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged.
Hasan’s case comes amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the US following the botched lethal injection of Tennessee death-row prisoner Christa Pike last week. Her lawyers said she awoke in hospital “angry and confused” and remained seriously ill and shackled to her hospital bed.
Media have sought to televise US executions in the past, but have been blocked by the courts. No other country is known to televise or livestream legal executions, experts said.
Indeed, public executions have largely disappeared around the world. Amnesty International recorded at least 17 in 2025, including 11 in Iran and six in Taliban-run Afghanistan.
In the US, executions have been conducted privately for about nine decades. The hanging of Rainey Bethea in Kentucky in 1936, witnessed by thousands, is generally regarded as the country’s last public execution, although another hanging took place in Missouri the following year.
Experts said there was no known precedent for livestreaming a legal execution. The execution of the Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh in 2001 was made available to victims’ relatives through closed-circuit television, but was not broadcast publicly.
The proposed live stream has prompted criticism from religious leaders. Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, said it was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”.
Politicians from both sides of the aisle also spoke out. Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives armed services committee, said the plan was “disturbing and makes a mockery of our legal system”. The Democratic senator Chris Murphy described public executions as “medieval”.
The Republican senator Thom Tillis said Hasan should face the death penalty but that broadcasting his execution was “beyond disgusting”, arguing that public executions were associated with oppressive regimes.
Others warned that the spectacle would be counterproductive and act as a recruiting sergeant for US enemies seeking fresh propaganda.
Ned Price, a former deputy to the US representative to the United Nations, posted on X: “You can take it from those of us who’ve spent years working on terrorism: the surest way to spawn more radicalized zealots is to glorify violence, embrace a cult of death, and create a martyr for the cause.
“Or take it from [al-Qaida] and ISIS, whose tactics offer the closest modern-day approximation of Hegseth’s proposal. Either way, it’s hard to conjure a more vivid example of his trademark performative bravado, which routinely damages America’s image and, in this case, so ghoulishly leaves us more vulnerable.”
Some experts have raised questions about whether the live stream could be challenged in court. Eugene Fidell, a military law specialist at Yale Law School, said Hasan could seek legal action to block the public display of his death.
Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at the University of California, Berkeley, said the announcement raised serious questions about the dignity of the condemned prisoner and the government’s motivation for staging such an unusual spectacle.
“This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” she told the Associated Press.
Justin Mazzola, deputy director of research at Amnesty International USA, said: “Livestreaming the taking of a life by firing squad would only compound the cruelty of the death penalty and perpetuate the cycle of violence that the authorities purportedly seek to end.
“This announcement adds to the display of cruelty that we have just witnessed in the senseless pursuit of the execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee. The US death penalty is irredeemably broken. It is high time that the US authorities, at all levels, use their power to show human rights leadership and end this ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment once and for all.”
Other experts argued that public access could increase transparency around capital punishment. Deborah Denno, a death penalty specialist at Fordham University, told the AP that a live stream could make the process more transparent at a time when the botched execution in Tennessee had renewed questions about how the state puts prisoners to death.
It remains unclear whether Hasan will seek to challenge his execution in civilian court, a move that could significantly delay the proceedings.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: US used meeting with us to strike deal with Putin behind our backs
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: US used meeting with us to strike deal with Putin behind our backs
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused US President Donald Trump's team of acting dishonestly by inviting a Ukrainian delegation to talks in the United States before striking a deal with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin behind its back to lift sanctions on Russian diesel.
Source: Zelenskyy in a telephone interview with Axios
Details: Zelenskyy said that a few days ago, US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff proposed a meeting in Florida to discuss new American ideas for ending the war. However, during talks between the Ukrainian delegation and Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the US side did not once suggest that it was considering a deal with Russia to purchase millions of tonnes of diesel fuel.
It was only an hour before Trump's official announcement that the Ukrainian negotiators were informed that the US president planned to speak to Putin and lift sanctions. Zelenskyy stressed that this was unfair to Ukraine.
Quote: "Steve proposed to meet in Florida. And of course I accepted to go there and speak about the possibilities of negotiations. The Americans said they have some ideas and we agreed to come to discuss.
It's not honest, really, because we tried to build our relations in the best way. It looks like that they used this opportunity to meet us from one side, and from the other side called Putin and negotiate this."
Details: Zelenskyy stressed that he would support easing energy sanctions only in exchange for an energy ceasefire. Instead, he said, the current situation demonstrated US weakness, as Washington had secured no concessions in return.
Quote: "What did [Trump] get? That he will have more diesel? For whom? More Russian diesel for Americans? It shows weakness of the world. It looks like Alaska No. 2.
You know, it looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible."
Details: Zelenskyy also suggested that Trump's representatives were trying to secure another visit to Moscow through the agreement.
Quote: "If you allow them to export diesel, and you think before that you have to go to Russia to negotiate, it looks that you are buying this meeting. Maybe I'm not right. But it looks this way. Otherwise, why do it?"
Details: Zelenskyy said he plans to obtain a full briefing from the Ukrainian negotiating team to establish whether the agreement is connected to the planned visit to Russia by Trump's envoys.
Despite his anger, Zelenskyy refrained from stating that Ukraine would reject US mediation. He stressed that "we need the Americans to try to stop this war".
Background:
- On the evening of 9 October, Trump said he had spoken by phone with Putin and agreed on supplies of millions of tonnes of Russian diesel to US and global markets.
- The US Department of the Treasury, through its Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), issued General Licence No. 135, authorising transactions involving the sale, delivery, unloading and import of Russian-origin diesel fuel into the US until 17 April 2027.
- Zelenskyy strongly criticised Trump's actions, describing the easing of sanctions as an "absolutely terrible" move. He stressed that this "happy birthday present for Putin" will provide Russia with billions more to continue the war.
- Zelenskyy said Ukraine's negotiating team in the US was being used as "cover" while Trump and Putin reached agreements on fuel supplies.
- Following his conversation with Trump, Putin confirmed that Russia is ready to supply petroleum products to the US and global markets. He also expressed hope for continued cooperation between the two countries.
