articles.title: Saudi Arabia says three killed at airport as Yemen war expands
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia says three killed at airport as Yemen war expands
Saudi Arabia said on Friday that three people including a pilot were killed in attacks on Riyadh international airport the day before when Yemen's Houthis claimed hits on the facility.
Houthi media reported on Friday that Saudi attacks on Sanaa airport killed two people, while the civil defence agency in the Yemeni capital reported extinguishing fires caused by Saudi strikes, including one that it said destroyed a factory.
The conflict between the Iran-backed Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognised government -- supported by Saudi Arabia -- surged in July, and has since spilled over into the neighbouring kingdom.
In addition to seizing territory along the Red Sea coast in Yemen, the Houthis have attacked transport hubs, oil facilities and other civilian targets in the world's largest crude exporter with drones and missiles.
The Saudi civil aviation authority said two attacks on Thursday on Riyadh airport and a Saudia airlines plane had "resulted in the martyrdom of three citizens".
The national carrier confirmed the death of the aircraft's captain.
The attacks on the Saudi capital forced diplomats stationed there to shelter in place and international schools to take safety measures, as explosions echoed across the city on Thursday.
Numerous flights at Riyadh airport were delayed or cancelled, and the civil defence agency said missile "interception debris" had damaged a kindergarten and a medical complex in the city.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree on Friday appeared to suggest that planes would need to seek the group's permission to fly in or out of Riyadh.
"Humanitarian flights to and from Riyadh Airport will be permitted for all flights authorised" by a Houthi coordinating body in Sanaa, he wrote on X.
'Advances are limited'
Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government forces it supports have struggled to reverse the Houthis' advance, despite a counter-offensive aimed at recapturing territory including the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, which is crucial to global shipping.
While a Saudi diplomat said on Friday that Saudi-backed forces had retaken the area, a military source on the ground gave a conflicting account, saying fighting was ongoing.
The Yemeni military source told AFP that government forces had launched a "major operation" in the strait region, supported by Saudi air power, but added that "fighting is fierce and advances are limited".
Houthi-affiliated media, meanwhile, said an attack by government forces south of the strait had been repelled.
A regional source told AFP on Friday that Saudi Arabia would not bow to the Houthis' "military blackmail" and would not agree to a truce until the Yemeni government regained all the territory it lost in recent weeks.
The Houthis' Al-Massirah TV channel reported fresh Saudi strikes on Sanaa, shortly after a large demonstration in support of the group in the city.
The raids targeted military positions far from residential neighbourhoods, according to an AFP correspondent.
The Houthis, whose heartlands are among the Zaidi Shia Muslims in the northwest, had already controlled the capital Sanaa and most of Yemen's major population centres since the start of the war in 2014.
Riyadh's military coalition intervened to support the government the following year.
Evacuation warning
After declaring the start of their counter-offensive against the Houthis, Yemen's government claimed to have pushed the fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea coast and the port city of Mocha.
But the Houthis insist they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by AFP have not reported any major changes on the ground.
The Houthis have warned workers to evacuate Saudi Arabia's oil facilities, having days before hit a major refinery south of the capital.
Admissions by Saudi authorities of civilian targets being hit are relatively rare. There have been few statements on Houthi attacks in recent weeks.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
In Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, ordinary civilians are paying the price for the renewed fighting, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.

articles.title: US eases Russian diesel sanctions after Trump-Putin deal
articles.body:
The United States has temporarily eased sanctions on Russian diesel after President Donald Trump announced a supply agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin, drawing criticism from Ukraine that the move would help Moscow prolong the war.
The Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control issued a license on Oct. 9 authorizing the sale, delivery and import of Russian diesel, including shipments to the United States, until April 7, 2027.
Trump said on Truth Social that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons to U.S. and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons immediately afterward.
A further 3 million tons would follow, depending on the condition of Russian refineries, he said.
Trump predicted the supplies would bring down diesel prices, saying relief for American farmers, ranchers and truckers was a priority.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow would immediately begin lifting its own diesel export restrictions ahead of schedule.
He told TASS that exports could reach 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons in December, potentially rising to nearly 3 million tons a month later.
Putin separately confirmed Russia’s readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to U.S. and global markets, saying the shipments would benefit the world economy.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky criticized the agreement, arguing that easing sanctions without a clear and lasting agreement to reduce hostilities would give Russia more resources to continue fighting.
“Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged,” he wrote on social media.
Zelensky said Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries were a response to attacks on its energy infrastructure. Kiev was ready to halt those strikes if Moscow stopped targeting Ukrainian energy facilities, he said, urging Washington to broker a reciprocal agreement.
Asked about Zelensky’s criticism before departing the White House, Trump said the United States remained a strong partner of Ukraine. He also thanked Putin for the diesel agreement.

articles.title: Flight cancelled to Saudi capital Riyadh over Houthi attacks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Flight cancellations hit Saudi capital Riyadh amid Houthi attacks
Airlines have cancelled flights to Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and countries have issued warnings against travel to the country as Houthi ballistic missile attacks continue to target the kingdom's airports, leading to numerous casualties.
Among the airlines that have suspended flights are Lufthansa, which said that flights to Riyadh were suspended through to 16 October due to "current developments in the Middle East".
India's Indigo has also cancelled its flights to the city until 9 October, while Air India and Alaska Air have suspended flights until 10 October, according to Reuters.
Alongside airlines, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) announced on Friday that it has expanded the airspace within Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi attacks.
"These recurrent missile and drone attacks, together with the activation of air defence systems, create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft, as well as risks associated with missile and drone overflights, interception activity and falling debris," the agency warned.
EASA warned that while southern and south-western parts of Saudi airspace "remain particularly exposed," Riyadh, Tabuk, Medina and Yanbu were also flagged as risks for airlines.
The membership-based organisation OPSGROUP also issued its own warning against flying to Saudi Arabia on Friday.
The warnings against flying to Saudi Arabia come as the war in Yemen continues to escalate following a Houthi offensive launched in Taiz province in September.
On Sunday, Yemen's government announced a general offensive nationwide aimed at retaking the capital Sanaa, with Saudi Arabia providing airpower to support the campaign.
As part of the escalation, the Houthis have launched drone and ballistic missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, initially against energy installations, though this has escalated to the targeting of airports in the country.
This includes Riyadh airport, where Houthi attacks killed three people on Thursday, and a Saudia Airlines plane was also destroyed.
Saudia Airlines issued an obituary for one of their employees, a pilot, who was killed in an attack on Thursday.
The Houthis launched follow-up attacks on Friday, with their spokesperson posting on X that "humanitarian flights to/from Riyadh Airport will be permitted for all flights authorised by the Humanitarian Operations Coordination Center based in the capital Sana'a."
Flights to the airport continued throughout the day, despite strikes and Houthi threats.
Alongside flight cancellations, several countries warned their citizens to exercise caution when travelling to the country, including the UK’s Foreign and Commonwealth Development Office, which issued advice against all but essential travel to Aseer province, Riyadh province, Najran province, Jizan province, and Taif City and Taif International Airport.
Alongside the UK, both Japan and the US also issued travel warnings to Saudi Arabia amid the escalation.

articles.title: Major Drone Attack Paralyzes Moscow Airports, Flights Delayed
articles.body:
A major wave of Ukrainian strike drones targeted the Moscow region early Saturday morning, Oct. 10, prompting severe aviation restrictions that delayed or canceled hundreds of commercial flights across the Russian capital’s major international airports.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin claimed that Russian air defenses intercepted 403 unmanned aerial vehicles directed toward the capital region between 8:30 p.m. local time on Friday and 8:30 a.m. on Saturday.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Sobyanin stated that the vast majority of incoming drones were neutralized on distant approaches to the capital, while 25 were shot down within the immediate airspace approaching Moscow.
Russian monitoring networks and Ukrainian observers described the overnight assault as one of the largest coordinated drone operations directed against the Russian capital since the start of the full-scale war.
The drone barrage triggered temporary ground stops and flight restrictions across Moscow’s primary civil aviation hubs, with the most severe disruptions recorded at Vnukovo and Sheremetyevo, alongside secondary delays at Domodedovo.
Russia’s federal air transport agency, Rosaviatsiya, confirmed that flight suspensions were lifted at 8:50 a.m. local time, though airlines continued adjusting schedules throughout Saturday morning to clear mounting flight backlogs.
Estimates regarding the scale of the disruption varied across civil aviation tracking monitors.
Yabloko Leader Fined Over Anti-War Slogans on Duma Ballots
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported that approximately 300 scheduled commercial flights experienced cancellations or prolonged delays, while Russian regional news outlet MSK1 reported that at least 370 flights were delayed across the metropolitan airport cluster.
Systematic pressure on Moscow’s air corridors
The disruption across Moscow’s civil aviation network reflects an expanding Ukrainian operational campaign designed to degrade Russian rear logistics, overwhelm metropolitan air defense coverage, and impose tangible economic costs on the Russian heartland.
By forcing civil aviation authorities to repeatedly activate emergency air closure protocols – designated in Russian aviation procedures as the “Kover” (Carpet) plan – recurrent drone incursions disrupt commercial passenger operations, divert long-haul freight traffic, and strain radar tracking architectures deployed around the Russian capital.
The overnight strikes on the capital region coincide with wider Ukrainian precision strikes targeting Russian strategic logistical nodes and fuel infrastructure.
Overnight into Saturday, Ukrainian strike drones struck the Yug Rusi oil transshipment terminal in Rostov-on-Don, igniting a major fire at an export and military supply hub handling 2.5 million metric tons of petroleum products annually.
Consecutive strikes on Russian tech and data infrastructure
The overnight assault on Moscow follows consecutive Ukrainian drone strikes targeting foundational Russian digital and communications infrastructure in adjacent regions.
On Friday, Oct. 9, Ukrainian strike drones damaged a major data center belonging to Russian technology corporation Yandex in the regional capital of Kaluga, located southwest of Moscow.
Yandex confirmed that several hardware modules were completely disabled, warning users that disruptions to its search, ride-hailing, cloud storage, and corporate digital ecosystems could occur while technical teams assess physical damage.
Kaluga Regional Governor Vladislav Shapsha reported that the Oct. 9 drone waves injured nine people across the province, with five hospitalized following impacts in residential and industrial zones.
The Kaluga strike marked the second consecutive day of precision attacks targeting Yandex’s server infrastructure. On Thursday, Oct. 8, Ukrainian drones hit another Yandex data center situated in Sasovo within the Ryazan region, forcing a complete operational shutdown of the installation.
The resulting server outage produced cascading disruptions across major corporate networks and public services dependent on Yandex cloud hosting, including booking systems operated by Russian Railways (RZhD), mobile network operator MegaFon, and several national media organizations.
The compounding infrastructure damage prompted Yandex shares to drop roughly 4 percent on the Moscow Exchange.

articles.title: Zelenskyy, Estonia's Defense Minister discuss implementation of drone deal, new contributions to PURL
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met in Kyiv with Estonian Defense Minister Martin Herem, with whom he discussed possibilities for new contributions to the PURL program and the search for additional funding for the procurement of air defense systems, as well as the implementation of the "drone deal," according to the president's press service.
"The drone deal has opened up opportunities for exports from our country to yours. We are ready to discuss drones, electronic warfare systems, and other equipment we have," Zelenskyy said during the meeting.
According to the president, Estonia could receive proven weapons, while Ukraine could receive additional funds for its defense. The head of state and the Estonian defense minister agreed that teams from both countries would work promptly to finalize the details of such an export package.
Herem assured that Estonia will continue its military support for Ukraine. He also spoke about his trips to Ukraine and praised the courage of Ukrainians in defending their values.
"This year, I have visited many places in Ukraine. Usually, our citizens only see war on television. But I have seen with my own eyes your courage and how you stand up for your values," the minister said.
During the meeting, Zelenskyy and Herem also discussed Ukraine's European integration. The president thanked Estonia for its support of Ukraine's accession to the European Union.
In addition, the parties discussed the security situation in the region, Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure, Ukraine's preparations for the winter, and cooperation between the two countries' militaries.

articles.title: Germany Concerned About Threat Russian Satellites Pose to Starlink
articles.body:
The ability of Russian satellites to perform coordinated active maneuvers raises concerns about a potential attack on Starlink satellites.
Major General Michael Traut, commander of the German Space Command, spoke about this in an interview with Reuters.
According to him, in May 2026, a group of Russian military satellites tracked a Western satellite assisting Ukraine, demonstrating capabilities that could threaten commercial satellite constellations.
General Traut stated that a direct attack on a Starlink satellite would constitute a significant escalation, but Moscow could employ gray zone tactics.
He described a hypothetical scenario in which a Russian satellite would shift into Starlink’s orbital path and then break up into debris. This would force the satellites to perform evasive maneuvers, consuming fuel and potentially shortening their operational lifespan.
According to the U.S. Space Force, in May, Russia maneuvered four military satellites — Cosmos 2610–2613 — bringing them closer to a commercial radar imaging satellite operated by the Finnish company ICEYE.
ICEYE CEO Rafal Modzewski told Reuters that the company subsequently changed the position of its satellite, after which the Russian satellites performed additional maneuvers.
According to him, this incident demonstrated that satellites are increasingly likely to maneuver close to one another to observe or potentially cause damage. Modzewski noted that this incident underscores the need to monitor activity in orbit and raises questions about the need for protection.
According to Western military officials, Russia’s interference with Western space systems has significantly intensified since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
They note that this includes jamming via ground-based assets and in-orbit surveillance to gather intelligence and test the West’s limits of tolerance.
In early September, the U.S. simulated a Russian nuclear explosion in space and its impact on satellites. The simulation shows that the radiation belt created by the explosion could cause 11,000 satellites to fail within a week.
Separately, the authors suggest that Moscow could use a space-based nuclear threat against Starlink to force Washington or SpaceX to limit their support for Ukraine.

articles.title: Head of Russian military propaganda network to be expelled from Montenegro over suspected anti-EU operation
articles.body:
Montenegro has ordered the expulsion of Mikhail Zvynchuk, head of the pro-Kremlin military information network Rybar, and four other Russian citizens over national security concerns following a security operation targeting suspected Russian hybrid influence activities, Vijesti reported on 9 October.
Zvynchuk is the founder and head of Rybar, a prominent Russian military-focused information network known for its Telegram channels covering Russia's war against Ukraine. The network promotes pro-Kremlin narratives and has been associated with Russian propaganda and influence operations.
Montenegrin police announced on 9 October that the five Russians had their residence rights revoked and were ordered to leave the country on national and internal security grounds.
Montenegro investigates suspected Russian hybrid activity
The operation involved Montenegro's police and National Security Agency (ANB), which seized drones, high-resolution recording equipment, cameras, and several mobile phones for further examination, according to Vijesti.
According to Montenegrin authorities, the five had arrived in the country less than two days before the operation. The investigation is being conducted with support from international partners.
Montenegrin police identified the five Russian citizens as Zvynchuk, his wife Valeria Zvynchuk, Sergei Belous, Pavel Lekatorchuk, and Kira Doroshenko. Authorities said the case had been referred to prosecutors in Podgorica and Kotor.
The European Union has sanctioned Zvynchuk over activities that undermine or threaten Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence. He has also been sanctioned by the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Australia, and Ukraine, according to Vijesti.
Suspected influence operation targeting EU integration
Vijesti reported, citing security sources, that Montenegrin authorities suspected the group of planning a documentary intended to undermine public support for the country's European integration.
According to the outlet, the planned material would portray Montenegro's expected alignment of its visa policy with EU standards as a politically imposed measure that threatens tourism, economic stability, and national interests.
Security services had monitored the group's arrival before carrying out the operation in Risan, in the Bay of Kotor area, Vijesti reported. The equipment seized from the group will undergo expert analysis to establish its intended purpose and use in Montenegro.
Medvedev threatens imprisoning “European and American idiots” for prisoner exchanges
Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev responded to the operation by suggesting Moscow might need to expand its pool of prisoners to exchange for Europeans and Americans to secure Zvynchuk's return.
“We will probably have to replenish our pool of prisoners for exchange with European and American idiots,” Medvedev said, according to Vijesti.
Montenegro, a NATO member and EU candidate, has aligned itself with EU sanctions against Russia following Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The expulsion comes amid broader European concerns over Russian intelligence activity, propaganda, and other forms of hybrid interference.

articles.title: Electronic warfare is driving the move to autonomy
articles.body:
The spread of localised electronic warfare across the front in Ukraine is what is pushing drones towards autonomy, the head of UK land at Helsing told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday.
Mike Wilmot said: “We see the action of denial of GPS leads to the reaction of flying by FPV, so you don’t need GPS. That sees the counteraction of localised EW that denies comms, and with that exponential increase of EW, we see a corresponding move towards greater autonomy.”
Full autonomy is not there yet, he said, agreeing with the Ukrainian officer who spoke before him, and most Western militaries are watching the same sequence and working out how to respond to it. The British Army’s answer is its 20-40-40 construct, which moves the balance away from exquisite survivable platforms and towards the attritable and the consumable.
What that means for suppliers is more software-defined systems and lower unit prices. “It also means what the army calls affordable mass, and what most economists call value, much cheaper systems, where the expectation isn’t necessarily that it will return,” he said, describing the question Helsing is working on as how to deliver more platforms at a lower price per unit that still do what is asked of them in a heavily contested electronic warfare environment.
“One of the points that is not actually often discussed there is the ethical element of being able to send a platform forward without a human operator, as well as the efficiency element,” he said.
“There isn’t just a financial expense of sending an F-35 across the forward line of enemy troops. There is also a potential human expense, and if we have that safety confidence in a platform to be able to deliver its task, then there does become an ethical consideration of why send a human pilot or a collection of human pilots when you could first send autonomous platforms,” he said.
Safety works the same way in his account, since there are tasks where an automated process earns more confidence than a person, air defence engagement being the obvious case.
Helsing has about fifty people in an office in Ukraine, set up in response to feedback from the Ukrainian armed forces, and runs a monthly software update to the hardware platforms it has fielded. “The hardware isn’t necessarily changing very much over a protracted period of time, but the software is, and it’s only through that proximity to the end users,” he said. “They’re not going to be pushing much feedback for us. We need to be pulling it from them.”
Western militaries will have to get comfortable with contractors working closer to the fighting than they have in recent conflicts, he suggested, which is a commercial problem as much as a military one and an area where Ukraine offers a working example.
Asked what he would tell a national armaments director, he reached for a high street. “If people buy sweets, sweet shops will open on a high street. If they buy enough sweets, a sweet factory will open nearby. And if they buy even more, then someone will open a sugar refinery, and even dentists will start popping up,” he said, citing the phrase capital follows contracts from reflections on the writing of the strategic defence review.

articles.title: Ukrainian Air Defense downs 117 targets as strikes hit 14 locations
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defense Forces shot down 117 enemy drones overnight into Saturday, but impacts by enemy aerial attack weapons were recorded at 14 locations, the Ukrainian Air Force said.
"According to preliminary data, as of 09:00, air defenses had shot down or suppressed 117 enemy UAVs of the Shahed type (82 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and drones of other types," the statement said.
Overall, during the night of October 10, starting at 18:00 on October 9, the enemy launched attacks using 160 Shahed-type attack UAVs (110 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parodiya-type decoy drones from the following directions: Oryol, Kursk, Shatalovo, Millerovo, and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia; the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk; and the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea, from Hvardiiske.
The aerial attack was repelled by aircraft, surface-to-air missile units, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
Meanwhile, impacts by enemy aerial attack weapons were recorded at 14 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 10 locations.

articles.title: Russia Strikes Dnipropetrovsk Region Nearly 40 Times, Killing 1 and Setting Warehouses Ablaze
articles.body:
Russian forces struck the Dnipropetrovsk region nearly 40 times on Friday, Oct. 9, killing one person.
Head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration Oleksandr Hanzha reported the attacks in a series of updates. Russia used drones, artillery and a missile against communities in the Kryvyi Rih, Nikopol and Synelnykove districts throughout the day, before striking a logistics company’s warehouses near Dnipro twice.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
One person was killed in the Synelnykove district. However, local authorities did not provide further details about the victim at the time of the report.
Kryvyi Rih district
Kryvyi Rih, President Volodymyr Zelensky’s hometown and a major industrial center, repeatedly faces Russian missile and drone attacks.
The latest strikes damaged infrastructure in the city, while the nearby Zelenodolsk community suffered damages on private houses.
On Tuesday, Oct. 6, Russian forces attacked central Kryvyi Rih with two Banderol loitering munitions, striking the grounds of a city hospital and wounding three people.
Russian forces launched an overnight Russian barrage on Kryvyi Rih on Sept. 11-12, killing two people and wounding three. The strikes also damaged an industrial facility and civilian infrastructure, including private homes.
In August, a Russian strike on a shopping center in the city killed at least 16 people and wounded more than 130, including several children.
Among the deadliest strikes in the Kryvyi Rih was recorded on July 30, when Russian forces launched a missile on the village of Radushne, killing an entire family of 10, including two parents, seven children, and an 18-month-old grandson.
US Congress Delegation Backs Expanded Starlink Access for Ukraine
Nikopol and Synelnykove district
The Nikopol district bore the brunt of today’s strikes as Russian forces struck the city of Nikopol along with the Pokrovske, Marhanets, Myrove, Mozolevska and Chervonohryhorivka communities.
According to Hanzha, the strikes damaged private homes and an apartment building, as well as businesses and an infrastructure facility. Several fires were sparked.
Russian attacks targeted the Zaitseve and Petropavlivka communities in the Synelnykove district, damaging an agricultural enterprise and infrastructure facilities.
Double strike on Dnipro district warehouses
Later in the evening, Russian forces struck the Dnipro district, setting a logistics company’s warehouses on fire, Hanzha reported at 8 p.m. local time.
The company’s name had not been made public at the time of reporting.
Less than an hour later, at 8:50 p.m. local time, Hanzha confirmed the same warehouses were struck for a second time. Authorities are still determining whether anyone had been hurt.

articles.title: Trump says Russia to 'immediately supply' 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to US, global markets
articles.body:
Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the US and other global markets, US President Donald Trump announced in a Truth Social post on Friday.
Another 500,000 are expected to be supplied in November, and another 1,000,000 “immediately thereafter,” according to Trump.
“Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump wrote in the post.
The announcement came following a "highly successful" discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Putin's envoy praises US-Russian cooperation on diesel, energy after call with Trump
Russian President Vladimir Putin's envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, praised cooperation between Russia and the United States on diesel and energy in a post on X/Twitter on Friday, shortly after Putin spoke by phone with US President Donald Trump.
After Putin and Trump spoke, the US leader said Russia agreed to immediately supply over 300,000 metric tons of diesel fuel to the American and global market.
"Russia-US cooperation on diesel and energy will benefit the world," Dmitriev wrote on X.
Zelensky responded, calling the decision an 'investment in war'
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky criticized an accord on Friday between the US and Russia allowing Moscow to provide the US with diesel as "an investment in a war that must be ended."
"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Zelenskiy wrote on the X social media platform.
"Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis," Zelenskiy said.
UK responds to the US-Russia diesel deal
The United Kingdom remains committed to supporting Ukraine and will maintain pressure on Russia through sanctions, a government spokesperson said on Friday, after US President Donald Trump announced a deal for Russia to supply diesel to the US and the global market.
"The UK's position could not be clearer. We will continue working closely with international partners to ensure Ukraine has the military and financial support it needs to defend itself. We will also maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by the UK," the spokesperson said.

articles.title: Hundreds protests at FedEx Oakland over Israel arms shipments
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Hundreds protests at FedEx in California over arms shipments to Israel
Three years after the outbreak of Israel’s war on Gaza, hundreds of demonstrators gathered in front of a FedEx building in Oakland, California to protest the shipping company’s arms deliveries to Israel.
FedEx, one of the world’s largest package shipping companies, currently sends weapons parts to Israel for its F-35 fighter jets, which has led to demonstrations against their role in Israel’s assault on Gaza. The shipments have been tracked from Oakland International Airport to their final destination of Nevatim Air Base in Israel.
On a warm Friday morning, demonstrators – represented by members of the Palestinian diaspora, labour unions, students, faith leaders and environmentalists – gathered in front of the FedEx entrance, holding signs reading: “No jets for genocide”, “Stop arming Israel” and “Arms embargo now”.
Speakers of different backgrounds took turns talking about their opposition to FedEx’s shipments of weapons parts to Israel, as well as other grievances with the corporation. Mohamed Shehk, an organiser with Arab Resource and Organising Centre (AROC) Action, spoke before a large crowd of demonstrators,
“We know that this did not start three years ago,” he said. “This genocidal apartheid state of Israel has been attempting to erase us, has been engaged in an ethnic cleansing campaign for 70 years.”
He said, “We’re here demanding that FedEx, this war profiteer, put an immediate end to military cargo being shipped to the apartheid state of Israel.”
He also criticised FedEx’s role in union crackdowns and alleged voter disenfranchisement in their home state of Tennessee.
“It’s also worth noting that FedEx isn’t just engaged in complicity in genocide. They are notoriously anti-union and anti-worker,” he said.
“Everyone remembers earlier this year when the Supreme Court shamefully gutted the Voting Rights Act of 1964. The state of Tennessee was the first state to exploit this ruling. Far-right politicians took the only majority Black district and split it up to weaken the Black vote and silence the Black voice,” he said.
“This why it is important for us to unite across all of these issues in this powerful coalition,” he said. “Solidarity with Palestine means solidarity with workers, solidarity with Black communities, and all communities that are oppressed by the capitalist and colonial class.”
Mick Glenn, a local resident, told The New Arab: “I wanted to make whatever difference I could by being there.”
He added, “The speeches were heartbreaking and motivating. I keep going to these demonstrations, but I hope they don’t have to go on much longer.”
A report by the Palestinian Youth Movement published in August 2025 noted that the Oakland airport is second only to Dallas-Fort Worth for the shipment of weapons parts to Israel.
The 15-page report, based on human rights investigations and on data exports, has found that since January, at least 280 military cargo shipments via FedEx have departed from Oakland International Airport, with Nevatim Airbase in Israel as the final destination. These shipments, supplied by Lockheed Martin, have included F-35 fighter jet components for carrying and releasing munitions and guided weapons.
More specifically, the report found that the shipments were consistently frequent (with only one week of a lull in transfers in six months); the materials delivered are wide-ranging, from lethal systems to small bolts; Nevatim is identified as the final destination for the materials; the shipments are coming from the Defence Logistics Agency in San Joaquín; and F-35s are confirmed to be used by Israel in Gaza.
